public_statements.boeing:
Five years ago I told you the case for a new airplane was better than it had been, and that it wasn't there yet. I'll tell you plainly where it stands today.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. Here's what has changed. Demand for single-aisle airplanes is running above what the industry can build, and the case for a new Boeing airplane is the best it has been.
- Technology is ready. The engines we'd want are in service, and our engine partners have answered our invitation on standard terms.
- Our balance sheet is ready. It's been repaired for twenty years, and it's staying repaired.
- Our production system has held full rate for three years.

The leg that isn't there is the market case itself. When we plan for the way new airplanes really come together, including the chance that it takes longer than we think, it doesn't clear the bar we hold ourselves to. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. Two out of three isn't three.

So the work keeps going, in stages, and it will be ready when the case is. We're designing the production system together with the airplane. The plan is a conservative one with headroom in it:
- a ten-year development;
- the type certificate before we build at rate;
- no fixed-price development;
- a choice of two engine sources, CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

On the 737, the line has been at full output, 57 a month, for three years. That's where it stays. It's gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA, and we'll keep our suppliers and our engine supply ahead of it. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

We turned this big ship. The job now is to keep it pointed in the right direction. Our dates are set by our own readiness, and it is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s and is now in production at its planned rate. Production stays disciplined and controlled. Every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family has completed an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers, and we support Rolls-Royce's work on time on wing for the Trent fleet. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. We fund our programmes from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041 and flies on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We've set out the standard we hold that engine to. On any new airframe, durability proven before entry into service is our standard, and our customers'. We claim no result here. The test and field record goes to our customers and our Board first, through our cross-functional team. It doesn't go into a press line.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and that's the airframer's call.

Boeing has asked us for a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware where they compete for the same parts.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support: the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits, and the gear and core we build for every Joint Venture engine.

Airbus has asked both its engine sources to commit capacity for its next step. Our answer is yes, on conditions. We will commit capacity, in steps, sized to Airbus's own firm volumes, with no exclusivity, on standard terms, with the allocation agreed jointly with Airbus and our fleet's spares protected. Where we fall short, we will tell Airbus early. Airbus speaks for its own rates and dates.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our answer to Boeing's invitation stands. The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, as one engine source, in the standard now in service, with each partner standing behind its own modules. It is offered on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On Airbus's next capacity step, we commit Rolls-Royce's own part, for Airbus's own volumes, with no exclusivity and no concession: our support capacity, and our share of the Joint Venture's investment and risk. Only what we are sure to deliver. We speak for Rolls-Royce, not for our partner. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (unchanged)
boeing.detail:
We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

Recorded internally: the dual-source enabler is unmet in 2050 on every plan (the MAX flies CFM only), and no order on this board can cure it.

boeing.move: 737 MAX held at its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
boeing.detail:
The 737 has held full output, 57 a month (684 a year), since 2047. This is the ceiling, not a Rate Increase. It stays gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA [B-2236].

We renew the LEAP-1B allocation of 1,368 engines a year in each annual round with CFM [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Supplier output stays proven ahead of the line. No dates or numbers beyond the ceiling are published.

boeing.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
boeing.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for NGSA at rate
airbus.detail:
This continues the programme from earlier rounds, now for NGSA in steady production.
- The NGSA wing stays in-house.
- Aerostructures come through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites.
- Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts.
- The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist continues.
It serves our own production only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: NGSA engine supply: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, at our own volumes
airbus.detail:
NGSA is fitted with CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine: two sources from three engine makers.
- The capacity agreements with both cover only our own NGSA volumes, with no exclusivity and nothing above our own production.
- We plan with each maker's published allocation rules: P&W puts fleet spares and MRO material ahead of new OE, and CFM puts LEAP durability kits first. P&W has said it will tell us early where it falls short.
- The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Prepare the next step in industrial capacity, gated on safety, quality and supply (kept prepared, not committed)
Widebody position for the 2050s: the A350 family and the A350F
airbus.detail: On widebodies we focus on the A350 family and the A350F, kept current for our customers. We support Rolls-Royce's time-on-wing work for the Trent fleet. We claim no Trent XWB programme that Rolls-Royce has not announced, promise no widebody engine and give no Re-engine timing. The A350 Re-engine is not tabled, so no widebody-engine invitation is issued [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0302].
We keep working with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

airbus.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2050s
airbus.detail: We continue apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe. They staff NGSA production at rate, the capacity step being prepared and widebody work, all from our own pipeline. There is no targeted hiring from any rival's team [AX-0073, A-0330].

cfm.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
cfm.detail: H5: no cancel and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it, on its schedule [CX-0469, CX-0205]. Continuing it as technology with Safran is joint practice. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP [CX-0162]. The one RISE allowance closes unused.

cfm.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of everything else
cfm.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it [CX-0613, CX-0540].

pratt_whitney.move: Fleet first: the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and the GTF fleet; Hot Section kit sold at value; fleet spares ahead of new hardware where they compete for the same parts
pratt_whitney.detail:
The fleet comes before any new hardware [PX-0080][PX-0084].
- The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign or capacity answer [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100].
- Fleet spares and MRO material are allocated ahead of NGSA OE, ahead of any new Airbus capacity step and ahead of any Joint Venture block hardware where they compete for the same parts.
- We fix forward through shop-visit upgrades. Any durability fix for the NGSA engine enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.
- Pacing parts and spares for the gear and the core are being sized to every Joint Venture engine that carries them, not only to our counted share, and to the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits.
- OE allocation is agreed jointly with Airbus, and we tell Airbus early where we fall short [PX-0099][PX-0066].
No date is given for any ramp or recovery. The move has no effect on the game board.

pratt_whitney.move: Answer to Airbus's next capacity step: P&W commits capacity, in steps, sized to Airbus's own firm volumes, standard terms, no exclusivity, fleet spares protected
Standing answer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine as one engine source, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts
pratt_whitney.detail:
This answers Boeing's standing invitation, which now names the Joint Venture as one of two engine sources in its plan at launch. It is Boeing's plan, not a selection, and nothing is booked on it.
- We offer the Joint Venture engine, ready since 2036, in the standard now in service on NGSA, with each partner standing behind its own modules.
- Standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer [P-0768].
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing, either way.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture governed to its published terms; 'never' restated as the public floor
pratt_whitney.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms published in 2035 and restated in 2045:
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233]. Gear and core modules are repaired in P&W's network under P&W data.
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

rolls_royce.move: Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 time-on-wing and durability work continues inside a flat R&D envelope
rolls_royce.detail: Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, and life-limited part extensions on the installed fleet. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat envelope, not added. Time on wing is reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. This is our answer on the widebody, not a new programme. No widebody programme is launched [RX-0123, RX-0214, RX-0101, RX-0246].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops: live for the NGSA fleet and sized for a second airframe
rolls_royce.detail: A partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team. The plan is Rolls-Royce's own. It is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service, and it is sized for a second airframe before that airframe enters service. The shops scale ahead of the fleet's shop-visit wave and ahead of any extra Airbus volume. Our partner's shops add capacity after that and never replace this plan. No dates are disclosed [RX-0283, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: Answer to Boeing's engine-sourcing invitation, renewed
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce offers its part of the Joint Venture engine for a future Boeing single-aisle. Standard terms, no launch discount, no concession. Durability is proven before entry into service, as a contract condition, and support through partner shops is in place before entry into service. No dates and no new spend. The answer implies no date for Rolls-Royce content and no Rolls-Royce content on the airframe by its entry into service. Rolls-Royce speaks only for its own part [RX-0058, RX-0081, RX-0283, R-1005].

rolls_royce.move: Answer to Airbus's next capacity step, for Rolls-Royce's part only

rolls_royce.detail: No concession to buy narrowbody or widebody share: not to Boeing, not in Airbus's capacity talks, not to our partner. Terms are win-win, value is paid for, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

Cash from the Trent and Joint Venture fleets goes first to the balance sheet, then to a 30-40% dividend payout, then to investment and further distributions on fit, value and timing, through the Investment Committee at mid-to-high-teens hurdles. No equity raise, no leverage above about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions [RX-0242, RX-0213, RX-0215, RX-0261].

boeing.move: Standing fps plan beyond this board (authority-to-offer work)
boeing.detail:
This is the company's plan to go on day one when a case clears. It is not a launch.
- Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP, capacity or strain relief we lack, at $2.45-2.57B below Solo.
- The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.47-0.68 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.
- Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition [BX-1298].
- The production system is designed with the airplane. The type certificate comes before building at rate, each fps rate break is proven before it is taken, and there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].
- The site is decided with the launch. Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
  1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
  2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
  3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
  4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers follow the actual wind-down.
  5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.
- Decide any fps and 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4.

What a case must show before it comes to the Board:
- the item more than +$1B in the expected column, with no plausible column below -$1B;
- Malave's buffer and 'Fundable' tests passed;
- the slip priced once on his baseline (the clean-sheet prior of +3 years at a realistic cost per year, with the marginal penalty included);
- Pope's readiness results;
- evidence that demand holds above slots through the 20-year market window, not only to the last printed year.

boeing.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded
boeing.detail:
- Keep the trained workforce on the MAX line.
- Keep a small, protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line.
- Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers carrying 57 a month are the ones an fps would load next.

Pope noted candidly that the brief carries no KPI readings. Ask her seat to put the six FAA-agreed KPIs in front of the Board each quarter, so that 'stable' rests on data, not on the absence of a reported problem [BX-1259].

Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: alone the item is +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, which is 2045's +0.74 discounted five years. It never clears ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine (+0.24 at Malave's 20% read). This hold very probably closes it on this board.

If it is ever re-tested beyond the board, it comes only as one pair with any fps under H4, and only while H3's second half is open. No programme spend is committed.

Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress through 2060. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board [BG-0044]. Headroom stays visible for a future staged fps (the 10-year's peak year is about $8.44B, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

airbus.move: NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
airbus.detail:
The review continues in steady production, with a standing watch on the Joint Venture engine.
- Durability and full life on life-limited parts. GTF2's tested configuration is in service; Rolls-Royce content comes only on a later block, after its own durability proof.
- CFM is the backstop source. Wagner notes that at about 27% of our NGSA engines (a proxy) it is a thin one, and could not cover a Joint Venture shortfall at once.
- Any quality finding goes to the Board at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AG-0038].

airbus.move: Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review
Audit Committee: net cash, rating and returns
airbus.detail:
Toepfer reports on a proxy, labelled as such, with FCF at 0.688 of operating profit.
- Net cash is about $61-94B at end-2050 on hold, against FY2025's $13.4B. The policy-consistent path, with the payout scaled within 30-50%, gives about $61B.
- The A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout are fundable with no debt, no raise and no cut.
- No change to shareholder returns is proposed this round. Any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter, with these lines shown [AX-0104, AX-0102, A-0402, AG-0062].

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine: held at the final gate and closed for this game, with the stopping tests recorded
airbus.detail:
It is not tabled. Two tests stopped it:
- Toepfer's binding robustness test. The item is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6/S7: negative in plausible columns and short of $1B everywhere.
- The company's own launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), met in no column.
Wagner's widebody-engine supply flag weighed but did not bind.
It is recorded as a strategic choice: holding at the last decision year closes the A350 Re-engine for this game. Any future Re-engine comes only with an engine committed and its durability proven [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0440].

cfm.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's code-7 sourcing invitation for its next single-aisle, through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail:
We offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted, ready since 2041, nine years in service on NGSA), with a LEAP derivative as the floor (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185].
- Durability proven before entry into service is our own standard. Accepting it as a contract condition is a commercial term, so it goes to Safran first, along with any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty, and it is modelled conservatively (Ghai) [CX-0184, CX-0979].
- We stand behind what test and field data back: the LEAP-1A kit (HPT hardware certified by the FAA and EASA in December 2024, in every LEAP-1A delivery and shop visit, more than doubling time on wing) [CX-0209, CX-0225], and the test gate as our standard.
- We make no Ducted durability claim until the cross-functional team releases the hot-and-harsh, dust and field record (Ali, H6).
- No price, no concession, no number. No ready year before 2041, and no year by which durability will be 'proven'.
- When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call [CX-0307].

cfm.move: LEAP-1B built to deliveries at 57 a month; any step above it through CFM with Safran, gated on floor data
cfm.detail:
The allocation at 57 a month (1,368 engines a year) has been fully used since 2047. Capacity and volume now match, so there was no overcapitalisation.
- Nothing above 57 a month until Boeing launches and agrees volumes with CFM, GE and Safran together. No number to Boeing before Safran agrees, and no price in it [CX-0184, CX-0160].
- If Boeing launches (S2), we plan the floor to the grid-implied step: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year on average over 2051-2056 (about 1,625 LEAP-1B and about 2,273 CFM NB engines a year). That is inside the 2,592 we delivered in 2030-2036. We do not plan to the 2,400 cap (3,048 in all, 17.6% above anything we've delivered).
- Each step is gated on floor data reported to the Board first, with kits ahead of rate. We never get ahead of Boeing or the FAA [CX-0307, CX-0197, CX-0540].

cfm.move: Airbus's next industrial step: capacity talks on product and supply only, for Airbus's own extra volumes, through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail:
Scope as Airbus states it publicly: its own NGSA volumes and the A320neo tail, no exclusivity, nothing drawn from any other allocation.
- No capacity or price number before Safran agrees. Any price term is a joint decision on standard terms [CX-0184].
- Any commitment is gated on floor data at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, with LEAP kits and the LEAP-1B rate first.
- This is upside we don't book.

cfm.move: Partner Embraer: terms worked through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: No Embraer number goes to the market or to an airframer until terms are agreed with Safran (Ghai's condition) [CX-0184]. Partner Embraer has counted since 2042 and stays on hold.

Three gaps, none closed on our record. Each is handed on as a standing management action, with an internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting and no public date [CX-0012, CX-0633].
(1) The Ducted: hot-and-harsh and dust results (turn on, turn off) and every test or field event on NGSA since 2041. Our sources hold 0 of each. Owner: Mohamed Ali, with the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team and Safran.
(2) The LEAP-1B durability-kit outcome. Not in our record; certification was due in the first half of 2026. Owner: Ali, with Boeing and the FAA [CX-0210, CX-0656].
(3) RISE durability and dust after October 2025. Owner: Ali, with Safran [CX-0216, CX-0222].
Absence of failure is not clearance. Any event becomes a flag and goes to the cross-functional team (root cause, inspection, a fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator) before any date, statement, offer or capacity step moves. A report date promises a report, not a result (Ali's test passes).

cfm.move: End-of-game hand-on: supplier floor margin and long-lead release (Ali owns, with me accountable)
cfm.detail:
This is the fourth time the Board has asked for the floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages, and it is still not shown [CX-0613]. Whether the Ducted's long-lead orders were released on floor data cannot be shown either.
- Owner: Ali, with the cross-functional team and Safran. Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting.
- The report covers three loads: 2,016 engines a year today, about 2,273 if S2 comes on the grid's volume, and 3,048 at the 100-a-month cap.
- Until then, no capacity is committed above 57 a month or for Airbus's step. Kits first, lean before capital. That is doctrine, since Ali's floor record ends in 2025 [CX-0540, CX-0653].

cfm.move: End-of-game hand-on: the Ducted's ledger cash curve and Airbus capacity-agreement status (Ghai owns)
cfm.detail:
(1) The Ducted's 2035-2040 ledger cash curve against the $1.0B a year approved. The board books $6.0B ($4.0B of R&D in 2035 plus $2.0B of strain) against $6.0B approved, with no overrun and no write-off. The yearly cash curve is not in our brief, so we don't invent it. Owner: Rahul Ghai, with GE Aerospace controllership and CFM finance (Safran on the CFM share).
(2) Whether the Airbus capacity agreements are signed. Airbus's public word covers scope only. Our signature status and terms are not in our brief. Owner: Ghai, with CFM commercial and Safran.
Both go in an internal report to the Audit Committee at its next regular meeting, with no public date. No booking rests on either.

pratt_whitney.move: Closing whole-programme NPV review to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Final decision year. Mitchill presents; all derived figures labelled derived, Finance only, never booked, never public.
(a) Booked: -0.14 = engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00 charged undiscounted, unchanged since 2045 (rounded table re-discounted gives +1.85, a rounding difference). 'Capitalise on the GTF' is reported as NOT MET, exactly as the GM reports it, with no re-measurement and no substitute figure.
(b) Run rate: +0.6 a year nominal over 2046-55 (8.8 against 8.2 in 2050), +0.7 in 2056. Nominal cumulative above the status quo +12.0 by 2056, crossing $2.0B nominal in 2041 (derived, not a payback claim). On the board's convention, cumulative PV reaches only +1.85 by 2056: no PV payback inside the count.
(c) S2 at -0.75, -0.61 below S1 (against -0.59 in 2045). The code-7 slot books nothing (EIS 2060, after the count ends in 2056); removing the last two slot-years moved the gap by only -0.02. Mitchill's arithmetic (inference): placed in 2051-56 it needs 134 engines a year lost while NGSA is above its ceiling; placed in 2038-49, when Boeing had 160-275 free slots, it needs about 28 a year. Read as a re-score of delivered years through the two-airframe preference rule, not cash at risk in 2051-56. Booked as neither. It becomes cash at risk only if NGSA's backlog drains below Airbus's ceiling: a watch item.
(d) Against a buyback (PV 0): -0.14, not met. Against Do Nothing: no grid row; direction only. Without a new P&W engine ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS, our NB OE flow would have run toward zero as the A320neo wound down; the 876 a year now carry about $8.8B a year of lifecycle value at 2050 prices. The 2030 grid priced 'NGSA without us' at -16.25: order of magnitude only, not rolled forward or booked. The programme sits far above Do Nothing and just below a status quo that assumes the A320neo flies our GTF forever.
(e) Derived, R&D discounted at 10%: +0.77 (spent evenly 2030-35), +1.01 (2035 lump), +0.49 (2030 lump).
(f) The lesson on the record: our 2030 and 2035 grids had no CFM column. In 2035 we put the low end on Airbus moving NGSA to code 5; the loss came from CFM's ducted engine (2041) and Embraer partnership (2042), about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half from us, which took the 2035 +0.48 to -0.14. The 2035 'Rolls-Royce commits' upside (+2.63) never showed. A grid shows one round of rivals' moves; we put the low end in the wrong place, and I own that.

pratt_whitney.move: In-service durability report and Rolls-Royce block gate to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Bad news first: after thirteen years in service, the time-on-wing record we would need to say the NGSA engine is where it needs to be is not in front of us. No time on wing by environment, removal intervals, severe-environment or fleet-leader findings, life-limited-part lives against full life, AOG count, shop-visit rate or turn times appear on the record we hold. What the record shows is narrower: no P&W fleet, AOG or quality event in any public bulletin 2037-2050, and our 876 counted engines delivered each year at Airbus's rate. That is OE supply at rate, not durability, and we claim nothing more [PX-0022].
The Committee gets the data as they exist: time on wing cooler against hot-and-sandy; removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage; life-limited-part lives against full life; configuration percentages, AOG, shop-visit rate, turn times and pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly. If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so and fleet lift goes ahead of the Airbus step.
Rolls-Royce block gate, unchanged: joint configuration board with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core; no intermix until the block is certified and its own spares stocked; at least 3x base-programme testing at severe-environment conditions; time on wing no worse than the fitted standard, with gear-and-core interface load tests; full-life parts at EIS; Rolls-Royce parts capacity qualified before rate; support in place before EIS; data to the Committee; no date. If the data are late, the block waits [PX-0035][PX-0073].
For Finance and the Committee: the Joint Venture's MRO split. Under term 4 the engine in service is GTF2's configuration, so shop load on the half counted to Rolls-Royce may fall on our network today. Shown, priced at value, and our fleet first.

pratt_whitney.move: Airbus capacity capex and shortfall pricing to the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail:
Capex for the Airbus step comes to Finance as a capital item, released in tranches only against Airbus's firm extra volumes, inside the roughly $6B self-funded envelope with the dividend covered; the one-time stretch is not used [PX-0081][P-0686].
Internal illustrative unit, never public: each 10 NGSA a month is about 240 engines a year, about 88 counted to P&W and about 175 gear-and-core sets (+10% on about 1,752), plus later spares for that fleet; about $0.88B a year nominal of lifecycle value at 2050 prices, off the board and not booked.
Pacing parts (Eddy, inference from the company record): turbine airfoil castings (shared with the Hot Section kit and GTF heavy visits; CFM competes for castings), powder-metal disks (life-limited, full life at ship), forgings, and the gear, where we hold no capacity data. Lead time to add forging and casting capacity: 2 to 2.5 years in the company record, read as a floor.
Shortfall pricing, part by part when it bites: a lost install costs about $10.05M of lifecycle value and does not come back; a fleet shortfall costs AOG compensation plus about $3.8M of aftermarket at risk per flying engine, plus the credibility the in-service engine now carries. We cannot net the two without AOG data. The tie-break stays fleet first where parts compete [PX-0080]; the way to avoid the trade is to size the spares for the larger fleet before each OE step.

pratt_whitney.move: Closing update of the enterprise risk register
pratt_whitney.detail:
(1) Rolls-Royce alignment: its public answer to Boeing, 'Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine', and 'The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service' are recorded as alignment on one engine on the public record. The Boeing half of our private written-confirmation request is closed by that record. The block-route half (through the joint configuration board and our gate) stays open as a Joint Venture configuration-control document. The watch is kept, not retired. Tells: a block bringing its own gear or core [P-1875]; any request for gear or core data, repair data included; an offer to Boeing by product name; pressure to put Rolls-Royce content in service before its proof.
(2) In-service durability of the NGSA engine: data gap after thirteen years; owner Eddy.
(3) CFM share pressure on NGSA (ducted engine and Embraer partnership).
(4) Airbus capacity commitment against fleet spares, airfoils and disks first.
(5) S2 preference shift: cash at risk only if NGSA's backlog drains below Airbus's ceiling.
(6) Heavy-visit wave: about 12,100 GTF engines delivered since 2026 (derived; excludes the pre-2026 fleet, spares and retirements) and about 16,250 Joint Venture engines carrying our gear and core by end-2050.

pratt_whitney.move: Counsel review of the GTF paragraph and the full disclosure
pratt_whitney.detail: Given the derivative claims over GTF oversight and the compliance monitor, counsel reviews the GTF paragraph before release. The 2045 draft sentence 'We make no claim that the GTF investment has paid back' is taken out on Mitchill's advice: it characterises a private result and could read as an admission. We make no payback claim by making none.

rolls_royce.move: Rolls-Royce-module durability gates and P&W's spares-first rule reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee
rolls_royce.detail:
Watson reports the gates with no date: module rig durability, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. Our modules keep their own test programme through to entry into service. No pacing is bent to any airframer's ramp, Airbus's capacity step included, and there is no concession to P&W.
His read on P&W's rule: it can slow our block's hardware but cannot compress the proof, and it does not reach our spare pool or our intervention team.
Watch items: P&W's GTF time-on-wing record and the GTF heavy shop-visit wave. If a gate fails or a fleet finding opens, the block waits, the capacity answer drops to 'only what we are sure to deliver', and we tell Airbus and P&W early [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476, R-0970, R-0318].

rolls_royce.move: Internal ask to P&W: our spare-pool modules count as fleet spares
rolls_royce.detail: We ask that P&W modules bound for Rolls-Royce's partner-shop spare-engine pool are allocated as fleet spares under P&W's own spares-first rule, not as OE. It is an ask, not a concession, and nothing is offered for it. Partnership needs to work, and alignment is what we watch [R-1010, R-0318, RX-0287].

rolls_royce.move: Internal capacity sizing and the close of the widebody watch
rolls_royce.detail:
Capacity: the narrowbody load is 84% of Watson's round-2 sizing. Partner shops scale ahead of the shop-visit wave through the 2050s. Internal sizing figures never go public. If castings, forgings or partner-shop capacity fall short, the capacity answer shrinks to match.
Widebody watch: it closes with the game. A Re-engine announced at this round's adjudication cannot be answered, and we accept that knowingly. Even with both Re-engines, UltraFan WB loses $3.32B before the strain, and it would be ready a year after a 2050 Re-engine's entry into service. No order of ours is left open.

other_moves.move: Standing fps plan beyond this board (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail:
This is the company's plan to go on day one when a case clears. It is not a launch.
- Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP, capacity or strain relief we lack, at $2.45-2.57B below Solo.
- The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.47-0.68 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.
- Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition [BX-1298].
- The production system is designed with the airplane. The type certificate comes before building at rate, each fps rate break is proven before it is taken, and there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].
- The site is decided with the launch. Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
  1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
  2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
  3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
  4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers follow the actual wind-down.
  5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.
- Decide any fps and 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4.

What a case must show before it comes to the Board:
- the item more than +$1B in the expected column, with no plausible column below -$1B;
- Malave's buffer and 'Fundable' tests passed;
- the slip priced once on his baseline (the clean-sheet prior of +3 years at a realistic cost per year, with the marginal penalty included);
- Pope's readiness results;
- evidence that demand holds above slots through the 20-year market window, not only to the last printed year.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (unchanged)
other_moves.detail:
We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

Recorded internally: the dual-source enabler is unmet in 2050 on every plan (the MAX flies CFM only), and no order on this board can cure it.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX held at its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
other_moves.detail:
The 737 has held full output, 57 a month (684 a year), since 2047. This is the ceiling, not a Rate Increase. It stays gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA [B-2236].

We renew the LEAP-1B allocation of 1,368 engines a year in each annual round with CFM [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Supplier output stays proven ahead of the line. No dates or numbers beyond the ceiling are published.

other_moves.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded
other_moves.detail:
- Keep the trained workforce on the MAX line.
- Keep a small, protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line.
- Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers carrying 57 a month are the ones an fps would load next.

Pope noted candidly that the brief carries no KPI readings. Ask her seat to put the six FAA-agreed KPIs in front of the Board each quarter, so that 'stable' rests on data, not on the absence of a reported problem [BX-1259].

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
other_moves.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: alone the item is +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, which is 2045's +0.74 discounted five years. It never clears ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine (+0.24 at Malave's 20% read). This hold very probably closes it on this board.

If it is ever re-tested beyond the board, it comes only as one pair with any fps under H4, and only while H3's second half is open. No programme spend is committed.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress through 2060. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board [BG-0044]. Headroom stays visible for a future staged fps (the 10-year's peak year is about $8.44B, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I told you the case for a new airplane was better than it had been, and that it wasn't there yet. I'll tell you plainly where it stands today.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. Here's what has changed. Demand for single-aisle airplanes is running above what the industry can build, and the case for a new Boeing airplane is the best it has been.
- Technology is ready. The engines we'd want are in service, and our engine partners have answered our invitation on standard terms.
- Our balance sheet is ready. It's been repaired for twenty years, and it's staying repaired.
- Our production system has held full rate for three years.

The leg that isn't there is the market case itself. When we plan for the way new airplanes really come together, including the chance that it takes longer than we think, it doesn't clear the bar we hold ourselves to. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. Two out of three isn't three.

So the work keeps going, in stages, and it will be ready when the case is. We're designing the production system together with the airplane. The plan is a conservative one with headroom in it:
- a ten-year development;
- the type certificate before we build at rate;
- no fixed-price development;
- a choice of two engine sources, CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

On the 737, the line has been at full output, 57 a month, for three years. That's where it stays. It's gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA, and we'll keep our suppliers and our engine supply ahead of it. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

We turned this big ship. The job now is to keep it pointed in the right direction. Our dates are set by our own readiness, and it is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever
- Orders: fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.
- Submitted row: -1.01 / -1.10 / -1.01 (S1 / S2 / S3).
  - S3 against Do Nothing: 0.00, with headroom of +2.00 over the -3.01 line.
  - The worst column is S2, at -1.10.
  - Net debt reads '2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B)' in every column.
- No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.
- This is the last round, and I say it plainly: this hold means no fps on this board, and very probably no 787 Re-engine either.

TEAM RULE (teams.md §9)
- Malave's buffer veto binds on the two via-Embraer hold rows (S3 -3.14 and -3.11, 0.13 and 0.10 past the line). Neither is chosen.
- The via-Embraer + Re-engine rows pass his buffer by only 0.06-0.08. His advice is against them, and so are the Board's Downside and Rating-first lines. Closed.
- The KPI doctrine has no object (rate_737 is hold only), and no problem is live. Pope did not invoke her veto.
- Pope flagged H4 on the 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years of overlap). Not chosen, and struck from the option set.
- No flag needs a strike, and there are no overrides.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes: the brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271], and the FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. Pope says candidly that the brief carries no KPI readings: 'stable' rests on no reported problem and three years at 684. I take that as a pass with a caveat, and I've asked for the KPIs in front of the Board.
2. Are market, technology and Boeing all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
   - Technology: yes. CFM, and the Joint Venture with 13 years of in-service data on NGSA.
   - Balance sheet: yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress. 'Fundable when the 777X turns' passes [BX-0547], and every 10-year row holds stress at $0.
   - Operations: yes, for one development. A lone 10-year passes Pope's gates and her own 2045 test (a 2% overrun and +3 years), leaving +0.22.
   - Market: closer than it has ever been, but not there.
     - The 10-year at Renton is +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35, and about $0.31B of that gain since 2045 is real.
     - But Pope shows that our own preference demand (446-460 a year) sits below our 684 slots. The excess is the rival's flexible customers, and the fps's capacity arrives after 2060.
     - Malave adds that 19 of the fps's 20 market years are past what the brief prints, and the excess demand is already falling at EIS (416 in 2053, 245 in 2060).
     - So the market leg rests mostly on overflow demand in years the brief does not show. That is lower confidence [BX-0548].
3. What if certification takes longer? I plan for the reset, once [BX-1318, BX-1319]. Malave corrected my arithmetic: with the marginal penalty on the extra spend (0.59, not the average 0.32), the 10-year at Renton breaks even at about $6.4B all in, 10.6% of the bill, not $10.4B. On a +3-year clean-sheet slip:
   - Case A, one 777X-size reset ($4.9B): the item keeps +0.06.
   - Case B, three years at the 777X's cost per year ($14.7B): the item falls to -0.35.
   The $4.9B bought one year on a derivative [BX-0550], and a clean sheet's prior is +3 years (range +2 to +5). The reset I would actually plan for is nearer case B. The edge survives only the optimistic reset.
4. Is this doing less, better [BX-1239]? Every plan is within ε of Do Nothing in S1. Doing less wins, and Do Nothing is the higher-confidence plan: it has nothing to slip [BX-0548].

DEBT FIRST
The grid already nets each penalty, so I do not subtract it again. No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in S1:
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.65.
- 10-year + Re-engine: +0.62.
- Re-engine alone: +0.45.
- 10-year at Renton: +0.35.
- 10-year at new site: +0.32.
Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B; the pair $22.2B; Re-engine $0.6B.

WORST-COLUMN TIE-BREAK, REPORTED PLAINLY
- On the printed grid, the 10-year at Renton has the higher worst column: -0.76 against -1.10, so Do Nothing fails this tie-break by $0.34B.
- Slip-priced, case A keeps the 10-year ahead by +0.05. Case B reverses it: Do Nothing is higher by $0.36B.
- The two cases straddle the $6.4B break-even, so this test does not settle the order. My first tie-break, doing less, decides it, and Malave's balance-sheet tie-break (advice) agrees: Do Nothing adds no penalty.

PER-ROW RESULTS (item value against the default, S1 / S2 / S3)
- 10-year at Renton: +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35. At a new site: +0.32 / +0.31 / +0.32.
  - Passes: buffer (S3 -0.66, headroom +2.35), Downside, H4, Fundable, stress at $0.
  - Fails my debt-first ε and the Board's +$1B line, by $0.65B. The Board would veto it.
- Re-engine alone: +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, or +0.24 weighted at Malave's 20%. It never clears ε at any p, and the Board would veto it.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.65 / -0.40 / +0.65 against Do Nothing.
  - The Re-engine item beside the fps is only +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30.
  - H4 sits at its 2-year limit with no slack: 3 years on a +1-year derivative slip, 4 on the +2-year prior.
- 7-year rows: closed.
  - -0.12 at Renton and -0.23 at new sites, 0.47-0.68 below the 10-year, with no overrun room.
  - With the Re-engine, 5 years of overlap breaches H4.
  - Stress peaks of $0.7B and $2.0-3.1B. Malave corrects these to development-year peaks, not scored failures.
- Via Embraer: closed.
  - The buffer veto binds on the hold rows. The Re-engine rows sit -1.92 to -3.00 against Do Nothing.
  - $52.5B undiscounted penalty, and it fails Pope's IP test.

RED LINES AND HARD RULES
- H1 and H3's first half: lifted in my 2030 ruling, not re-made.
- H3's second half: confirmed open. There is no A350 Re-engine on the record.
- H4: no overlap on the submitted plan.
- H5: nothing launched, nothing cancelled.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: logged below.
- H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger.
- My own: no production-certification concurrency, no fixed-price development, no rate change without stable KPIs, no blame on the FAA, and no attribution to suppliers or Airbus.

PREMIUMS (H8)
- fps hold: $0.35B in S1 and S3, $0.34B in S2, as a doctrine premium against the cap.
- Re-engine hold: logged as a Board hold, separately. It gives up $0.45B in S1 and S3 and saves $0.60B in S2.
- At plan level, against the best plan in S1: $0.65B.
- All inside $2B. The objective premium is $0.

RECORD OR DOCTRINE
- My record drove the four questions, doing less, the one conservative reset and debt first.
- Inference or doctrine drove:
  - the $1B ε threshold;
  - Malave's 20% read of an A350 Re-engine;
  - the H4 pairing;
  - code 7 at any launch;
  - the new_site preference.
- The Board's +$1B line would force the same orders.

COST OF WAITING (information, not a reason)
- On the grid: $0.35B for the fps and $0.45B for the Re-engine in S1. There is no later round on this board.
- Unscored: a later EIS lowers the long-run split under the lead-edge rule. The 50/50 and incumbency objectives stay unmet at 20% preference, and no order this round moves a scored year (the earliest EIS is 2057).
- Building a new future is on my list [BX-1245]. On this board's demand path the case came closer every round and never cleared the line. I won't force an airplane to end a game. 'I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned' [BX-1300] was true of the market leg to the end.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave is a thin seat: one call, Low confidence. His buffer test binds under the team rule. Everything else he says is advice, and I weighed it as advice.

What I took:
- Buffer: his confirmation, and the veto on the two via-Embraer hold rows (-3.14 and -3.11).
- Why S3 equals S1: slots bind, so Delay Tactics move preference, not deliveries.
- His correction of my overrun arithmetic, which was the most useful finding in either memo. The marginal penalty (0.59 a dollar, not 0.32) cuts the break-even to about $6.4B all in, 10.6% of the bill, not my $10.4B or the Board's 13-17%. I adopted it.
- His two slip cases. Case A ($4.9B, +0.06) and case B ($14.7B, -0.35) straddle the break-even. I lean to case B as the planning case for a clean sheet, because the $4.9B bought only one year on a derivative.
- His market-or-timing answer: the sign of the item rests on the board's booking at EIS, and the brief prints only one of the fps's 20 market years. I read that as lower confidence, not as a reason.
- His 20% A350 Re-engine read (doctrine, range 15-25%).
- His correction that the stress peaks are development-year peaks, not scored failures.
- Fundable: pass. Cancel: nothing to cancel.
- His classification of the premiums (fps hold as doctrine, Re-engine hold as a Board hold).

His balance-sheet tie-break is advice. It agrees with my doing-less tie-break, so it changed nothing. He also concedes the printed Meet-and-beat test favours the 10-year at Renton by $0.34B, and I report that plainly.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope is a thin seat: Very low airplane-business evidence, and the seat runs on operations doctrine. Her KPI veto binds only on a Rate Increase under a live problem, and it had no object this round. I weighed the rest as readiness evidence.

What I took:
- KPI gate clean, with her candid note that the brief carries no KPI readings. I asked for them to go to the Board.
- The MAX at 684 a year for three years, with 1,368 LEAP-1B engines a year demonstrated in deliveries but to be re-confirmed annually.
- One development can sit beside a stable line.
- Her H4 results: 0 years on the submitted plan; 2 for a 10-year pair, 3-4 on a derivative slip; 5 for a 7-year pair, a breach.
- No production-certification concurrency, read sensibly as the production system designed with the airplane and each rate break proven before it is taken.
- new_site over Renton. She estimates the +0.03 already gives up about $0.07B of MAX deliveries against a ~$0.10B capex saving. It also risks up to 504 MAX deliveries a year if Renton converts early, and the board does not price that.
- Via Embraer fails her IP test.

Most weight went to two findings:
- Her 2045 test now passes: the 10-year survives a 2% overrun and +3 years at +0.22, so operations would not stand in the way of a lone 10-year.
- Our own preference demand (446-460 a year) sits below our 684 slots. The fps's market leg is mostly overflow demand from the rival's flexible customers after 2060.

The first says Boeing is ready. The second says the market leg is lower-confidence than +0.35 suggests. She says plainly that the business case is not her seat.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1, rivals hold.

From the bulletin:
- Airbus's widebody focus 'stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve'.
- Rolls-Royce: 'No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table', and 'No widebody programme is launched' (Trent work inside a flat R&D envelope).
- Airbus's capital is going into its narrowbody capacity step.
- No A350 Re-engine has been launched in twenty years of play.

I take Malave's read of an A350 Re-engine at about 20% (range 15-25%; doctrine, not his record) as S2's weight. S3 (Delay Tactics) equals S1 on every row, because slots bind.

The probability-weighted value of the submitted plan is about -1.03 (0.8 x -1.01 + 0.2 x -1.10).
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:

board_response.recommendation: Do not let Airbus set our dates; decide on Boeing's own readiness.
board_response.response:
Taken up. Neither the hold nor any line of the statement cites Airbus. The orders rest on our own tests: the market leg inside ε, the slip priced once, and doing less, better.

The bulletin's Airbus wording informs only the expected-column read (about 20% for an A350 Re-engine), not the order.

priorities: Safety and production readiness come first. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the 737 MAX has delivered at full output (684 a year, 57 a month) since 2047. We approve no launch without Pope's results on KPIs, engineering capacity, suppliers and two-front strain. There must be no production-certification concurrency, and her five-step MAX bridge plan is needed if fps_site is renton [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069].

One well-founded launch, not a bet. The fps item value is the best it has been. The 10-year ramp is +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35 at Renton and +0.32 / +0.31 / +0.32 at a new site, positive in every column. Discounting alone would have taken 2045's +0.07 down to +0.04, so about $0.31B of the gain is real. It comes from demand running above both makers' slots: 2,232 against 1,884 in 2050. It is still $0.65B short of our +$1B business-case line. 2050 is the last decision year, so the grid's assumption that nobody moves after this round is now the whole game. On this grid our line means no fps on this board, and we say so plainly [BG-0021, BG-0022, B-0581, BG-0068, B-2303].

The balance sheet stays repaired. Do Nothing scores -1.01 in risk-case column S3, so the line is -3.01. Every Solo row passes (worst S3 is -1.24). The via-Embraer rows without the Re-engine fail (-3.14 and -3.11). With the Re-engine they pass by only $0.06-0.08B (-2.95 and -2.93), so Malave's buffer veto would not bind there. Our Rating-first clause does: via Embraer is $2.45-2.57B below the best Solo row in every column. Stress-case net debt stays at $0 on every 10-year row and on the Re-engine alone. It fails on the 7-year at a new site ($0.7B), on the 7-year with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B) and on every via-Embraer row ($1.5-6.3B). The stress results are advice, not a veto ground [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BG-0034, B-2259].

One development at a time, and the 787 Re-engine judged on its own case. Alone it is +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, which is exactly 2045's +0.74 discounted five years. Its worst column is inside our -$1B line, but its case is below +$1B. With a 10-year fps it is +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30, and the 2-year overlap passes H4. With a 7-year fps it is +0.17 / -0.87 / +0.17, and the 5-year overlap fails. H3's second half is still open: there is no A350 Re-engine on the record [BG-0066, B-2167, BX-0410, BG-0022].

Decide on Boeing's own case, never as a reply to Airbus. NGSA at its planned rate, Airbus preparing its next capacity step and any A350 move are read from the bulletin only. Neither a launch nor a hold should give them as its reason [B-2313, B-2315, BG-0068].

frame.question:
2050 is the last of four rounds. What we order now is where this board ends. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and that assumption is now the whole game. A hold means no fps on this board, and very probably no 787 Re-engine either.

What has changed is real, and I want it said plainly:
- The 10-year fps at Renton is +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35 against Do Nothing. It is positive in every column and has the highest worst column on the grid (S2 -0.76, against Do Nothing's -1.10).
- Discounting alone would have taken 2045's +0.07 to about +0.04. So about $0.31B of the gain is real, and it comes from the market: demand of 2,232 in 2050 against 1,884 slots for both makers together, peaking at 2,300 in 2053.
- On my own arithmetic, it would now survive a reset the size of the 777X's. In 2045 it would not have.

But +0.35 is still inside ε:
- It is $0.65B short of what my debt-first test needs, and the same distance short of the Board's +$1B line.
- The best plan in my expected column, the 10-year at Renton with the 787 Re-engine, is +0.65. That is also inside ε, and it costs 0.40 in S2.

So I'm asking the same question one last time: are the market, the technology and Boeing all ready? If the market leg is still short, we hold, say so plainly, and leave the company a standing plan rather than force an airplane. We decide on our own case. NGSA's planned rate, Airbus's next capacity step and any A350 move do not set our date.
frame.situation:
Round 4, decision year 2050, the last round. We have launched nothing and are on today's products: the 737 MAX, at its 57-a-month ceiling (684 a year) since 2047, and the 787.

**Public record**
- NGSA has been in service since 2037, fitted with CFM and the P&W-RR Joint Venture. Airbus says it is reaching its planned rate and is preparing a gated next capacity step.
- Airbus's widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, so H3's second half has not closed the 787 Re-engine.
- Engine programmes: the Joint Venture's engine has been ready since 2036, CFM's ducted engine since 2041, and CFM-Embraer since 2042.
- All three engine makers have answered our invitation on standard terms, with durability proven before EIS.

**Market on Do Nothing: -1.01 / -1.10 / -1.01**
- Narrowbody operating profit is -3.64, offset by +2.63 from supply and demand.
- Preference share has been 20% since 2043.
- Delivered share is 36.3% from 2047. Airbus's capacity of about 1,200 a year binds, and its flexible customers take our slots.
- Demand runs above both makers' 1,884 slots: 2,232 in 2050, 2,300 in 2053, 2,274 in 2055 and 2,129 in 2060.
- Do Nothing's S2 is now -1.10 (it was -1.34): an A350 Re-engine launched this year would enter service in 2055.

**Balance sheet**
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029, in base and stress, through 2060.
- Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year, and profit is back at the game baseline by 2050.
- Allocating the surplus is the Board's call.

**Objectives**
- Met: the balance-sheet lines, and three narrowbody engine makers in the market.
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (20%), and two sources on our narrowbody (the MAX flies CFM only).
- Every plan shows 1 engine source in 2050. The earliest fps EIS is 2057, so no order this round moves a scored year.

**KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. rate_737 is hold only.

**Grid columns**
- S1: rivals hold. S2: Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine. S3: the risk case, covert Airbus Delay Tactics.
- S3 equals S1 on every row. My reading, for Malave to confirm: demand exceeds the slots through 2060, so Delay Tactics move preference but not deliveries. The slip leg is therefore a level test, and S2 is the worst column on every row.

**Board guidance (not binding, but its veto binds after my decision)**
- It would veto:
  - every fps launch, on the business case (the best item is +0.35, against +$1B);
  - via Embraer, on Rating first, with Malave's buffer binding on the hold rows;
  - re787: launch, on the business case; with a 7-year fps it also fails H4.
- It would approve a hold on both, with new_site.
- It wants to see:
  - item values in S1-S3;
  - S3 against Do Nothing, with S2 as the worst column;
  - Malave's buffer, Fundable, net-debt and slip/overrun results;
  - Pope's gates;
  - H3's second half confirmed;
  - premiums logged, with Board holds logged separately;
  - code 7 at any launch;
  - no reason that cites Airbus;
  - no dividend or buyback signal.
- I carry these as Board risks, not red lines.

frame.initial_lean:
**Do Nothing on every lever:** fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.

**Why**
- On my four questions:
  - The KPIs are clean.
  - Technology is ready: CFM and the Joint Venture are both in service on another airframe.
  - Our balance sheet is ready: net debt $0 since 2029, in base and stress.
  - The market leg is closer than it has ever been, but it isn't there. "We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready" [BX-1296].
- No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in my expected column, S1. The best is the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine at +0.65, then the Re-engine alone at +0.45, then the 10-year at Renton at +0.35.
- Within ε, doing less and doing it better wins [BX-1239].
- The Board would veto every launch on its +$1B line, and I have no override. Bringing an item I know it will veto is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
- No order moves a scored year: the earliest EIS is 2057.

**What I am weighing honestly**
- This is the last round, and building a new future is on my list [BX-1245].
- Unlike 2045, the 10-year's edge may now survive a priced slip. If Jay's slip-priced test points to the 10-year at Renton, I'll report it plainly.
- My first tie-break is still doing less, and the market leg is what the Board's line measures.
- I won't force an airplane to end a game.

**Premiums**
- fps hold: $0.35B, doctrine, logged against the cap (unless Jay classifies it as a Board hold).
- Re-engine hold: a Board hold, $0.45B given up in S1 and S3, $0.60B saved in S2, about $0.19B weighted at 25%. My ε rule picks it too, and this very probably closes the Re-engine for good.
- If both counted as soft, the total is $0.80B, inside $2B. The objective premium is $0.

**Close**
- Every 7-year row: below the 10-year, H4 with the Re-engine, and stress failures.
- Every via-Embraer row: Malave's buffer on the hold rows, the Board's lines on the rest.

**What would move me**
- A finding from Jay or Stephanie, in the brief's own numbers, that puts a Solo launch more than ε ahead in S1 with no column below -$1B. Nothing on this grid does.
- A live problem would only confirm the hold.

**Public statement**
- No fps date.
- What's changed, said plainly: the market case is better than it has ever been, it still isn't there, and the market leg is what holds it back, not technology or the balance sheet.
- The staged work stays our standing plan: authority to offer first, a conservative ramp with headroom, two engine sources, and the production system designed with the airplane.
- The MAX stays at 57 on its KPIs.
- No Re-engine this year; Charleston capacity as customers need it.
- No dividend or buyback signal, and no reason that cites Airbus [B-2313].

"I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" [BX-1300]. And it is still so much more important that we do this right than fast [BX-1241].

- Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year, and profit is back at the game baseline by 2050.
