The gate is met for any 10-yr launch and for the 7-yr at Renton. The grid holds the fps back, not the cash.

tests.name: Cash path of each bill (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: When each bill lands (the board books it at EIS; the tracker spends it over development on the standard curve), and whether two land together.
tests.numbers:
The recommended plan has no bill and no programme cash.

Each bill:
- 10-yr fps: $60.32B over 2050-60. Year 1 at 5% is $3.02B. The peak at 14% is $8.44B in year 7 (2056-57): 61% of base ($13.8B) and 92% of stress ($9.2B) free cash flow. The tracker counts 79% of programme cash, so the net peak hit is $6.67B, or 48% of base and 73% of stress, which is why stress holds at $0. Booked in 2060.
- 7-yr fps: $65.00B over 2050-57, about $9.29B a year: 67% of base and 101% of stress (80% after the 79% factor). Its peak years take stress net debt to $0.7B at a new site; Renton's ~$3.0B saving keeps it at $0. Booked in 2057.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2050-55, about $1.0B a year. Booked in 2055.
- Strain: $1.2B for a 10-yr pair (2053-55, at H4's limit) and $3.0B for a 7-yr pair (5 years, a breach).

On the board's booking, no two bills land in the same year. In cash, a same-round pair runs together: the Re-engine's whole $5B falls inside the fps spend.

Renton: choosing it now, at least 3 years before EIS, captures the full ~$3.0B. On a hold it is worth 0.00, so keep new_site.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel (CEO ask 9)
tests.threshold: Cancel write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, and the debt penalty stays; cost it once, in full. H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine.
tests.numbers: Nothing is launched, so nothing can be cancelled. There is no later round on this board in which to order a cancel. Any launch now is irreversible under H5, so we launch only what we will finish.

tests.name: Rate step
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA. Never as a reply to Airbus, and never under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem (H6).
tests.numbers: rate_737 is hold only, and the brief reports no live problem. The MAX at 57 a month (684 a year) since 2047 is the ceiling, not a Rate Increase, and it stays KPI-gated, as we took 38 to 42 with the FAA [BX-0554]. The KPI gate is Pope's to state.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (H8; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Report every doctrine or objective premium in $B; the soft total must stay within $2B. Board holds are logged separately with their known cost. Name the condition that would break each number.
tests.numbers:
- fps hold: $0.35B in S1 and S3 and $0.34B in S2, against the 10-yr at Renton. I classify it as doctrine, against the cap: our own ε rule and my balance-sheet tie-break choose it before the Board's line applies. Note in the Board-hold log that the +$1B line would force it too, and count it once.
- Re-engine hold: a Board hold, logged separately. It gives up $0.45B in S1 and S3, saves $0.60B in S2, and is worth $0.24B weighted at my 20% read ($0.19B at 25%).
- At plan level, against the best grid plan in S1 (the 10-yr at Renton + Re-engine, -0.36), Do Nothing gives up $0.65B, not $0.80B, because next to the fps the Re-engine adds only +0.30. In S2 the best plan is the 10-yr at Renton (-0.76), and the figure is $0.34B.
- Soft total against the $2B cap: $0.35B. Counting both as soft, it is at most $0.80B (sum) or $0.65B (plan level), still inside the cap. The classification changes no decision.
- Objective premium: $0. No plan moves a scored year: the earliest fps EIS is 2057, and every plan shows one engine source in 2050.
- What breaks my numbers: an A350 Re-engine (S2) takes Do Nothing to -1.10. The fps-hold premium becomes a saving if the launch would have slipped at an all-in cost above $6.4B.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_via_embraer with 787 hold, at a new site or at Renton
vetoes.ground:
Buffer test (slip leg). Risk-case column S3 against Do Nothing's -1.01; the line is -3.01.
- Via Embraer + 787 hold: -3.14, which is 2.13 below Do Nothing and 0.13 past the line.
- Via Embraer at Renton + 787 hold: -3.11, which is 2.10 below and 0.10 past.
Both fail. The team rule (teams.md §9) makes this binding, and the CEO must revise within it.

Advice on top, not part of the veto: the undiscounted penalty is $52.5B, and stress-case net debt peaks at $3.3-3.7B (new site) and $2.5-2.9B (Renton).

vetoes.plan: fps launch_via_embraer with the 787 Re-engine, at a new site or at Renton
vetoes.ground: Advice only, NOT a veto. These rows pass my buffer narrowly: S3 -2.95 (headroom +0.06) and -2.93 (+0.08). Against Do Nothing they sit at -1.94 / -3.00 / -1.94 and -1.92 / -2.97 / -1.92. The undiscounted penalty is $52.5B, and stress-case net debt peaks at $1.7 / $6.3 / $1.7B and $1.5 / $5.3 / $1.5B. I advise against them. On the buffer ground alone I would have to concur, but the Board's Downside and Rating-first lines veto them.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_10yr rows (new site or Renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, NOT a veto. All four pass my buffer, with headroom of +2.32, +2.35, +2.62 and +2.65. They are fundable, and stress net debt holds at $0.
- The 10-yr at Renton is +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35, inside ε. It has the higher worst column on the printed grid (+0.34) and keeps it after one 777X-size reset (+0.05).
- It turns negative at an overrun above about $6.4B all in (10.6% of the bill) or a slip cost above the same figure. At the 777X's rate, three years of clean-sheet slip ($14.7B) takes it to about -0.35.
- It adds a $19.1B undiscounted penalty, and on cash as spent it is negative.
- With the Re-engine, S2 falls to -0.40 against Do Nothing, and the 2-year overlap ($1.2B) sits at H4's limit with no slack.
I advise hold. If the Board ever accepts a launch, I would concur on the buffer ground: the 10-yr ramp, Renton with Pope's bridge plan, and code 7 (CFM plus the Joint Venture). That last part is doctrine, not my record.

vetoes.plan: fps launch_7yr rows (new site or Renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, NOT a veto. All four pass my buffer: S3 -1.24, -1.13, -1.07 and -0.96.
- The item is -0.23 at new sites and -0.12 at Renton, below zero in every column, on a larger bill ($65.00B) and penalty ($22.0B). It has no overrun room.
- Stress net debt peaks at $0.7B at new sites and $2.0-3.1B with the Re-engine.
- With the Re-engine the overlap is 5 years ($3.0B), an H4 breach the CEO must strike.
Close these rows.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (alone or with any fps)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, NOT a veto. Alone it passes my buffer (S3 -0.56, headroom +2.45), and net debt holds at $0 in base and stress.
- Its item is +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, worth +0.24 at my 20% read. It never clears ε, even at p = 0.
- Its worst column (-1.70) is 0.60 below Do Nothing's, so Meet and beat holds.
- Next to a 10-yr fps it adds only +0.30 / -0.74, with $3.1B of extra undiscounted penalty and $1.2B of strain.
- A +2-year derivative slip takes S1 to about +0.37, worsens S2, and would push the overlap to 4 years.
If the CEO brings it, I concur on the buffer ground.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
fps:
- I would back the 10-yr at Renton if the staged case showed, in numbers, that a three-year clean-sheet slip or overrun would cost no more than about $6.4B all in, penalty included. That is roughly one 777X reset, not three years at its rate. It would take a type-certificate-first plan with a proven production system and fixed scope. Then Meet and beat points to the 10-yr at Renton under my baseline as well, and only my balance-sheet tie-break (advice) stands against it. I would not oppose a launch the Board accepts.
- Equally, a grid where a Solo row sits more than ε above Do Nothing in S1, with no column more than $1B below and S3 within $2B.
- Brief evidence that demand stays above both makers' slots, with an fps at rate, through the 2060-79 window would raise my confidence in the +0.35. The brief prints only 2060.

787 Re-engine: nothing on this board moves me. I would back it only on a grid that shows it more than ε above Do Nothing with its worst column within -$1B, and with H3's second half still open.

Balance sheet: if any chosen row's stress-case net debt rose above $0 in a scored year, I would hold whatever drives it.

A live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem would only confirm the hold.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the buffer as the baseline: S3 no worse than -3.01, $2B under Do Nothing's -1.01. Your list is right. Every Solo row passes; the tightest, the 7-year at new sites, has $1.77B of headroom. The two via-Embraer hold rows fail at -3.14 and -3.11, and that veto binds. With the Re-engine they pass by $0.06-0.08B, so there I give advice, not a veto.

S3 equals S1 because Airbus's slots bind: Delay Tactics move preference, not deliveries. The leg prices no slip, so I priced it, once.

Straight numbers on the 10-year at Renton. Count the penalty on the overrun itself and the +0.35 survives about $6.4B, 10.6% of the bill, not 13-17%. Slipped three years, it survives one 777X-size reset with about $0.05B to spare and keeps the higher worst column. But that $4.9B bought one year on a derivative. Three years at that rate is $14.7B, and the item goes to about -0.35. On cash as spent it is negative too, and 19 of its 20 market years lie past what the brief prints.

It is fundable: net debt holds at zero in base and stress. The edge sits inside ε, and balance sheet first decides: Do Nothing adds no penalty.

So, hold on every lever: a higher confidence plan we can meet and potentially beat, barring an A350 Re-engine (-1.10), which I now put at about 20%. Log the fps hold at $0.35B against the cap; the Re-engine as a Board hold.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read risk-case column S3 (Airbus Delay Tactics) against S1, read the worst column, and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. The doctrine slip priors (clean-sheet +3 years, range +2 to +5; derivative +2, range +1 to +4) are not priced on the board.
tests.numbers:
S3 equals S1 on every row:
- Do Nothing -1.01 / -1.01;
- Re-engine alone -0.56 / -0.56;
- 10-year at Renton -0.66 / -0.66;
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -0.36 / -0.36.
So 100% of every plan's value survives Delay Tactics. My reading (inference): demand runs above both makers' 1,884 slots (2,232 in 2050, 2,300 in 2053, 2,129 in 2060), so our 684 slots fill whatever preference does. Delay Tactics move preference, not deliveries. S2 is the worst column on every row.

Slip sensitivity, discounting at the 10.5% WACC only (inference; each year of later EIS takes about 9.5% off):
- fps 10-year at Renton on the clean-sheet prior: EIS 2060 becomes 2063 central (range 2062-65), and +0.35 becomes about +0.26. Each year of slip also costs 1 pp of long-run split under the lead-edge rule (27% to 24% at +3), which the grid does not price.
- fps 7-year: EIS 2057, central 2060 (range 2059-62). Its item is negative before any slip (-0.12 at Renton, -0.23 at new sites).
- 787 Re-engine on the derivative prior: EIS 2055 becomes 2057 central. +0.45 becomes +0.41 at +1, +0.37 at +2 and +0.30 at +4 (S1 and S3).
The fps value no longer hangs wholly on the nominal date and bill (see my 2045 overrun test below).

The recommended plan (hold) has no EIS to deliver. Its delivery commitment is the MAX at 684 a year, delivered as planned in 2047, 2048 and 2049. Result: pass.

tests.name: KPI gate (doctrine; my veto) - answers the CEO's ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of +5 a month or less, at least 6 months apart, each after 2-3 stable months on the FAA-agreed KPIs and an FAA review. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The menu offers only rate_737: hold, because the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. My veto therefore has neither a ground nor an object, and I do not invoke it.

Watch items, not live problems on our line:
- CFM says LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first, and that it works capacity with both airframers. The LEAP-1B is our sole MAX engine.
- P&W's GTF fleet and Hot Section work sits on the A320neo side, not the MAX.

tests.name: MAX at 57 a month since 2047, LEAP-1B allocation, and a development beside the line (doctrine) - answers ask 2
tests.threshold: The line holds its rate on stable KPIs agreed with the FAA, with engine and supplier output proven at that rate. A development may sit beside a stable line. A production change (rate break or line conversion) beside a development is a second front.
tests.numbers:
Board deliveries: 684 in 2047, 2048 and 2049 (36.3% delivered share), and 684 a year planned to 2060. That is three years at the 57-a-month ceiling, against the doctrine's 2-3 stable months before any step, with no problem reported.

For the Board, candidly: the brief carries no KPI readings. 'Stable' rests on no reported problem and a flat delivery record, not on KPI data. This is the ceiling, not a Rate Increase, and it stays KPI-gated with the FAA [B-2236].

LEAP-1B:
- 684 x 2 = 1,368 engines a year before spares, delivered three years running. The allocation is demonstrated in deliveries; the contract itself is not in the brief.
- In 2047-49 CFM's narrowbody engines were 53.5% of 3,768, about 2,016 a year. The MAX took about 68% of them, and CFM also carries NGSA at rate.
- Re-confirm 1,368 a year in each annual allocation round [BX-1264, BX-1325].

Can the line carry a development beside it? Yes, one:
- The front is engineering, not the line. With new_site the MAX line is untouched until the fps's own rate breaks after 2060.
- With Renton, the MAX wind-down becomes a second production front from 2060. That is why the bridge plan is needed.
- The suppliers carrying 57 a month are the ones an fps loads next. Supplier output is a gate at each fps rate break [B-2308].

tests.name: Two-front strain / engineering capacity, H4 (doctrine) - answers ask 3
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5. The fps window runs from EIS-7 to EIS, the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS. Engineering starts at launch; a slip extends the end.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (both held): 0 years, $0.

Same round, all pairs (there is no later round, so no cross-round pairs):
- 10-year fps alone (window 2053-60): 0 years, $0. Confirmed.
- Re-engine alone (2050-55): 0 years, $0.
- 10-year fps + Re-engine: 2053-55, 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted. At the limit with no slack. Confirmed.
  - On a +1-year derivative slip (to 2056): 3 years, $1.8B, past H4.
  - On the +2-year central prior (to 2057): 4 years, $2.4B. Confirmed.
- 7-year fps (2050-57) + Re-engine: 5 years, $3.0B. H4 breach, to be struck. Confirmed.

Result: pass for the recommended plan and for any lone launch. The pair passes on the board only at the limit.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers:
No fps on the recommended plan.

A 2050 launch:
- 7-year: EIS 2057, central 2060 on the clean-sheet prior (range 2059-62).
- 10-year: EIS 2060, central 2063 (range 2062-65).

Strain is $0 for either alone. With a same-round Re-engine it is $3.0B for the 7-year (a breach) and $1.2B for the 10-year (the limit).

The 10-year beats the 7-year in every column: by 0.55 (new site) and 0.47 (Renton) on the hold rows, and by 0.68 and 0.60 with the Re-engine. It also has the higher worst column (S2 -0.76 against -1.23 at Renton).

Cash:
- 7-year: about $9.29B a year on average, 101% of stress free cash flow. Stress net debt fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B).
- 10-year: a peak of about $8.44B in year 7 (2056), 92% of stress. Net debt $0 in base and stress.

If an fps is brought, operations backs only the 10-year.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference) - answers ask 7
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds IP or capacity Boeing lacks, at a cost within $1B of Solo.

tests.name: Engine and supplier readiness by a 2060 EIS, or 2057 on the 7-year (doctrine; supplier readiness is a hard gate) - answers ask 4
tests.threshold: Each named engine maker is ready by EIS, with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Supplier output is proven before each rate break. A sole source is a risk to reduce.
tests.numbers:
The engine code is null with the hold.

At any launch, code 7. The brief's table gives 2 fitted sources at a 2060 EIS: CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture. Codes 5 and 6 also give 2; codes 1-4 give 1.

Readiness:
- The Joint Venture's engine has been ready since 2036 and in service on NGSA since 2037. That is 13 years of in-service data now, 20 by a 2057 EIS and 23 by 2060.
- CFM's ducted engine has been ready since 2041.
- All three makers answered on standard terms, with durability proven before EIS [BX-1298]. P&W reports durability as the in-service data show it, and any RR content comes on a later block with its own proof. The item to watch is the durability evidence, not the date.

Today 100% of MAX engines are CFM. Every plan shows 1 source in 2050, and no order on this board can change that.

Suppliers: the brief has no supplier data, so supplier output is a gate before each fps rate break [B-2308], not a fail.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a launch now, EIS 2055, and H3's second half (doctrine) - answers ask 8
tests.threshold: Engineering is free, Charleston has capacity, the engine is ready with durability proven, the supplier gate is met on new parts, and the type certificate comes before building at rate. H3: no Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the record.
tests.numbers:
Engineering: nothing is in development, so a lone Re-engine (2050-55) would be the one development.

Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table; at 6 years from launch it could not be ready before 2056, after a 2055 EIS. The date therefore rests on the GEnx.

Charleston: the footprint covers 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. The 787 builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone Re-engine gaining 1 pp a year from 58.8% reaches about 108 a year (9.0 a month) in 2060 and 144 (12.0 a month) at the 85% cap. That is inside the footprint.

Supplier gate on new parts at the rate break [B-2308]. Type certificate before rate. Central EIS on the derivative prior: 2057.

H3, second half, confirmed open: no A350 Re-engine is on the public record.

Operations does not hold the Re-engine back. It fails the Board's +$1B line at +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45 (+0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30 beside a 10-year fps). That is a business-case test, not a readiness one.

tests.name: No production-certification concurrency (doctrine) - answers ask 5
tests.threshold: The type certificate comes before building at rate on any new airframe or derivative. No Renton conversion before the fps type certificate. Each rate break is proven before it is taken.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan: nothing is in certification and nothing is built early.

For any launch:
- the type certificate comes before building at rate;
- no Renton line converts before the fps type certificate;
- the Re-engine is built at rate in Charleston only after its type certificate.

On 'production system proven at rate before authority to offer': for a launch this round, the launch is the authority to offer, and no fps line can run at rate before the airplane exists. Read literally, the gate would bar any launch. I read it as follows: the production system is designed with the airplane, and each fps rate break (KPIs, suppliers, FAA) is proven before it is taken.

The 787-8 (planned for May 2008, delivered in September 2011) is the record behind the +3-year clean-sheet prior.

tests.name: Renton or new site, with the five-step MAX bridge plan (inference) - answers ask 6
tests.threshold: Renton only alongside a launch, and only with a bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp. Otherwise new_site.
tests.numbers:
With the hold, Renton is worth 0.00: keep new_site.

With a launch, Renton is worth +0.03 on the 10-year (-0.66 vs -0.69, every column) and +0.11 on the 7-year. It was +0.15 on the 10-year in 2045.

My reading (inference): valued at EIS, the ~$3.0B capex saving is worth about $0.10B at the 2060 discount factor of 29.8. So the wind-down already gives up roughly $0.07B of MAX deliveries on the nominal ramp, now that demand is above our slots. There is no later round, so Renton counts on the board only if chosen now.

The risk is not priced. All 684 MAX slots are full, and Renton carries 47 of the 57 a month. If Renton converts ahead of the fps's actual ramp (on a 3-year clean-sheet slip, say), the MAX falls to the Everett North Line at up to 15 a month (180 a year). That is a gap of up to 504 deliveries a year. At +0.03, operations prefers new_site even with a launch.

If Renton is chosen, the five-step bridge plan:
1. No Renton line converts before the fps type certificate.
2. Each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps line has held its rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month, about 4 years after EIS.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers follow the actual wind-down, not the planned one.
5. The Everett North Line carries the tail, at up to 15 a month.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (inference, one remark [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column. Otherwise, not applicable.
tests.numbers:
There are no Rate Increase rows on this grid (it was a 2030-only order).

Demand is visible. New demand runs above both makers' 1,884 slots by 348 in 2050, 416 in 2053, 390 in 2055 and 245 in 2060.

But our own preference demand (446, 460, 455 and 426 a year) sits below our 684 slots. The rest of our line (238, 224, 229 and 258 a year) is the rival's flexible customers.

The excess peaks in 2053 and is falling by 2060. The fps's capacity arrives from 2060 (rate 50 about 2064, 100 about 2068), in years the brief does not print.

Information for the Board (inference): the market leg under the fps is mostly overflow demand after 2060, not our own preference.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash and net debt, as numbers rather than adjectives.
tests.numbers:
Base free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in stress). Profit is back at the game baseline by 2050.
- Do Nothing: no bill. Net debt $0 in base and stress to 2060.
- Re-engine alone: $5B over 2050-55, about $1.0B a year (7% of base, 11% of stress free cash flow). Booked in 2055 at a factor of 18.09 (PV $0.28B), with a $0.6B undiscounted penalty. It returns +$90M of PV per $1B of bill in S1 and S3, and -$120M in S2. Net debt $0.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2050-60. Year 1 is about $3.02B (22% of base, 33% of stress). The peak is about $8.44B in year 7, 2056 (61% / 92%). Booked in 2060 at 29.81 (PV $2.02B). It returns +$5.8M of PV per $1B at Renton and +$5.3M at new sites (2045: +$1.2M and -$1.3M). Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- 10-year + Re-engine: both bills run over 2050-55, plus $1.2B of strain in 2053-55. Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2050-57, about $9.29B a year (67% / 101%). It returns -$1.8M per $1B at Renton and -$3.5M at new sites. Stress fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B).
- Via Embraer: a peak of about $14.0B (102% / 152%). Stress fails ($1.5-6.3B).
- Renton: ~$3.0B of capex saved, and only with a launch.

tests.name: The overrun and slip test I set in 2045 (inference) - answers ask 9
tests.threshold: Set by me in 2045: the fps item must survive a 2% overrun and the +3-year clean-sheet prior. Discounting at the 10.5% WACC, with the bill booked at EIS. Where I scale the debt penalty, I take it at 31.7% of the bill (19.1 / 60.32).
tests.numbers:
Discount factor: 29.81 for 2060, 40.22 for 2063.

On the 10-year at Renton (+0.35):
- Overrun break-even: $10.4B (17.3% of $60.32B) before any penalty on it, or $7.9B (13.1%) if the penalty scales with the bill. That matches the CEO's ~$10.4B and the Board's 13-17%.
- A 2% overrun ($1.21B) leaves +0.30 to +0.31.
- A +3-year slip to 2063, on discounting alone, leaves +0.26. Break-even slip cost: $7.9-10.4B.
- A 2% overrun and +3 years together leave +0.22.
- A 777X-size reset ($4.9B) on top of the 3-year slip leaves +0.10 to +0.14. It survives, but further inside ε.

In 2045 the same item was +0.07 at a factor of 18.09, and a 2.1% overrun ($1.27B) erased it. At new sites (+0.32) every figure is about 9% lower; the overrun break-even is about $9.5B before the penalty.

Result: pass. It changes my readiness view: operations no longer finds the 10-year's value hanging on the nominal bill and date. It does not change the business case. +0.35 is against the Board's +$1B line, and that test is not my seat.

tests.name: Standing plan beyond this board: workforce, production system, suppliers, Renton bridge (doctrine and inference) - answers ask 10
tests.threshold: What the company keeps ready so that, if a case clears, Boeing goes on day one.
tests.numbers:
There is no order here; this is the plan.
1. Workforce: the line has held 57 a month since 2047, so keep the trained workforce on it. Form a protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line.
2. Production system: designed with the airplane. Each rate break is proven before it is taken, and the type certificate comes before rate.
3. Suppliers: keep fragile suppliers funded, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. They carry 57 a month now and would carry an fps next.
4. Engines: renew the LEAP-1B allocation at 1,368 a year. Keep the code-7 proposals (CFM plus the Joint Venture) current, with durability evidence before EIS.
5. Renton: keep the five-step bridge plan on the shelf, and decide the site with the launch.
6. Base case: the 10-year ramp, Solo, code 7. Decide any future Re-engine and fps together as one pair under H4.
7. Stability first, then go.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (KPI veto NOT invoked)
vetoes.ground: No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The KPI doctrine has neither a ground nor an object this round, so I do not invoke it. As doctrine advice, not a board order: the MAX stays at its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated with the FAA, and any future step waits while a KPI is out or while LEAP-1B or supplier output is short of the next rate.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (fps 2050-57, Re-engine 2050-55), with $3.0B of strain undiscounted, past the 2-year limit. The CEO must strike it.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a breach on the board. The overlap is 2 years (2053-55), with $1.2B of strain, at the limit with no slack. It becomes 3 years ($1.8B) on a 1-year derivative slip and 4 years ($2.4B) on the 2-year central prior, both past H4. Beside the fps, the Re-engine item falls to +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30.

vetoes.plan: fps_site: renton (with a launch, or without one)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. Without a launch, Renton is worth 0.00. With a 10-year launch it is worth +0.03, and on my reading it already gives up about $0.07B of MAX deliveries against a ~$0.10B capex saving. If Renton converts ahead of the fps's actual ramp, the MAX falls to the Everett North Line at up to 180 a year, a gap of up to 504 deliveries a year. Prefer new_site. If Renton is chosen, the five-step bridge plan in my memo is a condition.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any row)
vetoes.ground: Operations advice. It sits 0.47-0.68 below the 10-year in every column and has a negative item value (-0.12 at Renton, -0.23 at new sites). Its spend averages about $9.29B a year, 101% of stress free cash flow. Stress net debt fails at new sites ($0.7B) and with the Re-engine ($2.0-3.1B).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: IP advice, not binding. The partner brings no airframe IP, capacity or strain relief on the board. It has the same EIS as the Solo 10-year (2060) and sits $2.45-2.57B below it in every column, with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Stress net debt fails ($1.5-6.3B). Malave's buffer binds on the hold rows (S3 -3.14 and -3.11); my seat does not.

vetoes.plan: Any fps or re787 launch this round
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule reminder H5, not a veto. Nothing is launched, so nothing can be cancelled. Under company doctrine, any launch now is never cancelled, only re-baselined once, so we launch only what operations will finish. The lone 10-year passes my readiness gates; the 7-year rows and the via-Embraer rows do not earn that commitment.

ops.memo:
Four results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes. The KPI, supplier and strain gates run on operations doctrine; the delivery, IP and cash tests apply my 2022 record by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The MAX has built 684 a year, 57 a month, since 2047, on 1,368 LEAP-1B engines a year. The KPI gate is clean, and my veto has nothing to act on.

Second, engineering capacity. A lone 10-year fps or a lone Re-engine is one front. Together they overlap 2 years and $1.2 billion, at H4's limit, and 4 years on a 2-year derivative slip. A 7-year fps with the Re-engine overlaps 5 years: a breach.

Third, the test I set in 2045. Then, a 2% overrun erased the fps. Now the 10-year at Renton survives an overrun of 13-17%, about $8-10 billion, and keeps about +$0.26 billion on a 3-year slip. It passes. Operations does not hold a lone 10-year back.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. The 10-year returns about $6 million of value per billion of bill. Renton adds $0.03 billion but risks up to 504 MAX deliveries a year if it converts early, so new_site. Embraer brings no IP we lack, at $2.45-2.57 billion below Solo.

The business case is not my seat: +$0.35 billion is $0.65 billion short of the Board's line. Orders: fps hold, new_site, no code; Re-engine hold; 737 hold.

other_moves.move: Standing fps plan beyond this board (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail:
This is the company's plan to go on day one when a case clears. It is not a launch.
- Solo by default. Pope's IP test finds that Embraer brings no airframe IP, capacity or strain relief we lack, at $2.45-2.57B below Solo.
- The base case is the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by 0.47-0.68 in every column, has the higher worst column, and holds stress net debt at $0.
- Code 7 (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture), with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition [BX-1298].
- The production system is designed with the airplane. The type certificate comes before building at rate, each fps rate break is proven before it is taken, and there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].
- The site is decided with the launch. Renton only with Pope's five-step MAX bridge plan:
  1. No conversion before the fps type certificate.
  2. Each Renton line comes down only after the fps line has held rate for 2-3 stable KPI months.
  3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month.
  4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers follow the actual wind-down.
  5. The Everett North Line carries the tail at up to 15 a month.
- Decide any fps and 787 Re-engine together, as one pair, under H4.

What a case must show before it comes to the Board:
- the item more than +$1B in the expected column, with no plausible column below -$1B;
- Malave's buffer and 'Fundable' tests passed;
- the slip priced once on his baseline (the clean-sheet prior of +3 years at a realistic cost per year, with the marginal penalty included);
- Pope's readiness results;
- evidence that demand holds above slots through the 20-year market window, not only to the last printed year.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (unchanged)
other_moves.detail:
We continue to invite the narrowbody engine makers to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Our plan at launch is a choice of two engine sources: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (code 7). Selection is on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment.

Recorded internally: the dual-source enabler is unmet in 2050 on every plan (the MAX flies CFM only), and no order on this board can cure it.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX held at its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA
other_moves.detail:
The 737 has held full output, 57 a month (684 a year), since 2047. This is the ceiling, not a Rate Increase. It stays gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA [B-2236].

We renew the LEAP-1B allocation of 1,368 engines a year in each annual round with CFM [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Supplier output stays proven ahead of the line. No dates or numbers beyond the ceiling are published.

other_moves.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers funded
other_moves.detail:
- Keep the trained workforce on the MAX line.
- Keep a small, protected fps production-system team that does not draw on the line.
- Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources [BX-1243, B-2330]. The suppliers carrying 57 a month are the ones an fps would load next.

Pope noted candidly that the brief carries no KPI readings. Ask her seat to put the six FAA-agreed KPIs in front of the Board each quarter, so that 'stable' rests on data, not on the absence of a reported problem [BX-1259].

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine: study only, no launch
other_moves.detail:
Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. Recorded candidly: alone the item is +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, which is 2045's +0.74 discounted five years. It never clears ε at any probability of an A350 Re-engine (+0.24 at Malave's 20% read). This hold very probably closes it on this board.

If it is ever re-tested beyond the board, it comes only as one pair with any fps under H4, and only while H3's second half is open. No programme spend is committed.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress through 2060. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board [BG-0044]. Headroom stays visible for a future staged fps (the 10-year's peak year is about $8.44B, 92% of stress free cash flow). Nothing is said publicly.

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago I told you the case for a new airplane was better than it had been, and that it wasn't there yet. I'll tell you plainly where it stands today.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. Here's what has changed. Demand for single-aisle airplanes is running above what the industry can build, and the case for a new Boeing airplane is the best it has been.
- Technology is ready. The engines we'd want are in service, and our engine partners have answered our invitation on standard terms.
- Our balance sheet is ready. It's been repaired for twenty years, and it's staying repaired.
- Our production system has held full rate for three years.

The leg that isn't there is the market case itself. When we plan for the way new airplanes really come together, including the chance that it takes longer than we think, it doesn't clear the bar we hold ourselves to. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. Two out of three isn't three.

So the work keeps going, in stages, and it will be ready when the case is. We're designing the production system together with the airplane. The plan is a conservative one with headroom in it:
- a ten-year development;
- the type certificate before we build at rate;
- no fixed-price development;
- a choice of two engine sources, CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, with durability proven before entry into service.

On the 737, the line has been at full output, 57 a month, for three years. That's where it stays. It's gated on our KPIs and agreed with the FAA, and we'll keep our suppliers and our engine supply ahead of it. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

We turned this big ship. The job now is to keep it pointed in the right direction. Our dates are set by our own readiness, and it is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever
- Orders: fps hold, fps_site new_site, fps_engine_code null, re787 hold, rate_737 hold.
- Submitted row: -1.01 / -1.10 / -1.01 (S1 / S2 / S3).
  - S3 against Do Nothing: 0.00, with headroom of +2.00 over the -3.01 line.
  - The worst column is S2, at -1.10.
  - Net debt reads '2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B)' in every column.
- No order differs from the default, so there is no Board item.
- This is the last round, and I say it plainly: this hold means no fps on this board, and very probably no 787 Re-engine either.

TEAM RULE (teams.md §9)
- Malave's buffer veto binds on the two via-Embraer hold rows (S3 -3.14 and -3.11, 0.13 and 0.10 past the line). Neither is chosen.
- The via-Embraer + Re-engine rows pass his buffer by only 0.06-0.08. His advice is against them, and so are the Board's Downside and Rating-first lines. Closed.
- The KPI doctrine has no object (rate_737 is hold only), and no problem is live. Pope did not invoke her veto.
- Pope flagged H4 on the 7-year fps + Re-engine (5 years of overlap). Not chosen, and struck from the option set.
- No flag needs a strike, and there are no overrides.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes: the brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271], and the FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. Pope says candidly that the brief carries no KPI readings: 'stable' rests on no reported problem and three years at 684. I take that as a pass with a caveat, and I've asked for the KPIs in front of the Board.
2. Are market, technology and Boeing all ready [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
   - Technology: yes. CFM, and the Joint Venture with 13 years of in-service data on NGSA.
   - Balance sheet: yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress. 'Fundable when the 777X turns' passes [BX-0547], and every 10-year row holds stress at $0.
   - Operations: yes, for one development. A lone 10-year passes Pope's gates and her own 2045 test (a 2% overrun and +3 years), leaving +0.22.
   - Market: closer than it has ever been, but not there.
     - The 10-year at Renton is +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35, and about $0.31B of that gain since 2045 is real.
     - But Pope shows that our own preference demand (446-460 a year) sits below our 684 slots. The excess is the rival's flexible customers, and the fps's capacity arrives after 2060.
     - Malave adds that 19 of the fps's 20 market years are past what the brief prints, and the excess demand is already falling at EIS (416 in 2053, 245 in 2060).
     - So the market leg rests mostly on overflow demand in years the brief does not show. That is lower confidence [BX-0548].
3. What if certification takes longer? I plan for the reset, once [BX-1318, BX-1319]. Malave corrected my arithmetic: with the marginal penalty on the extra spend (0.59, not the average 0.32), the 10-year at Renton breaks even at about $6.4B all in, 10.6% of the bill, not $10.4B. On a +3-year clean-sheet slip:
   - Case A, one 777X-size reset ($4.9B): the item keeps +0.06.
   - Case B, three years at the 777X's cost per year ($14.7B): the item falls to -0.35.
   The $4.9B bought one year on a derivative [BX-0550], and a clean sheet's prior is +3 years (range +2 to +5). The reset I would actually plan for is nearer case B. The edge survives only the optimistic reset.
4. Is this doing less, better [BX-1239]? Every plan is within ε of Do Nothing in S1. Doing less wins, and Do Nothing is the higher-confidence plan: it has nothing to slip [BX-0548].

DEBT FIRST
The grid already nets each penalty, so I do not subtract it again. No plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in S1:
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.65.
- 10-year + Re-engine: +0.62.
- Re-engine alone: +0.45.
- 10-year at Renton: +0.35.
- 10-year at new site: +0.32.
Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B; the pair $22.2B; Re-engine $0.6B.

WORST-COLUMN TIE-BREAK, REPORTED PLAINLY
- On the printed grid, the 10-year at Renton has the higher worst column: -0.76 against -1.10, so Do Nothing fails this tie-break by $0.34B.
- Slip-priced, case A keeps the 10-year ahead by +0.05. Case B reverses it: Do Nothing is higher by $0.36B.
- The two cases straddle the $6.4B break-even, so this test does not settle the order. My first tie-break, doing less, decides it, and Malave's balance-sheet tie-break (advice) agrees: Do Nothing adds no penalty.

PER-ROW RESULTS (item value against the default, S1 / S2 / S3)
- 10-year at Renton: +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35. At a new site: +0.32 / +0.31 / +0.32.
  - Passes: buffer (S3 -0.66, headroom +2.35), Downside, H4, Fundable, stress at $0.
  - Fails my debt-first ε and the Board's +$1B line, by $0.65B. The Board would veto it.
- Re-engine alone: +0.45 / -0.60 / +0.45, or +0.24 weighted at Malave's 20%. It never clears ε at any p, and the Board would veto it.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: +0.65 / -0.40 / +0.65 against Do Nothing.
  - The Re-engine item beside the fps is only +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30.
  - H4 sits at its 2-year limit with no slack: 3 years on a +1-year derivative slip, 4 on the +2-year prior.
- 7-year rows: closed.
  - -0.12 at Renton and -0.23 at new sites, 0.47-0.68 below the 10-year, with no overrun room.
  - With the Re-engine, 5 years of overlap breaches H4.
  - Stress peaks of $0.7B and $2.0-3.1B. Malave corrects these to development-year peaks, not scored failures.
- Via Embraer: closed.
  - The buffer veto binds on the hold rows. The Re-engine rows sit -1.92 to -3.00 against Do Nothing.
  - $52.5B undiscounted penalty, and it fails Pope's IP test.

RED LINES AND HARD RULES
- H1 and H3's first half: lifted in my 2030 ruling, not re-made.
- H3's second half: confirmed open. There is no A350 Re-engine on the record.
- H4: no overlap on the submitted plan.
- H5: nothing launched, nothing cancelled.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: logged below.
- H2 cannot bind; H7 has no trigger.
- My own: no production-certification concurrency, no fixed-price development, no rate change without stable KPIs, no blame on the FAA, and no attribution to suppliers or Airbus.

PREMIUMS (H8)
- fps hold: $0.35B in S1 and S3, $0.34B in S2, as a doctrine premium against the cap.
- Re-engine hold: logged as a Board hold, separately. It gives up $0.45B in S1 and S3 and saves $0.60B in S2.
- At plan level, against the best plan in S1: $0.65B.
- All inside $2B. The objective premium is $0.

RECORD OR DOCTRINE
- My record drove the four questions, doing less, the one conservative reset and debt first.
- Inference or doctrine drove:
  - the $1B ε threshold;
  - Malave's 20% read of an A350 Re-engine;
  - the H4 pairing;
  - code 7 at any launch;
  - the new_site preference.
- The Board's +$1B line would force the same orders.

COST OF WAITING (information, not a reason)
- On the grid: $0.35B for the fps and $0.45B for the Re-engine in S1. There is no later round on this board.
- Unscored: a later EIS lowers the long-run split under the lead-edge rule. The 50/50 and incumbency objectives stay unmet at 20% preference, and no order this round moves a scored year (the earliest EIS is 2057).
- Building a new future is on my list [BX-1245]. On this board's demand path the case came closer every round and never cleared the line. I won't force an airplane to end a game. 'I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned' [BX-1300] was true of the market leg to the end.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave is a thin seat: one call, Low confidence. His buffer test binds under the team rule. Everything else he says is advice, and I weighed it as advice.

What I took:
- Buffer: his confirmation, and the veto on the two via-Embraer hold rows (-3.14 and -3.11).
- Why S3 equals S1: slots bind, so Delay Tactics move preference, not deliveries.
- His correction of my overrun arithmetic, which was the most useful finding in either memo. The marginal penalty (0.59 a dollar, not 0.32) cuts the break-even to about $6.4B all in, 10.6% of the bill, not my $10.4B or the Board's 13-17%. I adopted it.
- His two slip cases. Case A ($4.9B, +0.06) and case B ($14.7B, -0.35) straddle the break-even. I lean to case B as the planning case for a clean sheet, because the $4.9B bought only one year on a derivative.
- His market-or-timing answer: the sign of the item rests on the board's booking at EIS, and the brief prints only one of the fps's 20 market years. I read that as lower confidence, not as a reason.
- His 20% A350 Re-engine read (doctrine, range 15-25%).
- His correction that the stress peaks are development-year peaks, not scored failures.
- Fundable: pass. Cancel: nothing to cancel.
- His classification of the premiums (fps hold as doctrine, Re-engine hold as a Board hold).

His balance-sheet tie-break is advice. It agrees with my doing-less tie-break, so it changed nothing. He also concedes the printed Meet-and-beat test favours the 10-year at Renton by $0.34B, and I report that plainly.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope is a thin seat: Very low airplane-business evidence, and the seat runs on operations doctrine. Her KPI veto binds only on a Rate Increase under a live problem, and it had no object this round. I weighed the rest as readiness evidence.

What I took:
- KPI gate clean, with her candid note that the brief carries no KPI readings. I asked for them to go to the Board.
- The MAX at 684 a year for three years, with 1,368 LEAP-1B engines a year demonstrated in deliveries but to be re-confirmed annually.
- One development can sit beside a stable line.
- Her H4 results: 0 years on the submitted plan; 2 for a 10-year pair, 3-4 on a derivative slip; 5 for a 7-year pair, a breach.
- No production-certification concurrency, read sensibly as the production system designed with the airplane and each rate break proven before it is taken.
- new_site over Renton. She estimates the +0.03 already gives up about $0.07B of MAX deliveries against a ~$0.10B capex saving. It also risks up to 504 MAX deliveries a year if Renton converts early, and the board does not price that.
- Via Embraer fails her IP test.

Most weight went to two findings:
- Her 2045 test now passes: the 10-year survives a 2% overrun and +3 years at +0.22, so operations would not stand in the way of a lone 10-year.
- Our own preference demand (446-460 a year) sits below our 684 slots. The fps's market leg is mostly overflow demand from the rival's flexible customers after 2060.

The first says Boeing is ready. The second says the market leg is lower-confidence than +0.35 suggests. She says plainly that the business case is not her seat.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1, rivals hold.

From the bulletin:
- Airbus's widebody focus 'stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve'.
- Rolls-Royce: 'No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table', and 'No widebody programme is launched' (Trent work inside a flat R&D envelope).
- Airbus's capital is going into its narrowbody capacity step.
- No A350 Re-engine has been launched in twenty years of play.

I take Malave's read of an A350 Re-engine at about 20% (range 15-25%; doctrine, not his record) as S2's weight. S3 (Delay Tactics) equals S1 on every row, because slots bind.

The probability-weighted value of the submitted plan is about -1.03 (0.8 x -1.01 + 0.2 x -1.10).
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario:
fps launch_10yr at Renton + 787 Re-engine: S1 -0.36, which is +0.65 against Do Nothing.

Not chosen:
- It is inside ε.
- Its S2 is -1.50, which is -0.40 against Do Nothing.
- The Re-engine item beside the fps is only +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30.
- H4 sits at its 2-year limit with no slack, and the overlap becomes 4 years on the derivative prior.
- The Board would veto both items on its +$1B business-case line.

The best Solo fps row is the 10-year at Renton, which also has the highest worst column: -0.66 / -0.76 / -0.66, or +0.35 / +0.34 / +0.35 against Do Nothing.
decision.premium_reason:
The doctrine premium against the cap is $0.35B, for the fps hold.
- It gives up $0.35B in S1 and S3 and $0.34B in S2 against the 10-year at Renton.
- My own ε rule and doing-less tie-break [BX-1239] choose it before the Board's line applies, and so does Malave's balance-sheet tie-break. It is counted once.
- The Board-hold log notes that the Board's +$1B line would force it too.

The Board hold, logged separately, is the 787 Re-engine hold.
- It gives up $0.45B in S1 and S3 when the Re-engine is alone, or $0.30B when it sits beside the fps.
- It saves $0.60B in S2.
- Weighted, it is worth +$0.24B at a 20% read and +$0.19B at 25%.

At plan level, Do Nothing gives up $0.65B against the best grid plan in S1 (the 10-year at Renton + Re-engine, -0.36). In S2 it gives up $0.34B against the best plan there (the 10-year at Renton, -0.76).

Even counted entirely as soft, the total is $0.65B at plan level or $0.80B as a sum, inside the $2B cap. The objective premium is $0.

What breaks these numbers:
- An A350 Re-engine takes Do Nothing to -1.10.
- The fps-hold premium turns into a saving if the launch would have slipped at an all-in cost above about $6.4B.
decision.objective_note:
The PD-briefing objective is the company's mission, not on my own ranked list, and it never changes the payoff.

Status in 2050 on every plan:
- 50/50 split and incumbency: not met. Preference share is 20% and delivered share 36.3%.
- Balance-sheet lines: met. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 in base and stress.
- Enabler, three narrowbody engine makers in the market: met.
- Enabler, dual engine sources on our narrowbody: not met. The MAX flies CFM only.

No order this round can move a scored year: the earliest fps EIS is 2057, and every plan shows one engine source in 2050. The objective premium is therefore $0.

Beyond the board, the code-7 requirement (CFM plus the Joint Venture) stays our public plan for two sources at launch.
decision.predictions:
- Rivals hold (S1, about 80%). Airbus does not launch an A350 Re-engine this round (about 20% that it does).
- Airbus may prepare or take its gated narrowbody capacity step. It does not change our orders.
- Boeing's realized ΔPV: -1.01 in S1, -1.10 in S2 (about -1.03 weighted).
- The MAX holds 684 a year through 2060. Delivered share stays 36.3% and preference share 20%, while demand stays above both makers' slots (2,300 at its 2053 peak, 2,129 in 2060).
- Net debt stays $0 in base and stress through 2060.
- Objectives as in the brief:
  - balance-sheet lines met;
  - three engine makers met;
  - 50/50, incumbency and dual-source not met.
- No new engine-maker launches, since nobody selects them. CFM's RISE stays a technology programme.
- The Board confirms with no Board item, since every order is the default.
- Beyond this board, the 10-year Solo fps with code 7 remains the standing plan, waiting for a market case that clears the line.

ops.note:
I concur. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes. The KPI, supplier and strain checks below come from operations doctrine. The delivery, IP and cash points apply my 2022 record by inference.

First and foremost, the KPI gate (doctrine, my seat). The orders are fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold and fps_site new_site, which match my recommended orders on every field. The brief's menu offers rate_737 hold only (round4.md, line 301), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. My veto has no object and no ground, so I do not invoke it.

Second, hard rules (doctrine). There is no breach. H4 is 0 years and $0 of strain. H5 has nothing launched to cancel. H6 has no rate order.

Third, what the CEO says publicly against what operations can show. "Held full rate for three years" matches the record: 684 a year since 2047, on 1,368 LEAP-1B engines a year. The 57-a-month line is called a ceiling, not a Rate Increase, and it stays KPI-gated with the FAA [B-2236, B-2221]. I accept the ask to put the six FAA-agreed KPIs in front of the Board each quarter. That cures the caveat I raised: today "stable" rests on the absence of a reported problem, not on KPI data.

Fourth, a correction for the Board's file (inference). Malave's marginal-penalty figure of about 0.59 a dollar cuts the 10-year's overrun break-even to about $6.4B, 10.6% of the bill. My memo said $7.9-10.4B. I accept his figure. A 2% overrun still passes. On a +3-year slip the item holds only at one 777X-size reset. That changes the business case, which is not my seat. It does not change my readiness results.

And finally, the standing plan is the one operations can deliver: the 10-year Solo fps with code 7, durability proven before EIS, the type certificate before rate, a supplier gate at each rate break, new_site, and the five-step bridge plan on the shelf for Renton. Under H4, any future Re-engine and fps are decided together as one pair. I concur, with no veto and no red line [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308, B-0341, BX-1331].

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s and is now in production at its planned rate. Production stays disciplined and controlled. Every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family has completed an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers, and we support Rolls-Royce's work on time on wing for the Trent fleet. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. We fund our programmes from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION: the company default on every lever, on our own clock, at the final gate.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (in service since 2037, engine code fixed), `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`, `a320_plan: alt`.
- Every field is at its default, so there are no Board items and no override. The game's single override ends the game unspent, as the Board asked.
- The A350 Re-engine got a full hearing at this last gate and is not tabled. The tests that stopped it are named below and in `board_response`. Holding closes it for this game, and I record that as a strategic choice.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: no order or public line contradicts them (Wagner, ask 7). No safety, quality, supply-crunch, engine-slip or inject event is on the record [AX-0073, AX-0081].
2. Ramp: NGSA has delivered 1,200 a year (100 a month) since 2047, and the A320neo transition is complete. Our own factory ceiling binds, not preference: delivered share is 63.7% against 80% preference, and the waiting backlog is 616 in 2050 and 2,297 in 2060. I keep the capacity step prepared, because Wagner's gate 2 is not met. Neither engine source has committed capacity for our extra volumes.
3. Airbus of the 2030s and beyond: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the technology-ready year, with no slip. The widebody question was the one strategic lever left. It does not clear our own launch bar.
4. Board: the default is never vetoed. A Re-engine tabled against an unresolved ExCo soft veto would be vetoed.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted as red lines or pillar failures (never traded for PV):
- Every Delay Tactics row. fps is not on the public record and this is the last round, so under rule 4 any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
- One move on the hold row: -7.80 / -0.13 / -0.13 / -0.15 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13. Both moves: -7.98 / -0.26 / -0.26 / -0.30 / -0.26 / -7.99 / -0.27. On the Re-engine row: -7.81 for one move and -8.00 for both.
- No column gains, even where fps launches, because our 1,200-a-year ceiling binds.
- `both` is two moves. `bottleneck` and `both` fail integrity. `poaching` on the hold row breaks rule 5. The team's stricter condition stays in force, and I record no set-aside.

Tested:
- Default:
  - passes every Toepfer test: peak cash $0.0B against $5.2B; worst column S7 at +12.85; net cash built, with no raise and no cut;
  - passes every Wagner test: NGSA at rate, no quality finding, 2 sources and 3 makers, no crunch, ramp shield, integrity of the other moves.
- `rea350: launch` passes:
  - peak cash: $1.0B a year over 2050-54, leaving $4.2B of headroom;
  - rule 6: one launch, zero overlap, $0 strain;
  - the teams.md robustness form: worst column S7 at +12.44;
  - the Board's -$2B downside;
  - all of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp-shield, supply-crunch, engineering-capacity and absorption tests. Absorption passes on the proxy only, because the record is silent.
- It FAILS Toepfer's robustness test, as written in rounds 2 and 3 and applied unchanged. The item is +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / -0.41 / -0.41: negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and short of $1B in every column and on every weighting. He marks the soft veto binding and finds no reason on the record to read a final round differently. I agree: a sealed last round cannot rule out S6/S7.
- It also fails the company's A350 launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), in every column.
- Wagner's widebody-engine finding is a supply flag, not a veto. Rolls-Royce gives "No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table", and UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5. With no later round, the board's 2055 date would not be an operating date. He recommends hold on that flag and on the $1B bar.

Survivor: the default only.

Doctrine check, which gives the same answer on its own:
- Even had Toepfer's test passed, the Re-engine is within $1B of the default on every weighting: +0.43 on my weights, +0.48 on round-2 weights, +0.30 equal-weighted, +0.58 at best. So the doctrine-default rule takes the default.
- Both tie-breaks favour hold: the later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2050) and fewer Board items (0, against 1 Qualified Majority item).

Override: not available, and not sought.
- The margin over the best passing option is +0.43 expected and +0.58 at best, under $1B.
- On a Qualified Majority item it is also behind in the worst column (-0.41).
- The Board would veto a Re-engine carried by an override or tabled against an unresolved objection.

WHAT HOLD COSTS, SAID PLAINLY
- About $0.43B on my weights, and $0.58B in S1-S5. In S6/S7 hold is $0.41B better.
- The rule allows that cost. It is not a premium.
- Nothing on the record prices a later launch, so hold closes the A350 Re-engine for this game.
- The derivatives-first instinct [AX-0082] argued for a launch, and the Board would have approved it if it had come cleanly. But a launch with no widebody engine committed, our own $1B bar unmet in every column and a binding CFO test is not a disciplined launch. A final round earns no last-chance premium: the doctrine's $3B premium covers only staying out after a 787 Re-engine or skipping a second Delay Tactics move.
- The item has shrunk from +0.90 in 2045 to +0.58 now. I take the Board's point that a later gate would not have helped.

SCENARIO TABLE (weight; default row; Re-engine row, not tabled)
- S1, Boeing holds, 35%: +13.71; +14.29
- S2, 10-year fps, 30%: +12.88; +13.46
- S3, 10-year fps at Renton, 5%: +12.88; +13.46
- S4, 7-year fps, 5%: +12.88; +13.46
- S5, fps via Embraer, 10%: +12.88; +13.46
- S6, 787 Re-engine, 10%: +13.68; +13.27
- S7, 10-year fps + 787 Re-engine (worst plausible), 5%: +12.85; +12.44

Weighted, the default is +13.25 (+13.11 equal-weighted) and the Re-engine row +13.68. S6+S7 carry 15%, against the Re-engine's break-even of about 59%.

BOARD GATE
There are no Board items. For the record, the default row:
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass on peak cash ($0.0B against $5.2B), robustness (worst S7 +12.85) and net cash ($61-94B at end-2050, proxy), with no raise and no cut.
- Wagner: pass on NGSA at rate, quality, 2 sources and 3 makers, no crunch, ramp shield and integrity.
- Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +13.68 / +12.85.

Not tabled, `rea350: launch` (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn):
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: peak cash pass; robustness FAIL, a binding soft veto.
- Wagner: pass, with a non-binding engine-supply flag, and he recommends hold.
- Item ΔPV against hold: +0.58 x5 / -0.41 x2.
- Stopped by Toepfer's robustness test and the company's $1B launch test.

FLAGS I CARRY
- Joint Venture durability and full-life parts: a watch item on the product-safety review, with CFM as a thin backstop.
- The capacity step: prepared, not committed. It needs a phased capex line, both engine sources committed and the Ethics Committee's written confirmation.
- The waiting backlog grows as our ceiling binds.
- Rule 3: no 787 Re-engine is on the record before our order.

frame.situation:
BOEING (public record)
- Boeing held for the third time: no fps and no 787 Re-engine. fps is still not on the public record.
- Its 2045 words: "Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready. The market is getting there, but it hasn't got there." It gives no date, works in stages, designs the production system together with the airplane, and wants "a conservative plan with headroom".
- It updated the fps engine requirement: a choice of two sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture (code 7), with durability proven before entry into service. These are the same two sources as NGSA's.
- On the 787: "We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year." Charleston is capacity growth for 787 rates in the teens, not a new programme.
- The 737 MAX returns to 57 a month, gated on KPIs and agreed with the FAA. Boeing says this is "not a Rate Increase".
- If fps launches now, a 7-year fps enters service in 2057 and a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2060. That is 20 to 23 years after NGSA.

ENGINES
- NGSA flies CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine: 2 sources from 3 makers.
- The Joint Venture engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Rolls-Royce content comes only on a later block, after its own durability proof and full life on every life-limited part.
- P&W allocates fleet spares and MRO material ahead of NGSA OE when they compete for parts, and says it will tell us early where it falls short.
- CFM puts LEAP durability kits and deliveries first. "On capacity, we work with both airframers."
- Widebody: Rolls-Royce says "No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table". Its answer is time-on-wing work on the Trent fleet inside a flat R&D envelope, with no widebody programme launched. UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5. Widebody engine shares have been CFM/GE 44.8% and Rolls-Royce 55.2% since 2042.
- Observed narrowbody engine shares in 2049: CFM 53.5%, P&W 23.3%, RR 23.3%.

OUR POSITION (brief)
- If nobody moves: +13.71 $B, yield 109.14%.
- Components: narrowbody operating profit +61.59, programme investment -15.23, debt penalty -0.53, supply and demand -31.78, Alt plan cost -0.32.
- Operating profit is $18.0B a year from 2046, against $7.6B in the status quo.
- NGSA delivers 1,200 a year (100 a month). The A320 Alt plan ran out by 2047.
- Our own factory ceiling binds. Delivered share is 63.7% against 80% preference, and the waiting backlog grows from 616 in 2050 to 1,384 in 2053 and 2,297 in 2060. That is why the fps columns cost us only $0.83B.
- No public events this round. No supply crunch, engine slip, quality event or inject is reported.
- Nothing is in development. NGSA spend ended in 2036, and no Board item has gone up since round 1. The game's single override is unspent.

- All four tests are met: worst preference year 72.0% (2040), and 80% in 2045 and 2050; the A320 family held 60% before NGSA entered service; 2 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Every grid row gives 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050, so no order this round moves the objective.

BOARD GUIDANCE (carried in)
- It would approve `rea350: launch` as a Qualified Majority item on three conditions: Lars's safety, quality, ramp-shield and supply-crunch tests pass; no ExCo soft veto is left unresolved; and any capacity step taken in the same round passes his supply and engineering-capacity test alongside it.

  - any Delay Tactics value;
  - a Re-engine carried by an override, tabled against an ExCo objection that was neither respected nor overridden, or tabled with a capacity step Lars fails;
  - any override short of $1B, or of Lars's safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch results;
  - any equity raise or dividend cut.
