The charge is shown beside the adjusted figure, not netted. The hold row books no charge.

tests.name: Final round: is a later launch priced, and what does hold cost? CEO ask 6
tests.threshold: Use only numbers from the brief
tests.numbers: Nothing on the record prices a later launch. 2050 is the last decision year, and the grid assumes nobody moves after this round. Hold therefore closes the A350 Re-engine for this game. The cost of hold on the grid: $0.43B on the CEO's refreshed and round-3 weights, $0.48B on his round-2 weights, $0.30B equal-weighted and $0.58B at best (S1-S5). In S6/S7 hold is $0.41B better. Nothing on the record says a later gate would have helped: the item fell from +0.90 in 2045 to +0.58.

tests.name: Board downside (the Board's own test, shown for its cash and risk read)
tests.threshold: No Board item loses more than $2B in any plausible column
tests.numbers: The Re-engine item's worst column is -0.41 (S6/S7), inside -$2B. This is the Board's test, not mine. Passing it does not clear my robustness test, and the Board's approval condition (no ExCo soft veto left unresolved) is not met while my veto stands.

tests.name: Board cash lines (the Board's form: five pillars, CFO test, Lars's test, grid ΔPV), CEO ask 8
tests.threshold: Every order that differs from the default goes to the Board with its S1-S7 row, the default row and the peak-year arithmetic [AX-0026, AG-0049]
tests.numbers: DEFAULT ROW (no Board items). Five pillars: pass. CFO: peak cash pass ($0.0B new programme spend against $5.2B); robustness pass (worst S7 +12.85); net cash $61-94B at end-2050 (proxy); no raise, no cut, payout fundable; buybacks a reserved matter. Lars: his result. Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +13.68 / +12.85; +13.25 on the CEO's weights, +13.11 equal. RE-ENGINE ITEM, if tabled (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn). Five pillars: no breach on my side. CFO: peak cash pass ($1.0B a year over 2050-54, $4.2B headroom, zero overlap, $0 strain). Robustness FAIL: a binding soft veto, with the item at +0.58 x5 / -0.41 x2 (+0.43 CEO, +0.30 equal), negative in S6/S7 and short of $1B. The company's $1B launch test fails; the teams.md form passes (worst S7 +12.44); the Board's -$2B downside passes. Not overridable: under $1B, and behind in the worst column. $5B charge at EIS 2055: about $13.0B reported against $18.0B underlying. Net cash $1.0B lower at end-2050. Lars: his result. Grid ΔPV: +14.29 / +13.46 / +13.46 / +13.46 / +13.46 / +13.27 / +12.44.

vetoes.plan: `rea350: launch` (NGSA hold, Alt plan, no Delay Tactics): the CEO's test case
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test (soft veto). Against the best passing option (hold) the item is +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / -0.41 / -0.41: +0.43 on the CEO's refreshed and round-3 weights, +0.48 on his round-2 weights, +0.30 equal-weighted. It turns negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and misses $1B in every column and on every weighting. The company's $1B launch test (profile §6) also fails in every column. Peak cash passes ($1.0B a year against $5.2B), so cash is not the ground. Grid margin over the best passing option: +0.43 expected and +0.58 at best, below the $1B an override needs, and on this Qualified Majority item the plan is also behind in the worst column (-0.41). I see no override that could carry it. Whether to override is the CEO's call. The Board's guidance says it would veto a Re-engine carried by an override or tabled against an unresolved ExCo objection.

vetoes.plan: Any `delay_tactics` value (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`) on the hold row or the Re-engine row
vetoes.ground: Company red lines, not overridable. (1) Rule 4: fps is not on the public record, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine (PV about $7.62B at the 2050 order year): -7.80 to -7.81 in S1/S6 for one move and -7.98 to -8.00 for both. (2) `both` is a second move. (3) Rule 5: on the hold row nothing is in development, so `poaching` has no programme to serve. (4) Integrity pillar: I could not defend `bottleneck` or `both` to the Audit Committee. No value gains in any column (best -0.13), so no $1B case exists, and the Board vetoes every value.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Re-engine: any one of three. (1) A grid that puts the item at least $1B over hold in the expected column, with no negative plausible column. (2) S6/S7 ruled out on the public record before our order. The item would then be positive in every remaining column and pass my robustness test, and taking it below $1B would be the CEO's doctrine call. A sealed final round cannot give us either. (3) A Board decision. Peak cash would stop the Re-engine only if programme spend went above the $5.2B line, for example a capacity step committed alongside it with capex above the $4.2B of headroom. Capacity step: I move from 'keep prepared' only when there is a phased capex figure as its own line, Lars's gates are met on the record (both engine sources committed for our own volumes, no open quality finding, no crunch) and the Ethics Committee has confirmed in writing. Net cash: my verdict would change only if actual FCF ran far below my proxy of 0.69 x operating profit. Delay Tactics: nothing on this board. No value gains in any column, fps is not public, and the Board vetoes all of them.
cfo.memo:
2050 gate, for the Audit Committee.

Recommendation: the company default on every lever. A350 Re-engine on hold, no Delay Tactics, the Alt plan as listed, NGSA in service (engine code fixed; on engines I defer to Lars). No Board items; the override ends the game unspent.

Peak cash: pass on both rows. The Re-engine is $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2050-54, zero overlap, $0 strain: $4.2B inside one year's FCF (EUR 4,753m at $1.10 = $5.2B). Cash does not stop it.

Robustness: fail on the Re-engine item. Against hold it is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6/S7: +0.43 on the CEO's weights, +0.30 equal-weighted. Negative in plausible columns and short of $1B in every one, so my soft veto is binding, as in 2045. The final round gives no reason on the record to read it differently. No override can carry it: under $1B, and behind in the worst column. The company's $1B launch test also fails.

Capacity step: no capex figure on the record, so I cannot test it. Keep it prepared and gated. Before any commitment: a phased figure as its own line, Lars's gates, the Ethics Committee's written confirmation; above EUR 300m, a Board item.

Net cash (proxy): $61-94B at end-2050, $1.0B lower with a launch. No raise, no cut, no change to returns.

A launch books $5B at EIS 2055: about $13.0B reported against $18.0B underlying.

Hold closes the Re-engine for this game, at $0.43B expected. Delay Tactics: deleted.

tests.name: NGSA at rate, quality and product safety; rule 1 (ask 1)
tests.threshold: NGSA in service at or after 2035 (rule 1). It holds a disciplined and controlled rate with no open quality finding, and stays on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
tests.numbers:
- EIS 2037, two years after the 2035 floor.
- Delivered: 1,219 in 2045, then 1,200 a year (100 a month) from 2046-47 to 2060 on every grid row. The A320 Alt plan ran out by 2047 as planned.
- The brief reports no quality finding, quality event, supply crunch, engine slip or inject.
- Confirmed: NGSA stays on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review, with the Joint Venture durability and full-life-parts watch and CFM as the backstop.
- The record holds proxies, not plant data: no KPI, escape or concession figures. 'No open quality finding' means none is reported, not that one has been measured.

tests.name: NGSA engine supply, the enabler and Joint Venture durability (ask 2)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second source on NGSA, with three narrowbody engine makers in 2050. No engine or block enters service before durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life
tests.numbers:
- Fitted sources: CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one source. That gives 2 sources from 3 makers in 2050 on every grid row and in every column. The engine code is fixed (None).
- Engine mix (proxy, derived from the observed 2049 shares, CFM 53.5% / P&W 23.3% / RR 23.3% of 3,768 narrowbody engines, with the 737 MAX's 1,368 all on CFM): the Joint Venture supplies about 1,756 of our 2,400 NGSA engines a year (73%) and CFM about 648 (27%).
- Joint Venture durability and full-life parts: the record holds no in-service durability or life-limited-part data. P&W says it will report durability 'as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them'. The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Rolls-Royce content comes only on a later block, after its own durability proof with every life-limited part at full life, and no date is given for that block.
- P&W puts fleet spares and MRO material ahead of NGSA OE, and CFM puts LEAP durability kits and deliveries first. Classification: watch items, not a supply crunch and not an engine slip. Neither is reported as a shortfall, and NGSA delivers 1,200 a year through 2060 on the board. P&W says it will tell us early where it falls short.
- CFM is the backstop, but a thin one: at about 27% of our volume (proxy) it could not cover a Joint Venture shortfall at once.

tests.name: Supply crunch (binding, never overridden)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch: no new concurrency
tests.numbers:
- No crunch is reported and the board has no injects, so the test is not triggered for the default or the A350 Re-engine.
- The waiting backlog (616 in 2050, 1,384 in 2053, 2,297 in 2060) and the 63.7% delivered share against 80% preference come from our own factory ceiling of 100 a month, not from a supplier crunch.
- The two engine makers' allocation rules (P&W spares first, CFM LEAP kits first) are watch items, not a crunch.

tests.name: A350 Re-engine: safety and quality (ask 3a)
tests.threshold: No order or public line that contradicts safety or quality
tests.numbers:
- No A350, A350F or NGSA quality or safety event is on the record.
- `rea350: launch` contradicts neither pillar on its own, provided the public line promises no engine and no date. Durability must be proven before entry into service.
- Classification: safety and quality tests, passed.

tests.name: Ramp shield (A320 and NGSA; ask 3a)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open ramp commitment
tests.numbers:
- No A320 ramp commitment is open: the end-2027 date is long past, and the Alt plan ran out by 2047.
- The NGSA ramp is complete at 100 a month since 2047.
- The Re-engine's $1.0B a year over 2050-54 buys widebody work and takes no narrowbody slots, no narrowbody engines and no wing capacity.
- Passes for the default and for the Re-engine. Classification: ramp-shield test, passed.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6 (ask 3b)
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round
tests.numbers:
- NGSA development ran 2030-37. A Re-engine launched in 2050 develops over 2050-55.
- Overlap: 0 years. Strain: $0. One launch, so rule 6 is met.
- It does not compete with NGSA at 100 a month: it is widebody work on a separate engine chain (Trent XWB today, UltraFan WB only if launched), with no narrowbody slots.
- The shared constraint is skilled engineering and industrial talent [A-0366, A-0485, A-0423]. That binds only if a capacity step runs at the same time (see the capacity test).
- Classification: engineering-capacity test, passed.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 work-package absorption (ask 3c)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: not in round 1 (2030); round 2 (2035) at the earliest
tests.numbers:
- Proxy: 2050 is three rounds after the earliest round the proxy allows, and 15 years after the company's 2033-35 window.
- On the record: still silent. No bulletin or brief reports A350F or Spirit A350 status. Widebody deliveries have been flat at 70 a year (41.2% share) from 2026 to 2049, with no widebody quality or supply event.
- At the last gate, absorption can never be shown complete on the record. The silence gives me no concrete production constraint, and a veto of mine must name one.
- Classification: production-readiness test, passed on the proxy only.

tests.name: Widebody engine committed in time (ask 3d). Classification: supply flag, not a safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch test, and not a soft veto
tests.threshold: A widebody engine committed on the record and ready by the Re-engine's entry into service (supply certainty)
tests.numbers:
- The A350 flies the Trent XWB. No widebody engine for a Re-engine is launched, and Rolls-Royce has launched no widebody programme.
- Rolls-Royce: 'No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table.' UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5.
- If Rolls-Royce launches in this sealed round, the engine is ready in 2056, against the board's 2055. If it does not, no widebody engine reaches the record before the game ends.
- On the board, the A350 Re-engine enters service 5 years after launch whatever the engine, so the grid's +0.58 assumes 2055. The operating date is set by the engine and is later. That gap is unpriced (inference).
- Because the engine never changes the grid, no $1B override could answer an engine objection, which is why it is a flag and not a veto.
- Do my tabling conditions resolve it? They respect it, but they do not resolve it in substance. A public invitation on standard terms, durability before entry into service and a window that follows the engine keep the public line honest, so the flag is not an unresolved objection. They cannot bring an engine onto the record in a final round.
- Result: not met. It binds nothing.

tests.name: Company A350 launch bar (profile §6): at least $1B over Do Nothing. Cited, not owned: the CEO's doctrine and the CFO's robustness test, not an operating-head soft veto
tests.threshold: Launch the A350 Re-engine only on at least $1B over Do Nothing in the grid
tests.numbers:
- Item against hold: +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / -0.41 / -0.41.
- +0.43 on the CEO's refreshed weights (0.432 on my check).
- Break-even: S6+S7 together at about 59% (0.58 / 0.99 = 0.586), against 15% on his weights.
- No column reaches $1B. My 'grid gain of at least $1B' trigger for changing my mind is not met.

tests.name: Capacity step beyond 100 a month: my gates (ask 4; unpriced other move)
tests.threshold: Take the step only when all three gates are met: (1) NGSA holds rate on its KPIs with no open quality finding; (2) both engine sources commit capacity for our own extra volumes, and the wing, titanium and forgings are sized; (3) no supply crunch is reported
tests.numbers:
- Gate 1: met on the proxy. 100 a month since 2047, and no finding reported.
- Gate 2: not met. Neither source has committed. CFM puts LEAP durability kits first. P&W puts fleet spares and MRO material ahead of NGSA OE, and its source carries about 73% of our NGSA engines (proxy). Boeing's fps now names the same two sources. The record holds no measurement of engine, wing, titanium or forging capacity above 2,400 engines a year.
- Gate 3: met. No crunch is reported.
- Need: the waiting backlog is 616 (2050), 1,384 (2053) and 2,297 (2060), with 63.7% delivered against 80% preference.
- Recommendation: keep it prepared and gated. A 'commit, gated' line adds a public expectation we cannot back with engines, which hurts the credibility of our rate. I do not veto it if the gates are written as conditions precedent, no volumes or capex are released, and no rate number is published.
- With a Re-engine: the Re-engine alone passes. A capacity step taken now alongside it fails my supply test on gate 2, so the pair fails. With the step kept prepared, the pair passes.
- Capex: no figure on the record. It is Thomas's line against the $5.2B line, and it goes to the Board above EUR 300m.

tests.name: Delay Tactics: rules 4 and 5 and the integrity pillar (ask 5)
tests.threshold: At most one move per game, only after fps is public and before its EIS. `both` counts as two. `poaching` only with an Airbus programme in development. `bottleneck` and `both` never (integrity)
tests.numbers:
- fps is not on the public record and this is the last round, so any move is naked and exposed to the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
- Hold row, one move: -7.80 / -0.13 / -0.13 / -0.15 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13. Both moves: -7.98 / -0.26 / -0.26 / -0.30 / -0.26 / -7.99 / -0.27.
- Re-engine row, one move: -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.16 / -0.14 / -7.81 / -0.14. Both moves: -8.00 / -0.28 / -0.28 / -0.32 / -0.28 / -8.00 / -0.28.
- No column gains, because our 1,200-a-year ceiling binds.
- On the hold row nothing is in development, so `poaching` also breaks rule 5.
- `bottleneck` and `both` breach integrity. My verdict stands.

tests.name: Integrity of the other moves (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Secure our own supply for our own production, never a claim on a rival's capacity. Recruit from our own pipeline, never by targeting a rival's team
tests.numbers:
- Capacity talks with CFM and the Joint Venture as published: our own extra volumes only, no exclusivity, and nothing drawn from any rival's allocation. That includes Boeing's LEAP-1B line and anything either source sets aside for Boeing's fps, which now names the same two sources. None can be read as `bottleneck`.
- Current agreements cover our own NGSA volumes only.
- Skills come from apprenticeships, graduates and universities in Europe, with no targeted hiring, so nothing can be read as `poaching`.
- I confirm the terms as published on the record. I hold no contract data. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee's written confirmation comes before any capacity step.

tests.name: Five pillars and the public statement (ask 7)
tests.threshold: No order or public line that contradicts safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security
tests.numbers:
- The default orders breach no pillar, and `rea350: launch` alone breaches none.
- Conditions on the public line:
  1. No widebody engine promised before one is committed.
  2. No Re-engine EIS date. If tabled, give a window that follows the engine and is gated on durability.
  3. No rate number (100 a month stays internal) and no date for the capacity step, only a gate.
  4. No reference to Delay Tactics.
  5. Describe the engines accurately: CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, two sources from three makers. The Joint Venture engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration, so do not imply Rolls-Royce content is in service.
  6. On the widebody line: Rolls-Royce's public time-on-wing work names the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000. Say 'time on wing for the Trent fleet', and do not claim a Trent XWB programme Rolls-Royce has not announced.
  7. 'Reaching its planned rate' becomes 'at its planned rate', with no number.

tests.name: Rule 3 (no A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine once a 787 Re-engine is on the record before our order
tests.numbers:
- Not triggered. Boeing: 'We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year.' Charleston is capacity growth.
- If Boeing launches one in this sealed round (S6/S7), both enter service in 2055 and the item is -0.41.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If reported: re-time, never cancel
tests.numbers: None is reported. NGSA has been in service since 2037. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, CFM ducted since 2041 and CFM-Embraer since 2042.

tests.name: Engine code recommendation
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker
tests.numbers: The code is fixed (None) with NGSA in service. Fitted: CFM plus the Joint Venture, 2 sources and 3 makers, on every row.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: The 737 returns to its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated with the FAA, and Boeing says this is 'not a Rate Increase'. None of our programmes changes.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics value (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`), on the hold row or the Re-engine row
vetoes.ground:
- Company red line, rule 4: fps is not public in the final round, so any move is naked and exposed to the $48.32B fine.
- `both` counts as two moves.
- On the hold row, `poaching` also breaks rule 5, because nothing is in development.
- `bottleneck` and `both` breach the integrity pillar.
- Margin against the best passing option: one move is -7.80 in S1/S6 on the hold row (-7.81 on the Re-engine row) and -0.13 to -0.16 elsewhere. Both moves are -7.98 / -7.99 (-8.00). No column gains.
- This is a red line and a pillar, so no override is possible.

vetoes.plan: Taking the capacity step beyond 100 a month in 2050, alone or alongside an A350 Re-engine. That means releasing capex or committing volumes before both engine sources commit
vetoes.ground:
- Failed supply and production-readiness test, gate 2: neither engine source has committed capacity for our extra volumes.
- CFM puts LEAP durability kits first. P&W puts spares and MRO ahead of NGSA OE, and its Joint Venture carries about 73% of our NGSA engines (proxy).
- The move is unpriced, so it has no grid margin, and no $1B override can be shown.
- If tabled with a Re-engine, the Board vetoes the pair.
- 'Keep prepared and gated' passes. 'Commit, gated' is not vetoed if the gates are conditions precedent, no capex or volumes are released, and no rate number is published.

vetoes.plan: `rea350: launch` in 2050 (Alt plan, no Delay Tactics)

ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence). Nothing of mine is on record, so I apply company doctrine.

NGSA: 1,200 a year, 100 a month, since 2047. No quality finding, crunch or engine slip is reported; these are proxies, not plant data. NGSA stays on the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review. Engines: CFM plus the Joint Venture, 2 sources and 3 makers on every row. On the observed 2049 shares, the Joint Venture carries about 73% of our NGSA engines and CFM about 27% (proxy). P&W puts spares ahead of our OE, and CFM puts LEAP kits first. Watch items, not a crunch, but CFM is a thin backstop.

A350 Re-engine: safety, quality, ramp shield, supply crunch and engineering capacity (zero overlap, $0 strain, one launch) pass. Absorption passes on the proxy; the record is silent. No soft veto, nothing to override.

The engine stays a supply flag. Rolls-Royce waits for a Re-engine on the table and needs six years: 2056 at best against the board's 2055, and with no later round perhaps never on the record. I recommend hold: no engine committed, and +0.58 at best, -0.41 in S6/S7, short of the company's $1B bar. If you table it with my conditions (open engine invitation on standard terms, durability before entry into service, a window that follows the engine), I concur.

Capacity beyond 100 a month: keep it prepared. Gate two fails: neither source has committed. Not alongside a Re-engine.

Binding: any Delay Tactics.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for NGSA at rate
other_moves.detail:
This continues the programme from earlier rounds, now for NGSA in steady production.
- The NGSA wing stays in-house.
- Aerostructures come through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites.
- Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts.
- The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist continues.
It serves our own production only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: NGSA engine supply: CFM and the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, at our own volumes
other_moves.detail:
NGSA is fitted with CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine: two sources from three engine makers.
- The capacity agreements with both cover only our own NGSA volumes, with no exclusivity and nothing above our own production.
- We plan with each maker's published allocation rules: P&W puts fleet spares and MRO material ahead of new OE, and CFM puts LEAP durability kits first. P&W has said it will tell us early where it falls short.
- The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Prepare the next step in industrial capacity, gated on safety, quality and supply (kept prepared, not committed)
Widebody position for the 2050s: the A350 family and the A350F
other_moves.detail: On widebodies we focus on the A350 family and the A350F, kept current for our customers. We support Rolls-Royce's time-on-wing work for the Trent fleet. We claim no Trent XWB programme that Rolls-Royce has not announced, promise no widebody engine and give no Re-engine timing. The A350 Re-engine is not tabled, so no widebody-engine invitation is issued [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0302].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: We keep working with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2050s
other_moves.detail: We continue apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe. They staff NGSA production at rate, the capacity step being prepared and widebody work, all from our own pipeline. There is no targeted hiring from any rival's team [AX-0073, A-0330].

other_moves.move: NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
other_moves.detail:
The review continues in steady production, with a standing watch on the Joint Venture engine.
- Durability and full life on life-limited parts. GTF2's tested configuration is in service; Rolls-Royce content comes only on a later block, after its own durability proof.
- CFM is the backstop source. Wagner notes that at about 27% of our NGSA engines (a proxy) it is a thin one, and could not cover a Joint Venture shortfall at once.
- Any quality finding goes to the Board at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AG-0038].

other_moves.move: Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review
Audit Committee: net cash, rating and returns
other_moves.detail:
Toepfer reports on a proxy, labelled as such, with FCF at 0.688 of operating profit.
- Net cash is about $61-94B at end-2050 on hold, against FY2025's $13.4B. The policy-consistent path, with the payout scaled within 30-50%, gives about $61B.
- The A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout are fundable with no debt, no raise and no cut.
- No change to shareholder returns is proposed this round. Any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter, with these lines shown [AX-0104, AX-0102, A-0402, AG-0062].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine: held at the final gate and closed for this game, with the stopping tests recorded
other_moves.detail:
It is not tabled. Two tests stopped it:
- Toepfer's binding robustness test. The item is +0.58 in S1-S5 and -0.41 in S6/S7: negative in plausible columns and short of $1B everywhere.
- The company's own launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), met in no column.
Wagner's widebody-engine supply flag weighed but did not bind.
It is recorded as a strategic choice: holding at the last decision year closes the A350 Re-engine for this game. Any future Re-engine comes only with an engine committed and its durability proven [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0440].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since the second half of the 2030s and is now in production at its planned rate. Production stays disciplined and controlled. Every step is gated on safety, on quality and on the readiness of our supply chain, and safety and quality come before schedule. Our customers have a choice of engine, from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, and our supply agreements are matched to our own volumes. The A320neo family has completed an orderly transition to the new aircraft. Demand for the new aircraft remains strong. With our suppliers we are preparing the next step in our industrial capacity, and we will take it when our safety, quality and supply indicators say so, not before. On widebodies, our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F, which we continue to improve for our customers, and we support Rolls-Royce's work on time on wing for the Trent fleet. We continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. We fund our programmes from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the company default on every lever, on our own clock, at the final gate.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (in service since 2037, engine code fixed), `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`, `a320_plan: alt`.
- Every field is at its default, so there are no Board items and no override. The game's single override ends the game unspent, as the Board asked.
- The A350 Re-engine got a full hearing at this last gate and is not tabled. The tests that stopped it are named below and in `board_response`. Holding closes it for this game, and I record that as a strategic choice.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: no order or public line contradicts them (Wagner, ask 7). No safety, quality, supply-crunch, engine-slip or inject event is on the record [AX-0073, AX-0081].
2. Ramp: NGSA has delivered 1,200 a year (100 a month) since 2047, and the A320neo transition is complete. Our own factory ceiling binds, not preference: delivered share is 63.7% against 80% preference, and the waiting backlog is 616 in 2050 and 2,297 in 2060. I keep the capacity step prepared, because Wagner's gate 2 is not met. Neither engine source has committed capacity for our extra volumes.
3. Airbus of the 2030s and beyond: NGSA entered service in 2037, two years after the technology-ready year, with no slip. The widebody question was the one strategic lever left. It does not clear our own launch bar.
4. Board: the default is never vetoed. A Re-engine tabled against an unresolved ExCo soft veto would be vetoed.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted as red lines or pillar failures (never traded for PV):
- Every Delay Tactics row. fps is not on the public record and this is the last round, so under rule 4 any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
- One move on the hold row: -7.80 / -0.13 / -0.13 / -0.15 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13. Both moves: -7.98 / -0.26 / -0.26 / -0.30 / -0.26 / -7.99 / -0.27. On the Re-engine row: -7.81 for one move and -8.00 for both.
- No column gains, even where fps launches, because our 1,200-a-year ceiling binds.
- `both` is two moves. `bottleneck` and `both` fail integrity. `poaching` on the hold row breaks rule 5. The team's stricter condition stays in force, and I record no set-aside.

Tested:
- Default:
  - passes every Toepfer test: peak cash $0.0B against $5.2B; worst column S7 at +12.85; net cash built, with no raise and no cut;
  - passes every Wagner test: NGSA at rate, no quality finding, 2 sources and 3 makers, no crunch, ramp shield, integrity of the other moves.
- `rea350: launch` passes:
  - peak cash: $1.0B a year over 2050-54, leaving $4.2B of headroom;
  - rule 6: one launch, zero overlap, $0 strain;
  - the teams.md robustness form: worst column S7 at +12.44;
  - the Board's -$2B downside;
  - all of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp-shield, supply-crunch, engineering-capacity and absorption tests. Absorption passes on the proxy only, because the record is silent.
- It FAILS Toepfer's robustness test, as written in rounds 2 and 3 and applied unchanged. The item is +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / +0.58 / -0.41 / -0.41: negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and short of $1B in every column and on every weighting. He marks the soft veto binding and finds no reason on the record to read a final round differently. I agree: a sealed last round cannot rule out S6/S7.
- It also fails the company's A350 launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), in every column.
- Wagner's widebody-engine finding is a supply flag, not a veto. Rolls-Royce gives "No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table", and UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5. With no later round, the board's 2055 date would not be an operating date. He recommends hold on that flag and on the $1B bar.

Survivor: the default only.

Doctrine check, which gives the same answer on its own:
- Even had Toepfer's test passed, the Re-engine is within $1B of the default on every weighting: +0.43 on my weights, +0.48 on round-2 weights, +0.30 equal-weighted, +0.58 at best. So the doctrine-default rule takes the default.
- Both tie-breaks favour hold: the later capex start (none, against $1.0B a year from 2050) and fewer Board items (0, against 1 Qualified Majority item).

Override: not available, and not sought.
- The margin over the best passing option is +0.43 expected and +0.58 at best, under $1B.
- On a Qualified Majority item it is also behind in the worst column (-0.41).
- The Board would veto a Re-engine carried by an override or tabled against an unresolved objection.

WHAT HOLD COSTS, SAID PLAINLY
- About $0.43B on my weights, and $0.58B in S1-S5. In S6/S7 hold is $0.41B better.
- The rule allows that cost. It is not a premium.
- Nothing on the record prices a later launch, so hold closes the A350 Re-engine for this game.
- The derivatives-first instinct [AX-0082] argued for a launch, and the Board would have approved it if it had come cleanly. But a launch with no widebody engine committed, our own $1B bar unmet in every column and a binding CFO test is not a disciplined launch. A final round earns no last-chance premium: the doctrine's $3B premium covers only staying out after a 787 Re-engine or skipping a second Delay Tactics move.
- The item has shrunk from +0.90 in 2045 to +0.58 now. I take the Board's point that a later gate would not have helped.

SCENARIO TABLE (weight; default row; Re-engine row, not tabled)
- S1, Boeing holds, 35%: +13.71; +14.29
- S2, 10-year fps, 30%: +12.88; +13.46
- S3, 10-year fps at Renton, 5%: +12.88; +13.46
- S4, 7-year fps, 5%: +12.88; +13.46
- S5, fps via Embraer, 10%: +12.88; +13.46
- S6, 787 Re-engine, 10%: +13.68; +13.27
- S7, 10-year fps + 787 Re-engine (worst plausible), 5%: +12.85; +12.44

Weighted, the default is +13.25 (+13.11 equal-weighted) and the Re-engine row +13.68. S6+S7 carry 15%, against the Re-engine's break-even of about 59%.

BOARD GATE
There are no Board items. For the record, the default row:
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass on peak cash ($0.0B against $5.2B), robustness (worst S7 +12.85) and net cash ($61-94B at end-2050, proxy), with no raise and no cut.
- Wagner: pass on NGSA at rate, quality, 2 sources and 3 makers, no crunch, ramp shield and integrity.
- Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +12.88 / +13.68 / +12.85.

Not tabled, `rea350: launch` (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn):
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: peak cash pass; robustness FAIL, a binding soft veto.
- Wagner: pass, with a non-binding engine-supply flag, and he recommends hold.
- Item ΔPV against hold: +0.58 x5 / -0.41 x2.
- Stopped by Toepfer's robustness test and the company's $1B launch test.

FLAGS I CARRY
- Joint Venture durability and full-life parts: a watch item on the product-safety review, with CFM as a thin backstop.
- The capacity step: prepared, not committed. It needs a phased capex line, both engine sources committed and the Ethics Committee's written confirmation.
- The waiting backlog grows as our ceiling binds.
- Rule 3: no 787 Re-engine is on the record before our order.

board_response.recommendation: R4-1: The last widebody gate. Table the A350 Re-engine with its grid and cash, or record which test stopped it, that holding closes it for the game, and the widebody position for the 2050s.
board_response.response:
Held, not tabled. Two tests stopped it:
1. Toepfer's robustness test, a binding soft veto that I respect. The item is +0.58 x5 / -0.41 x2 against hold: negative in plausible columns S6/S7 and short of $1B in every column (+0.43 on my weights, +0.48 on round-2 weights, +0.30 equal-weighted).
2. The company's own A350 launch test of at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6), met in no column.

What it passed: peak cash ($1.0B a year, $4.2B inside the $5.2B line), zero overlap, one launch, all of Wagner's safety, quality, ramp-shield and supply-crunch tests, and the Board's -$2B downside. Wagner's widebody-engine finding is a non-binding supply flag; he recommended hold on it and on the $1B bar.

No override is possible: the margin is under $1B, and it is behind in the worst column. The doctrine default (within $1B) and both tie-breaks (later capex, fewer Board items) point the same way.

Recorded as a strategic choice: holding at the last decision year closes the A350 Re-engine for this game. Hold costs about $0.43B on my weights and $0.58B at best. I accept the Board's point that a later gate would not have helped.

Widebody position for the 2050s:
- the A350 family and the A350F, kept current for our customers;
- support for Rolls-Royce's time-on-wing work on the Trent fleet, with no Trent XWB programme claimed that Rolls-Royce has not announced;
- any future Re-engine only with an engine committed and its durability proven.
No widebody-engine invitation is issued, since the item is not tabled.

other_moves.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's code-7 sourcing invitation for its next single-aisle, through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail:
We offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted, ready since 2041, nine years in service on NGSA), with a LEAP derivative as the floor (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185].
- Durability proven before entry into service is our own standard. Accepting it as a contract condition is a commercial term, so it goes to Safran first, along with any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty, and it is modelled conservatively (Ghai) [CX-0184, CX-0979].

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041 and flies on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We've set out the standard we hold that engine to. On any new airframe, durability proven before entry into service is our standard, and our customers'. We claim no result here. The test and field record goes to our customers and our Board first, through our cross-functional team. It doesn't go into a press line.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and that's the airframer's call.

Boeing has asked us for a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]
This is the last round, and the launch game ended for this board some time ago.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, and its code is fixed.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041. Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade have counted since 2042.
- The Joint Venture's engine has been ready since 2036.
- The one launch on the menu is an Open Fan. Launched now, it is ready in 2060: 23 years behind NGSA and 4 years after the board stops counting narrowbody engines (2056). Lobby only works with it.
So the game is the installed base we hold: the 737 slot at its 57-a-month ceiling, our share of NGSA, the A320neo tail and the GEnx. 'Our major economics happen in and around' that base [CX-0422]. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
Hold everything: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all on hold (option A, Do Nothing).
- Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]. Hold is the best row in both columns: -24.29 (S1) and -22.50 (S2).
- Open Fan + Lobby against hold: -12.83 / -12.83 on a $9B bill, $3.83B beyond it. The Open Fan inside it loses $4.83B beyond its $8B.
- Open Fan alone: -13.43 / -13.42 on $8B, $5.43B / $5.42B beyond the bill.
- Lobby on the Open Fan is +0.60 / +0.59, but only on a base that fails by $12.83B. Lobby alone is about -1.00 a column. That figure is an inference: the flat $2B strain is already in the hold row.
- In S1 there's no new narrowbody to defend, so the Open Fan buys nothing and costs its whole bill plus the wait loss. S2 shows the same, because NGSA sets the wait.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536].
- Expected column: S1, the record. Weights: S1 70 / S2 30. Weighted hold is -23.75 (-23.84 at Ghai's 75/25).
- Hold is best at every weight, so the weights set the booking, not the choice.
- I book -24.3, on S1. S2's +1.79 gets credit only once a Boeing fps is on the record.
- Last round's -24.3 matched the record (-24.29). Booking low held.

3. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]. Ready is max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060, confirmed by Ali. The first new narrowbody (NGSA, 2037) sets the wait, so S2's 2060 fps doesn't help. No Open Fan.

4. Ducted only as a defence (H3). It is in service and on hold only. It is called 'a step forward from today's LEAP' and never the next generation.

5. Strain. Hold adds no project and no strain; the flat $2B is already booked. An Open Fan would put a fourth programme on a supply base whose margin is not shown.

6. The next generation: my 20% line [CX-0217] arises only if an Open Fan is ordered. None is, and the statement makes no fuel-burn claim. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]: no plan here trades it.

7. Tie-break: not needed. The gap to the next plan is $12.83B, far outside my $1B ε.

THE RISE ALLOWANCE, TESTED ON ITS MERITS AND CLOSED
For the first time the cheapest Open Fan plan ($12.83B against hold) fits inside the one $15B allowance in dollars. It's the last round, and that's exactly where the installed-base lens tempts you to 'seed the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. Doctrine says the allowance 'still covers a launch you judge strategic' (dashboard_game.md §5). I judge this one is not.
- It fits only because seven narrowbody years are left to lose, not twelve (Ghai). There is less board left, not a better plan.
- It buys nothing inside the count. $9B of R&D buys a 2060 engine with no share gain on the board.
- The wait loss takes about 647 of our 648 NGSA engines a year alone, or about 456 with Lobby. That turns 2050 into a share miss (about 36%, or 41% with Lobby) while still missing the Open Fan objective. Confirmed by Ghai on the board's engine value of $8.39M of 2026 PV per engine a year.
- The gates fail:
  - G1: no airframer has launched an Open Fan or asked for one.
  - G2 and H2: NGSA has been in service since 2037.
  - G4: Ali can't show any RISE test progress after October 2025.
- Doctrine says do not let conviction launch RISE without G1 (profile §8). RISE becomes a product 'as our airframer and airline customers deem appropriate' [CX-0469], not on the hope of an order not yet won [CX-0248].
- RISE into a wait is not joint practice, and I have no reason to give why Safran would agree.
- The Board would veto it, and I have no override against the Board.
RISE stays 'all in' as technology [CX-0214], the seed corn [CX-0256], funded with Safran. If Boeing launches, RISE goes to Boeing on Boeing's schedule, through CFM with Safran.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
No CFM narrowbody order this round. The other moves (the Boeing reply, the LEAP-1B allocation, Airbus's capacity talks, the Embraer terms) go through CFM with Safran, on product and supply only, with no price or number before Safran agrees [CX-0184, CX-0160]. RISE continuing as technology is joint practice. GEnx is GE alone and stays on hold.

EXCO DELIBERATION
- Ghai confirmed every row and both share inferences. He sharpened my reading of S2's +1.79: it comes from capacity, not preference. Both lines sat at their ceilings in 2047-2049, so only the MAX top-up after 2050 moves a delivery: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year, roughly 11 MAX a month above 57. I adopt that, and we plan any step to it, not to the 2,400 cap.
- Ghai stays at 75/25; I hold 70/30. That's $0.09B, he doesn't object, and the booking is the same.
- Ali confirmed every date and raised no flag. He failed his own evidence checks plainly (the Ducted record, the LEAP-1B kit, RISE after 2025, the floor margin), and each is now handed on with a named owner and an internal report to the Board.
- His binding date veto on wording holds. Last round's 'durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included' stays out. It could read as a result dated before 2041, and no test in our hands backs that. The statement now says plainly that we claim no result.
- Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the Lobby rule; the Embraer terms; the floor gates on capacity (beyond my own 'lean before capital'); and the G1-G5 reading of the allowance.

SCORING LAST ROUND
My round 3 predictions held:
- Boeing held again, with no date.
- The Joint Venture held.
- There was no 787 Re-engine, no widebody UltraFan and no rival widebody upgrade (RR's Trent work stayed inside a flat envelope), so there was no GEnx re-test.
- The booking matched the record.
Ghai's 'build to deliveries' held too: LEAP-1B rose from 1,042 engines in 2045 to the 1,368 ceiling by 2047, with no capacity built ahead of it.

OFF-BOARD RISKS, NAMED FOR THE RECORD
(1) A Boeing code-4 selection (the Joint Venture alone) would take the 737 slot from fps entry: 1,368 engines a year, about 68% of our narrowbody engines. It falls outside the count but not outside the business, and only product answers it: the Ducted with whatever record test and field data support, plus a LEAP derivative.
(2) A Ducted durability or quality event would re-price the value booked from 2041. Ghai books it in the quarter we find it.
(3) The MAX above 57 a month, and Airbus's capacity step: new floor load, gated on floor data.

WHAT WOULD HAVE CHANGED MY MIND
- A durability or quality flag from Ali: the statement and the Boeing offer would change, though no order would.
- A firm airframer path for RISE on the record.
- Ghai showing the allowance buys something inside the count.
None came.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

This is the last round. The launch game ended for this board a while ago.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with all three makers fitted, and its code is fixed.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041. Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade have counted since 2042.
- The Joint Venture's engine has been ready since 2036.
- The menu offers one launch, an Open Fan. Launched now it is ready in 2060: 23 years behind NGSA, and four years after the board stops counting narrowbody engines (2056). Lobby only works with it.

So the game is the installed base we already hold: the 737 slot, which now runs at its 57-a-month ceiling, our share of NGSA, the A320neo tail and the GEnx. "Our major economics happen in and around" that base [CX-0422]. We win it the same way we have for two rounds:
- prove in test and in the field that what we launched does what we said, on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658];
- keep LEAP kits and deliveries first;
- earn our seat on Boeing's next single-aisle, on product, through CFM with Safran. We don't have a birthright on that order [CX-0564].

One thing is new this year. For the first time the cheapest Open Fan plan ($12.83B against hold) fits inside the one $15B RISE allowance in dollars. It's also the last round, so there is no later round in which to answer a Boeing launch. That is exactly when the installed-base lens tempts you to "seed the next 30 years" [CX-0555]. I want that case tested on its merits, so we can say plainly why the allowance closes unused, rather than just assume it.

The last-round job is also to close out what we owe. The Board has asked since 2030 for the Ducted's durability record, the floor margin at the suppliers and the ledger figures. Each gap gets closed, or handed on with a named owner and an internal report to the Board. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630]. Tell them what we know and what we don't [CX-0436].
