- Last round I said a third 'not yet' would lower S2. It came, with 'technology ready, Boeing ready', and both lines at their ceilings, which is confirmed data. They offset.
- 70/30 is -23.75 against -23.84 at 75/25, a difference of $0.09B. I don't object to 70/30. It changes neither the choice nor the booking.

S2's +1.79: I'd sharpen your reading (inference from the rules).
- In 2047-2049 both factories sit at their ceilings: the 737 at 684 (57 a month) and Airbus at 1,200 (100 a month) with a growing waiting backlog.
- Preference alone can't move a delivery. It decides who waits; capacity decides who delivers.
- The only new slots inside 2056 are the MAX top-up after 2050 ('tops Boeing up to the fps's full rate while the fps ramps'). The fps enters in 2060, so 2051-2056 is all MAX, all LEAP-1B.
- The size: $1.79B over $6.97M of 2026 PV per engine a year (2051-2056) is about 257 more LEAP-1B a year on average. That is about 128 MAX a year, roughly 11 a month above 57.
- So your part (b) is the mechanism, and part (a) at most decides whose customers fill the slots. Both mean more LEAP-1B, as you say.
- Planning implication: the grid implies about 1,625 LEAP-1B and about 2,273 CFM NB engines a year in S2. That is below the 2,592 we delivered in 2030-2036. The 2,400 / 3,048 figure is the cap, not the case.

tests.name: No overcapitalization, payout, rating and the two owed items (Ask 6)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over their development years, must fit in the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow (about $2.55B a year). The 2-3% band is advice. (Inference: an analogy from capex to R&D.)
tests.numbers:
- New spend on hold: $0 against $2.55B a year of room.
- OF+L would be $1.8B in 2050 ($0.8B plus Lobby's $1B), then $0.8B a year. It fits, because this test can't fail on this board, and passing it doesn't save the item.
- Payout: 70% of $8.5B ($5.95B) stays whole.
- R&D: 6-8% of sales with RISE inside (doctrine and Board guidance, not my words), held through shocks.
- No new debt and no new commitment, so no A-range risk.

Owed since round 2, neither closed:
1. The Ducted's 2035-2040 ledger cash curve. The board books $4.0B of R&D (2035) plus $2.0B of strain: $6.0B against $6.0B approved ($1.0B a year over 6 years), with no overrun and no write-off. The yearly ledger cash is not in my brief, and I won't invent it.
2. Airbus's capacity agreements. Airbus says publicly that 'the capacity agreements with both' cover only its own NGSA volumes and the A320neo tail, with no exclusivity. That is Airbus's word on scope. Our signature status and terms are not in my brief.

Handed on, with me as owner: the ledger curve with GE Aerospace controllership and CFM finance (with Safran on the CFM share); the agreements with CFM commercial and Safran. Each goes in an internal report to the Board (Audit Committee) at its next regular meeting, with no public date. No booking rests on either.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (Ask 7)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium of at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, stated apart (company doctrine, hard rule 9).
tests.numbers:
Hold: $0 this round, and $0 of $4.0B for the game.

The RISE allowance, stated apart: unused, and it closes unused. The cheapest Open Fan plan costs $12.83B against hold in both columns. That is inside $15B in dollars, but there is no airframer path, so it is not a pre-authorised launch.

tests.name: Terms: standard terms, no concession, no CFM narrowbody price or number without Safran (Ask 9)
tests.threshold: No public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or that talks CFM narrowbody price or capacity numbers without Safran.
tests.numbers:
Your draft line carries no price, concession, launch-era pricing or capacity number. 'On capacity we work with both airframers, together with Safran' and 'Together with Safran we've answered on product' pass.

Conditions on the other moves:
1. Boeing reply: product only. Boeing makes 'durability proven before entry into service' a contract condition. Accepting it, or any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty, is a commercial term: Safran first, modelled conservatively.
2. LEAP-1B allocation: 1,368 a year is a CFM narrowbody capacity number. Any step above 57 a month goes through CFM with Safran, with no number to Boeing before Safran agrees and no price in it.
3. Airbus's capacity talks: any price term is a joint decision, on standard terms. Launch-era pricing is behind us.
4. Embraer: no number until terms are agreed.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (advice)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores.
tests.numbers:
Hold's worst column is S1 at -24.29: 0.45 below 75/25, 0.54 below 70/30 and 1.79 below S2.

Not in the columns:
1. A Boeing code-4 selection (the Joint Venture alone). From fps entry the MAX gives way down to a 10-a-month tail. The 737 slot is 1,368 engines a year, 68% of our NB engines and about $17B a year of nominal lifecycle value at 2060 prices (inference). It falls outside the count, not outside the business, and only product answers it.
2. The MAX above 57 (S2): about +$1.79B, plus floor load.
3. Airbus's capacity step: upside, not booked.
4. A Ducted durability or quality event. It re-prices the value booked from 2041, and I'd book it in the quarter we find it.
5. Value past the 2056 NB count: 2,016 engines a year that the board stops counting.
6. An airframer slowdown, tariff escalation, a recession, or a widebody Re-engine.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence (advice)
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill year, ready year and first year of share gain inside the horizon (NB to 2056, WB to 2061 per the brief). (Inference.)
tests.numbers:
Hold: no new launch.

Live programmes:
- Ducted: counting since 2041, 16 years inside the NB count.
- Partner Embraer: since 2042, 15 years.
- GEnx: +5 pp WB since 2042 (44.8%), 20 years inside the WB count.

An Open Fan launched in 2050 would fail this test:
- bill 2050-2059;
- ready in 2060;
- no year of share gain on the board, and NB counting ends in 2056.
Lobby: $1B in 2050, with no gain on its own.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan that stacks two or more projects (the $2B strain). GE9X losses are not live. (Inference.)
tests.numbers: Hold adds no project. The Ducted, Partner Embraer and GEnx sit on the one $2B strain already booked. An Open Fan would add a fourth project on the floor at no extra board strain. The floor load is Ali's ground. GE9X losses are not live.

tests.name: Guide low (advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV at the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed. (Inference.)
tests.numbers:
Book -24.3: S1, the record, and the lowest column on hold.
- Scored: last round's -24.3 matched the record (-24.29).
- No credit for S2's +1.79, or for the -23.84 / -23.75 blends, until a Boeing fps is on the record.
- Your intended -24.3 is right.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, in any form (alone, or with lobby_emissions)
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding grounds 1 and 2.

Ground 1, pays for itself: the item doesn't beat hold in any column.
- Alone: -13.43 / -13.42 on $8B.
- Inside OF+L: -12.83 / -12.83 against $8B ($9B as a package).
- It loses more than its bill in every column.

Ground 2, premium above the cap (hard rule 9). The $12.83B fits $15B in dollars, but the allowance exempts only a pre-authorised RISE launch (§6, gates G1-G5). G1 fails (no committed airframer) and hard rule 2 as mapped fails (NGSA in service since 2037; ready in 2060). So the gap counts against the general cap: 6.4 times the $2.0B round cap and 3.2 times the $4.0B game cap. It buys neither objective and nothing inside the 2056 count.

This is a veto on the launch, not on the R&D: RISE stays funded as technology with Safran (H5).

It lifts only if an airframer path appears on the record and a grid row beats hold, or loses no more than its bill, with the gap declared within a pre-authorised allowance. Neither can happen on this grid.

Note: my veto right is an inference. teams.md §1 shows my tests, not a formal decision right; the GM reads a failed test as binding unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan that passes
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding ground 1. Alone it is about -1.00 in each column: $1B with no board effect, and the flat strain already sits in the hold row (an inference from the rules, not a grid row). On the Open Fan it is +0.60 / +0.59, but on a base that fails by $12.83B.

Note: my veto right is an inference. teams.md §1 shows my tests, not a formal decision right; the GM reads a failed test as binding unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement or other move (the Boeing reply, the LEAP-1B allocation, Airbus's capacity talks, the Embraer terms) that carries launch-era pricing, a price concession, or CFM narrowbody price or capacity numbers without Safran
vetoes.ground:
Terms, binding ground 3. This is a standing veto, not engaged by your draft. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision, and launch-era pricing is behind us. Accepting Boeing's durability contract condition, or any guarantee or time-on-wing term, goes to Safran first and is modelled conservatively.

Note: my veto right is an inference. teams.md §1 shows my tests, not a formal decision right; the GM reads a failed test as binding unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: A, hold everything, as framed (advice)
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a veto:
1. Book -24.3 on S1, with no S2 credit until a Boeing fps is on the record.
2. Weights: 75/25 rather than 70/30. It's $0.09B and changes nothing.
3. If S2 comes, plan the floor to the grid-implied volume (about 257 more LEAP-1B a year, about 1,625 in all), not the 2,400 cap. Commit no capacity until Boeing and Safran agree volumes.
4. Hand on the ledger curve and Airbus's signature status, with me as owner and an internal report to the Audit Committee at its next regular meeting, with no public date.
5. Keep a Boeing code-4 selection as a named off-board risk.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
What would make me back an Open Fan or Lobby? Neither is in sight:
1. An airframer path for RISE on the record: a new narrowbody that isn't in service before the engine would be ready. On this board none is possible before 2056, because NGSA has been in service since 2037.
2. A grid row in which an Open Fan plan beats hold in the expected column, or loses no more than its bill in every column, with the gap inside an allowance pre-authorised by G1-G5.

What would raise the booking above -24.3:
1. A Boeing fps on the record. S2's +1.79 then becomes creditable.
2. Boeing and Safran agreeing volumes above 57 a month. That's when we plan the capacity, to the agreed number, not the 2,400 cap.

What would lower it (booked the quarter we find it):
1. A Ducted durability or quality flag from Ali. It re-prices the value booked from 2041. Dates and readiness are his ground.
2. A Boeing signal toward code 4.
3. 737 deliveries falling back below 684.

What would change my weights:
- A firm Boeing date raises S2 above 25.
- A Boeing step back from 'technology ready, Boeing ready' lowers it.

What would engage my terms veto: any price, concession or capacity number going to an airframer before Safran agrees.
cfo.memo:
Larry, your rows are right, and there's nothing to hide. Hold is -24.29 in S1 and -22.50 in S2, best at every weight. The cheapest Open Fan plan costs $12.83B against hold. It fits $15B for the first time, but only because seven narrowbody years are left to lose, not twelve. It buys nothing inside 2056: $9B of R&D for an engine ready in 2060, plus about 456 of our 648 NGSA engines a year. Alone, it takes all 648 and 2050 share drops to about 36%. The allowance covers a pre-authorised launch. With no airframer this isn't one, so it's 6.4 times the round cap. My vetoes on any Open Fan and on Lobby alone stand. They're on the launch, not the R&D.

S2's +1.79 is capacity, not preference. Both lines sit at their ceilings, so only the MAX top-up after 2050 moves a delivery: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year. Plan to that, not 2,400, and commit nothing until Boeing and Safran agree volumes.

I said a third 'not yet' would lower S2. It came with 'technology ready, Boeing ready'. They offset, so I stay at 75/25. That's $0.09B. Book -24.3.

Capital: $0 new spend, $2.55B of room, payout whole. I still owe the Ducted's ledger curve and Airbus's signature status. Neither is in my brief. I own both and will report to the Audit Committee at its next meeting.

We missed share by about 24 engines, roughly $0.2B. But the good news is the installed base keeps paying.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): open_fan launched in 2050, alone or with Lobby (options B and C; Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 10 and not before 2045. Any order whose value depends on an earlier ready year fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times)
tests.numbers:
Confirmed: ready = max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA's 2037 entry and 4 years after the NB count ends (2056).

The Open Fan rows (-37.72 S1 / -35.92 S2; with Lobby -37.12 / -35.33) book no gain in any year. They carry only the wait penalty set by NGSA's 2037 entry: -35 pp NB, or -20 pp with Lobby. No value rests on a year earlier than 2060, so the date passes.

S2's fps would also enter in 2060, but that does not help: the first new narrowbody (NGSA) sets the wait. Lobby takes effect immediately and has no ready year.

To be ready by 2050, an Open Fan had to launch by 2040. The last round that allowed it was 2035 (ready 2045).

Calc: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-sd/work/r4_ali_calc.py

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): the hold row, i.e. Ducted, Partner Embraer and GEnx (Culp's ask 1, second part)
tests.threshold: Ducted ready no earlier than launch + 6. Partner Embraer counts 7 years after launch, on a CFM engine already ready. GEnx counts 3 years after launch, not before 2035, and on the widebody from 2042 if there is no Re-engine
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: 2035 + 6 = 2041. 'Ready since 2041' is on the public record, so there is no slip and no re-price.
- Partner Embraer: 2035 + 7 = 2042, on a Ducted ready a year earlier.
- GEnx: 2030 + 3 = 2033. It counts +5 pp WB from 2042 (44.8%). No widebody Re-engine or rival upgrade is on the record.

Confirmed: the hold row (-24.29 S1 / -22.50 S2; -23.75 at 70/30) rests on 2041 and 2042 and on no earlier year. Those years come from the board's development times. The test record behind 2041 is not in our sources (see the Ducted evidence test).

tests.name: Test, not analysis (veto: dates): Culp's draft statement, other moves and the internal Board report dates (Culp's asks 4 and 8)
tests.threshold: Every date must be one a test can back: no ready year before launch plus development years; no RISE or Open Fan date of any kind; no year by which a durability result is promised; no wording that dates a durability result no test in hand backs
tests.numbers:
- 'Ready since 2041': 2035 + 6, on the public record. PASS.
- 'We're not launching anything new this year': no date. PASS.
- RISE, 'We won't put a date on it ... that's the airframer's call': no demo, test or entry year. PASS. My own fly demo slipped from 'by the middle of this decade' to 'this decade', so we promise none.
- 'Its test and field record goes to our customers and our Board first': no result claimed. PASS.
- Boeing reply, 'we'll be at the table' and 'When we know, you'll know': no year. PASS.
- Internal reports to the Board 'at its next regular meeting': PASS. A private report date promises a report of what we hold, not a result by a date. It fails only if worded as a result ('proven by ...').

The dropped line (ask 8): keep it out as written. Next to 'ready since 2041' and 'flies on Airbus's new single-aisle', the words 'durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh included' read as a result dated before 2041. No hot-and-harsh or dust result in our hands backs that.

What we can say plainly: 'Last year we set out the standard we hold that engine to. We claim no result here: the record goes to our customers and our Board first, through our cross-functional team.'

As a forward standard it also passes: 'On any new airframe, durability proven before entry into service is our standard, as it is Boeing's.' No deny-then-reverse.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Open Fan
tests.threshold: Ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service. Otherwise the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap in years
tests.numbers:
The engine would be ready in 2060 against NGSA's 2037 entry. That is 23 years late in both S1 and S2, and 4 years past the NB count (2056). S2's 2060 fps does not close the gap, because the first new narrowbody sets the wait.

Item against hold:
- Open Fan alone: -13.43 / -13.42 on an $8B bill, so $5.43B / $5.42B beyond the bill.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -12.83 / -12.83 on $9B.
- Lobby on the Open Fan: +0.60 / +0.59.

Culp's share inference checks on my arithmetic: about 647 engines a year lost (456 with Lobby), which puts 2050 share near 36% (41%). That is Ghai's ground.

H2, from the readiness side: hold, and keep RISE whole as technology.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Ducted against Boeing's next single-aisle, and what the Boeing reply can stand on (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year, so a late date does not fail it. A customer claim stands only on test and field data in hand
tests.numbers:
Gap in years for the Ducted, ready in 2041:
- 4 years after NGSA's entry (it has earned since 2041);
- 19 years before S2's fps entry (2060);
- 16 years before a 7-year fps launched in 2050 (2057, off grid).
It has 9 field years on NGSA by 2050.

Boeing's contract condition is durability proven before entry into service.

What we can stand behind:
- the test gate, as our own standard;
- the LEAP-1A kit record. Its HPT hardware was certified by the FAA and EASA in December 2024. It is in all LEAP-1A deliveries and shop visits and more than doubles time on wing, matching the CFM56. Retrofits add no shop visits.

What we cannot stand behind: any Ducted durability number or 'proven' claim, until the hot-and-harsh, dust and field record is in hand and the cross-functional team releases it.

Any guarantee or time-on-wing term goes to Safran first; that is Ghai's ground. Product only, through CFM with Safran.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (evidence, advice): the Ducted's durability record since 2041 (Culp's ask 3; the Board's first priority)
tests.threshold: A durability claim needs the failure turned on in test and turned off by the design, plus field data. Absence of failure is not clearance
tests.numbers:
In our sources, which end in October 2025: 0 hot-and-harsh results, 0 dust results and 0 NGSA test or field events.

Field time: 9 years on NGSA (2041-2050), with NGSA at its planned 100 a month (1,200 a year since 2045).

Public record: no public events in 2045, and no engine slip or quality event named by Airbus or Boeing. That is absence, not clearance.

Not a veto: ducted is hold-only, and no order or date rests on the result.

Hand-on:
- Owner: Mohamed Ali, with the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team and Safran.
- Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting.
- No public date.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (evidence, advice): LEAP-1B durability-kit outcome (Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: Fix believed only when reproduced in test, removed by the new design, and accepted by the airframer and the regulator
tests.numbers:
Last in our record: certification with Boeing was expected in the first half of 2026 (Culp, October 2025), or the first quarter (Ghai, November 2025). That is a year after my own 2025 date. The 1B has flown fewer cycles than the 1A.

The outcome is not in our record.

Field facts: the 737 ran at 57 a month in 2047-2049 (684 aircraft, 1,368 LEAP-1B a year). Each step was KPI-gated, agreed with the FAA and taken only once engine output was proven. No durability event is named. That is delivery evidence, not durability evidence.

Hand-on:
- Owner: Mohamed Ali, with Boeing, the FAA and the cross-functional team.
- Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting.
- No public date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (advice): RISE after October 2025, and gate G4 for the RISE allowance (Culp's asks 2 and 4)
tests.threshold: G4: RISE test progress reported and no open durability failure, on test results only
tests.numbers:
The last items in our record:
- 350+ programme tests, with an early focus on durability (July 2025);
- 200+ hours of wind-tunnel tests with Safran;
- noise tests with Airbus, showing the open fan can be quieter than today's LEAP;
- dust testing on RISE HPT blades, begun in October 2025.

Nothing later: no dust result, and no outcome of the ground and flight test planned 'this decade'. No failure is in evidence either, and absence is not clearance.

G4 cannot be shown. That alone keeps RISE a technology programme, so the allowance closes unused.

Hand-on:
- Owner: Mohamed Ali, with Safran and the cross-functional team.
- Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting.
- No RISE date of any kind.

tests.name: Physics (advice): wording and Culp's 20% line (Culp's ask 8)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. Never call a ducted engine the next generation: it has 'less than half' the open fan's gain
tests.numbers:
Neither the brief nor the draft gives a fuel-burn figure.

- The draft calls the Ducted 'a step forward from today's LEAP', never the next generation. PASS (H3).
- RISE stays the engine of 20% or better, SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable. 20% is 'practically impossible' without the open fan.
- Culp's 20% line arises only if an Open Fan is ordered. If option B were ordered, the brief has no data to confirm it.

tests.name: Durability first (advice)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule (inference: Culp's line applied to my seat)
tests.numbers:
Hold trades nothing: no new programme and no new date. LEAP kits and deliveries stay first.

Yardsticks:
- CFM56: about 17,000 cycles benign, 7,000-8,000 harsh.
- LEAP fleet leaders in 2023: 9,882 benign, about 4,800 harsh.
- Kit targets: 8,000 harsh, 17,000 neutral.

The draft statement claims no Ducted durability result. An Open Fan's durability record after October 2025 is not in hand (see the RISE test).

tests.name: Safety call (advice): flags on the Ducted, LEAP and RISE (Culp's ask 5)
tests.threshold: A problem that touches safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, never one person
tests.numbers:
Flag: none on the Ducted, LEAP or RISE, because no failure is in evidence.

The three evidence gaps sit with the cross-functional team, not with one person, and that answers the safety call. Any test or field event goes to that team before any date, statement, offer or capacity step moves.

If the Board report shows an event, it becomes a flag and takes the usual path: root cause, inspection, and a fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator.

tests.name: Supply load (advice, doctrine): stacking
tests.threshold: Two or more projects bring $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only)
tests.numbers:
Hold adds no project, no R&D and no strain. The flat $2B is already in the hold row.

An Open Fan would put a fourth programme on the same supply base for -12.83 or worse against hold.

This follows doctrine, not my record.

tests.name: Supply load (advice): floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, long-lead release, and the gates on each step (Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Floor evidence that the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of shortages carry LEAP, the kits and the Ducted with margin; any step above what we have delivered gated on that data

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign (advice)
tests.threshold: Widebody: prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture. Narrowbody: keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures; this does not argue against the Open Fan
tests.numbers:
- GEnx: the 2030 upgrade is live and counts +5 pp WB from 2042 (44.8%). No widebody Re-engine or rival upgrade is on the record, so nothing triggers a re-test.
- RISE: its technology keeps flowing into LEAP.
- No cancel (H5).

vetoes.ground:
Dates not backed by real testing, binding ground 2: a public statement or move that gives a date no test backs.

2041 is 2035 + 6, on the public record, and may be stated.

RISE has no test record in our hands after October 2025, and my own fly demo slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade', so it gets no date of any kind.

No hot-and-harsh or dust result for the Ducted is in our sources. A line that says or implies the proof came before its 2041 entry into service therefore dates a result no test backs.

An internal report date to the Board is a reporting commitment, not a programme date, and passes.

Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My own words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results. Under the team rule the veto binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions (options B and C), declared as the one RISE allowance
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto: the 2060 date (launch + 10) passes.

What fails:
- Readiness: ready 23 years after NGSA's 2037 entry and 4 years past the 2056 count, in every column.
- G4: no RISE test progress after October 2025 is in our hands.
- Item against hold: -13.43 / -13.42 alone, and -12.83 / -12.83 with Lobby.
- Stacking: a fourth programme on a supply base whose margin is not shown.

Hold, and keep RISE whole as technology with Safran. Never cancel it: we failed twice, and we got it done.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan (option D)
vetoes.ground:
Advice. It raises no date issue, since it takes effect immediately, and it buys nothing on the board without a live Open Fan.

On whether to lobby I have no evidence: following Culp and Ghai.

The technical facts I can supply: RISE is designed SAF-ready and hydrogen-capable, and noise tests with Airbus showed the open fan can be quieter than today's LEAP.

vetoes.plan: Any capacity commitment above the LEAP-1B rate of 57 a month (1,368 engines a year), or for Airbus's next industrial step, before the floor margin is reported
vetoes.ground:
Advice, following doctrine and not my record (kits first, lean before capital).

The floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites has never been shown. The MAX at 100 a month would mean 3,048 engines a year, 17.6% above the 2,592 we have ever delivered.

Gate every step on floor data reported to the Board, through CFM with Safran, and never get ahead of Boeing or the FAA.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Test or field data only, never analysis.

(1) A hot-and-harsh or dust test result, or an NGSA field event, showing the Ducted short of the standard. I would raise a flag and take it to the cross-functional team with Safran, and the statement and the Boeing offer would change. No order changes, because ducted is hold only. A turn-on, turn-off record that meets the standard would let the Boeing reply cite it, once the team releases it.

(2) A LEAP-1B kit outcome showing the fix did not turn the problem off. I would flag it with Boeing and the FAA, and LEAP kits would stay ahead of every step above 57 a month.

(3) RISE results from Safran showing a durability or dust problem, or progress that clears G4. RISE stays technology either way: no airframer path exists on this board, because NGSA's 2037 entry sets the wait.

(4) Floor data at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites showing margin, which would clear a gated LEAP-1B step if Boeing launches. Floor data showing no margin would mean the LEAP rate and kits come first and every new load waits.
ops.memo:
Turn on, turn off. I recomputed every date.

Open Fan launched now: ready 2060, launch plus ten. NGSA has flown since 2037. That is twenty-three years late, and four years past the board's narrowbody count. The date passes. Readiness fails. Gate G4 fails on my own record: nothing on RISE after October 2025 is in my hands, not the dust results, not the ground test. So the allowance closes unused. RISE stays whole, as technology, with Safran. We failed twice. We got it done. Not by launching into a wait.

Hold row: Ducted 2041, launch plus six. Embraer and GEnx count from 2042. No veto.

Now what we owe. We told the market we hold the Ducted to durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh included. Nine years in service, and I cannot show one turn-on, turn-off result: not hot and harsh, not dust, not a field event on NGSA. Nor the LEAP-1B kit outcome. Absence of failure is not clearance. That line stays out; we say plainly we claim no result. I own all three gaps, with the cross-functional team, Safran, Boeing and the FAA. The report goes to the Board at its next regular meeting: a report date, not a result date.

Supply: 2,016 engines a year against the 2,592 we delivered. A MAX at 100 a month means 3,048. The floor margin at the nine suppliers is still not shown. Fourth time. I own it. No step above 57 without floor data.

other_moves.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's code-7 sourcing invitation for its next single-aisle, through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail:
We offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted, ready since 2041, nine years in service on NGSA), with a LEAP derivative as the floor (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185].
- Durability proven before entry into service is our own standard. Accepting it as a contract condition is a commercial term, so it goes to Safran first, along with any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty, and it is modelled conservatively (Ghai) [CX-0184, CX-0979].
- We stand behind what test and field data back: the LEAP-1A kit (HPT hardware certified by the FAA and EASA in December 2024, in every LEAP-1A delivery and shop visit, more than doubling time on wing) [CX-0209, CX-0225], and the test gate as our standard.
- We make no Ducted durability claim until the cross-functional team releases the hot-and-harsh, dust and field record (Ali, H6).
- No price, no concession, no number. No ready year before 2041, and no year by which durability will be 'proven'.
- When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call [CX-0307].

other_moves.move: LEAP-1B built to deliveries at 57 a month; any step above it through CFM with Safran, gated on floor data
other_moves.detail:
The allocation at 57 a month (1,368 engines a year) has been fully used since 2047. Capacity and volume now match, so there was no overcapitalisation.
- Nothing above 57 a month until Boeing launches and agrees volumes with CFM, GE and Safran together. No number to Boeing before Safran agrees, and no price in it [CX-0184, CX-0160].
- If Boeing launches (S2), we plan the floor to the grid-implied step: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year on average over 2051-2056 (about 1,625 LEAP-1B and about 2,273 CFM NB engines a year). That is inside the 2,592 we delivered in 2030-2036. We do not plan to the 2,400 cap (3,048 in all, 17.6% above anything we've delivered).
- Each step is gated on floor data reported to the Board first, with kits ahead of rate. We never get ahead of Boeing or the FAA [CX-0307, CX-0197, CX-0540].

other_moves.move: Airbus's next industrial step: capacity talks on product and supply only, for Airbus's own extra volumes, through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail:
Scope as Airbus states it publicly: its own NGSA volumes and the A320neo tail, no exclusivity, nothing drawn from any other allocation.
- No capacity or price number before Safran agrees. Any price term is a joint decision on standard terms [CX-0184].
- Any commitment is gated on floor data at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, with LEAP kits and the LEAP-1B rate first.
- This is upside we don't book.

other_moves.move: Partner Embraer: terms worked through CFM with Safran
other_moves.detail: No Embraer number goes to the market or to an airframer until terms are agreed with Safran (Ghai's condition) [CX-0184]. Partner Embraer has counted since 2042 and stays on hold.

other_moves.move: End-of-game hand-on: durability evidence (Ali owns)
other_moves.detail:
Three gaps, none closed on our record. Each is handed on as a standing management action, with an internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting and no public date [CX-0012, CX-0633].
(1) The Ducted: hot-and-harsh and dust results (turn on, turn off) and every test or field event on NGSA since 2041. Our sources hold 0 of each. Owner: Mohamed Ali, with the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team and Safran.
(2) The LEAP-1B durability-kit outcome. Not in our record; certification was due in the first half of 2026. Owner: Ali, with Boeing and the FAA [CX-0210, CX-0656].
(3) RISE durability and dust after October 2025. Owner: Ali, with Safran [CX-0216, CX-0222].
Absence of failure is not clearance. Any event becomes a flag and goes to the cross-functional team (root cause, inspection, a fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator) before any date, statement, offer or capacity step moves. A report date promises a report, not a result (Ali's test passes).

This is the fourth time the Board has asked for the floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages, and it is still not shown [CX-0613]. Whether the Ducted's long-lead orders were released on floor data cannot be shown either.

(2) Whether the Airbus capacity agreements are signed. Airbus's public word covers scope only. Our signature status and terms are not in our brief. Owner: Ghai, with CFM commercial and Safran.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Our new CFM engine, a step forward from today's LEAP, has been ready since 2041 and flies on Airbus's new single-aisle. We're working with Embraer, together with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe. We thank our customers for that.

We've set out the standard we hold that engine to. On any new airframe, durability proven before entry into service is our standard, and our customers'. We claim no result here. The test and field record goes to our customers and our Board first, through our cross-functional team. It doesn't go into a press line.

LEAP durability kits and deliveries still come first. On capacity, we work with both airframers, together with Safran.

We're not launching anything new this year. RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and that's the airframer's call.

Boeing has asked us for a proposal for its next single-aisle. Together with Safran, we've answered on product, and we'll be at the table. We don't have a birthright on that order. When and what Boeing launches is Boeing's call.

Here's what we don't know: when that airplane launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]
This is the last round, and the launch game ended for this board some time ago.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on code 7, and its code is fixed.
- Our Ducted has been ready since 2041. Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade have counted since 2042.
- The Joint Venture's engine has been ready since 2036.
- The one launch on the menu is an Open Fan. Launched now, it is ready in 2060: 23 years behind NGSA and 4 years after the board stops counting narrowbody engines (2056). Lobby only works with it.
So the game is the installed base we hold: the 737 slot at its 57-a-month ceiling, our share of NGSA, the A320neo tail and the GEnx. 'Our major economics happen in and around' that base [CX-0422]. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
Hold everything: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer, lobby_emissions and genx all on hold (option A, Do Nothing).
- Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]. Hold is the best row in both columns: -24.29 (S1) and -22.50 (S2).
- Open Fan + Lobby against hold: -12.83 / -12.83 on a $9B bill, $3.83B beyond it. The Open Fan inside it loses $4.83B beyond its $8B.
- Open Fan alone: -13.43 / -13.42 on $8B, $5.43B / $5.42B beyond the bill.
- Lobby on the Open Fan is +0.60 / +0.59, but only on a base that fails by $12.83B. Lobby alone is about -1.00 a column. That figure is an inference: the flat $2B strain is already in the hold row.
- In S1 there's no new narrowbody to defend, so the Open Fan buys nothing and costs its whole bill plus the wait loss. S2 shows the same, because NGSA sets the wait.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536].
- Expected column: S1, the record. Weights: S1 70 / S2 30. Weighted hold is -23.75 (-23.84 at Ghai's 75/25).
- Hold is best at every weight, so the weights set the booking, not the choice.
- I book -24.3, on S1. S2's +1.79 gets credit only once a Boeing fps is on the record.
- Last round's -24.3 matched the record (-24.29). Booking low held.

3. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]. Ready is max(2050 + 10, 2045) = 2060, confirmed by Ali. The first new narrowbody (NGSA, 2037) sets the wait, so S2's 2060 fps doesn't help. No Open Fan.

4. Ducted only as a defence (H3). It is in service and on hold only. It is called 'a step forward from today's LEAP' and never the next generation.

5. Strain. Hold adds no project and no strain; the flat $2B is already booked. An Open Fan would put a fourth programme on a supply base whose margin is not shown.

6. The next generation: my 20% line [CX-0217] arises only if an Open Fan is ordered. None is, and the statement makes no fuel-burn claim. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]: no plan here trades it.

7. Tie-break: not needed. The gap to the next plan is $12.83B, far outside my $1B ε.

THE RISE ALLOWANCE, TESTED ON ITS MERITS AND CLOSED
For the first time the cheapest Open Fan plan ($12.83B against hold) fits inside the one $15B allowance in dollars. It's the last round, and that's exactly where the installed-base lens tempts you to 'seed the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. Doctrine says the allowance 'still covers a launch you judge strategic' (dashboard_game.md §5). I judge this one is not.
- It fits only because seven narrowbody years are left to lose, not twelve (Ghai). There is less board left, not a better plan.
- It buys nothing inside the count. $9B of R&D buys a 2060 engine with no share gain on the board.
- The wait loss takes about 647 of our 648 NGSA engines a year alone, or about 456 with Lobby. That turns 2050 into a share miss (about 36%, or 41% with Lobby) while still missing the Open Fan objective. Confirmed by Ghai on the board's engine value of $8.39M of 2026 PV per engine a year.
- The gates fail:
  - G1: no airframer has launched an Open Fan or asked for one.
  - G2 and H2: NGSA has been in service since 2037.
  - G4: Ali can't show any RISE test progress after October 2025.
- Doctrine says do not let conviction launch RISE without G1 (profile §8). RISE becomes a product 'as our airframer and airline customers deem appropriate' [CX-0469], not on the hope of an order not yet won [CX-0248].
- RISE into a wait is not joint practice, and I have no reason to give why Safran would agree.
- The Board would veto it, and I have no override against the Board.
RISE stays 'all in' as technology [CX-0214], the seed corn [CX-0256], funded with Safran. If Boeing launches, RISE goes to Boeing on Boeing's schedule, through CFM with Safran.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
No CFM narrowbody order this round. The other moves (the Boeing reply, the LEAP-1B allocation, Airbus's capacity talks, the Embraer terms) go through CFM with Safran, on product and supply only, with no price or number before Safran agrees [CX-0184, CX-0160]. RISE continuing as technology is joint practice. GEnx is GE alone and stays on hold.

EXCO DELIBERATION
- Ghai confirmed every row and both share inferences. He sharpened my reading of S2's +1.79: it comes from capacity, not preference. Both lines sat at their ceilings in 2047-2049, so only the MAX top-up after 2050 moves a delivery: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year, roughly 11 MAX a month above 57. I adopt that, and we plan any step to it, not to the 2,400 cap.
- Ghai stays at 75/25; I hold 70/30. That's $0.09B, he doesn't object, and the booking is the same.
- Ali confirmed every date and raised no flag. He failed his own evidence checks plainly (the Ducted record, the LEAP-1B kit, RISE after 2025, the floor margin), and each is now handed on with a named owner and an internal report to the Board.
- His binding date veto on wording holds. Last round's 'durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included' stays out. It could read as a result dated before 2041, and no test in our hands backs that. The statement now says plainly that we claim no result.
- Where doctrine, not my record, drove a choice: the Lobby rule; the Embraer terms; the floor gates on capacity (beyond my own 'lean before capital'); and the G1-G5 reading of the allowance.

SCORING LAST ROUND
My round 3 predictions held:
- Boeing held again, with no date.
- The Joint Venture held.
- There was no 787 Re-engine, no widebody UltraFan and no rival widebody upgrade (RR's Trent work stayed inside a flat envelope), so there was no GEnx re-test.
- The booking matched the record.
Ghai's 'build to deliveries' held too: LEAP-1B rose from 1,042 engines in 2045 to the 1,368 ceiling by 2047, with no capacity built ahead of it.

OFF-BOARD RISKS, NAMED FOR THE RECORD
(1) A Boeing code-4 selection (the Joint Venture alone) would take the 737 slot from fps entry: 1,368 engines a year, about 68% of our narrowbody engines. It falls outside the count but not outside the business, and only product answers it: the Ducted with whatever record test and field data support, plus a LEAP derivative.
(2) A Ducted durability or quality event would re-price the value booked from 2041. Ghai books it in the quarter we find it.
(3) The MAX above 57 a month, and Airbus's capacity step: new floor load, gated on floor data.

WHAT WOULD HAVE CHANGED MY MIND
- A durability or quality flag from Ali: the statement and the Boeing offer would change, though no order would.
- A firm airframer path for RISE on the record.
- Ghai showing the allowance buys something inside the count.
None came.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily. On money I defer to Rahul's tests, and his profit calls land [CX-0910].

What I took:
- His confirmation of every row: hold -24.29 / -22.50; Open Fan + Lobby -12.83 / -12.83 against hold on $9B; Open Fan alone -13.43 / -13.42 on $8B. No Open Fan plan passes bounded downside.
- His reading of hard rule 9. The $12.83B fits $15B in dollars for the first time, but the allowance exempts a pre-authorised launch (G1-G5). G1 fails and H2 fails, so on any reading it's 6.4 times the round cap. He left the 'strategic' judgement to me, and I judged it isn't strategic.
- His share check: about 647 engines a year lost alone (2050 share 36.3%), or about 456 with Lobby (41.4%). The 2045 miss is about 24 engines, roughly $0.22B nominal ($0.05B of 2026 PV).
- His correction on S2's +1.79: it comes from capacity, not preference. That's about 257 more LEAP-1B a year (about 1,625 LEAP-1B and 2,273 CFM NB engines), and we plan to that, not the 2,400 cap. I adopted it and dropped my preference reading.
- His capital count: $0 new spend against $2.55B of room; the 70% payout ($5.95B) whole; R&D at 6-8% with RISE inside; no A-range risk.
- His ownership of the two items owed since round 2 (the ledger curve and the capacity-agreement status), each reported to the Audit Committee at its next regular meeting, with no public date.

His binding vetoes are respected: any Open Fan, Lobby alone, and any price, concession or capacity number without Safran. None is ordered, and the statement carries no number.

One difference: weights. He stays at 75/25 and I hold 70/30 on Boeing's 'technology ready, Boeing ready' and both lines at their ceilings. That's $0.09B, he doesn't object, and the booking (-24.3 on S1) is the same.

I scored him too. His 2045 call to build to deliveries held: volume rose to the 1,368 ceiling with no capacity built ahead of it.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed on dates and engineering. His record is thin elsewhere: his own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only (durability, the test standard, RISE physics). On supply and capacity his record is my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked that part of his memo against doctrine.

What I took in full:
- His dates. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060: the date passes, but readiness fails, 23 years behind NGSA and 4 years past the count. The hold row rests on 2041 (Ducted) and 2042 (Embraer, GEnx), and no earlier year.
- G4: no RISE test progress after October 2025 is in our hands. That alone keeps RISE a technology programme.
- His safety call: no flag, because no failure is in evidence. He also said plainly that absence is not clearance.
- His three evidence gaps and the floor margin. Each is handed on with him as owner, the cross-functional team, Safran (and Boeing and the FAA on the LEAP-1B kit), and an internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting. He confirmed that a report date passes his date test because it promises a report, not a result.

His binding wording veto holds:
- no RISE or Open Fan date;
- no Ducted year before 2041;
- no year by which durability will be 'proven';
- last round's line 'durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh included' stays out.
I used his plain line, with one change: I dropped 'last year', since the last statement was five years ago, so the line carries no date at all. I kept his forward standard ('on any new airframe ... our standard, and our customers''), which he cleared. The Boeing reply stands on the LEAP-1A kit record and the test gate only.

On supply, he failed his own floor-margin check for the fourth time. That's advice, not a veto. His grid-implied load (about 2,230-2,270) matches Ghai's 2,273. I accept his gates, which match doctrine (kits first, lean before capital, never ahead of Boeing or the FAA), and I put the gap in the Board's hands plainly.

The RISE allowance, stated apart: unused, and it closes unused.

Say so plainly if the record holds nothing, carry each gap as a standing management action with a named owner and an internal report date, and send any event to the cross-functional team.
board_response.response:

(a) The Ducted: our sources, which end in October 2025, hold 0 hot-and-harsh results, 0 dust results and 0 NGSA test or field events. It has nine field years on NGSA with no public event. That is absence, not clearance.
(b) The LEAP-1B kit: the outcome is not in our record (certification was due in the first half of 2026). The 737 reached 57 a month, KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA, with no durability event named. That is delivery evidence, not durability evidence.
(c) RISE: the last items are 350+ tests, 200+ wind-tunnel hours, noise tests with Airbus and HPT dust testing begun in October 2025. Nothing later is on our record.
Ali raises no flag. Each gap is a standing management action. Owner: Mohamed Ali, with the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team; with Safran on the Ducted and RISE, and with Boeing and the FAA on the LEAP-1B. Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting, with no public date. Any event becomes a flag and goes to the team, never to one person [CX-0012]. This also closes R3-1 and R2-1 as open management actions.

- If Boeing launches, RISE goes to Boeing only when Boeing wants it, on its schedule, through CFM with Safran. Our offer today is the Ducted with a LEAP derivative as the floor.

board_response.recommendation: R4-3 Delivery: show the floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites; account for the load if the MAX runs above 57 a month (up to 2,400 LEAP-1B); commit no capacity above today's rate without floor data reported to you, agreed through CFM with Safran; build to deliveries, kits first, lean before capital.
board_response.response:
Taken up, but not met, and I say so plainly: the floor margin is still not shown, for the fourth time, and neither is the Ducted's long-lead release on floor data.
- Owner: Ali, with the cross-functional team and Safran. I am accountable. Internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting.
- The report will cover three loads: 2,016 engines a year today; about 2,273 if S2 comes (about 257 more LEAP-1B a year, the grid's volume, per Ghai and Ali); and 3,048 at the 100-a-month cap, 17.6% above anything we've delivered.
- Until then: no capacity committed above 57 a month or for Airbus's step; any step through CFM with Safran; we plan to the grid's volume, not the cap; we never get ahead of Boeing or the FAA. Kits first, lean before capital [CX-0540].
This carries R3-5 and R2-2 forward as open management actions.

board_response.recommendation: R4-4 Customers and Safran: answer Boeing's code-7 invitation product-only (the Ducted, a LEAP derivative as the floor, durability proven before entry into service as our own standard, guarantees to Safran first and modelled conservatively); answer Airbus's capacity talks on product and supply for its own volumes; report whether Airbus's capacity agreements are signed; keep Embraer free of numbers.

Taken up.

Accepting the durability contract condition, and any guarantee, time-on-wing term or penalty, goes to Safran first and is modelled conservatively. We stand on the LEAP-1A kit record and the test gate. We make no Ducted durability claim until the team releases it.

This closes R3-4 and R2-4, and carries R2-5's signature question as an open action.

board_response.recommendation: R4-5 Weights and booking: reason the S1/S2 weights from the 2045 record; explain S2's +1.79; book on S1 (-24.29); raise the booking only once a Boeing fps is on the record.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
Weights: S1 70 / S2 30.
- For S2: Boeing's 'Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready'; Airbus's factory ceiling and growing waiting backlog; the 737 at its own ceiling since 2047; the code-7 invitation.

S2's +1.79 comes from capacity, not preference (Ghai's reading, adopted). Both lines sat at their ceilings in 2047-2049, so the only new slots inside 2056 are the MAX top-up after 2050 while the fps ramps: about 257 more LEAP-1B a year, about 11 MAX a month above 57.
Booked -24.3, on S1. Hold is best at every weight. Last round's -24.3 matched the record. No raise until a Boeing fps is on the record.

board_response.recommendation: R4-6 Cost and capital: no new R&D or strain on hold; at least 70% of free cash flow to shareholders; R&D at 6-8% of sales with RISE inside; bring the Ducted's 2035-2040 ledger cash curve against $1.0B a year approved; premium $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.

- No A-range risk.
- Premium: $0, and $0 of $4.0B for the game.

The board books $6.0B ($4.0B of R&D plus $2.0B of strain) against $6.0B approved, with no overrun and no write-off, but the yearly cash curve is not in our brief and we won't invent it. Owner: Ghai, with GE Aerospace controllership and CFM finance (Safran on the CFM share). Internal report to the Audit Committee at its next regular meeting, with no public date. board_response.recommendation: R4-7 Narrowbody share objective: state it as not met (63.9% / 49.3% / 53.5%); no order changes 2045, and the Open Fan would cut share by 35 pp (20 pp with Lobby); pay no premium for share.
board_response.response:

board_response.recommendation: R4-8 Public statement: name no rival and blame no one; nothing on another maker's fleet or the Joint Venture; nothing on Boeing's timing beyond 'Boeing's call'; no RISE or Open Fan date; the Ducted a step forward from LEAP, never the next generation; no durability or fuel-burn claim beyond the evidence; no price or capacity number without Safran; what we know and what we don't.
board_response.response:
Taken up.

board_response.recommendation: R3-3 (round 3) Say what the Joint Venture miss teaches about reading rivals; reason the weights from the record; raise the booking only on a Boeing fps.
board_response.response: Taken up. The lesson is to price a move a player can make alone as live. This round I applied it to Boeing's own conditions ('technology ready, Boeing ready') by moving S2 to 30, not by waiting for a date. I also keep a Boeing code-4 selection named as an off-board risk, which only product answers. The weights set the booking, not the choice, and the booking stays on S1.

board_response.recommendation: R3-5 (round 3) Show how LEAP and the Ducted run together through the NGSA ramp and Airbus's A320neo Alt plan.

What the record shows:

The margin itself is an open management action under Ali, in the same Board report as R4-3.

board_response.recommendation: Rounds 1-2 items still open: the end-of-game record of open management actions.
board_response.response:
Marked open, each with an owner and an internal report to the Board at its next regular meeting, with no public date:
(1) Floor margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites (R1, R2-2): Ali.
(2) The Ducted's long-lead release on floor data (R2-2): Ali.

Three items are closed:

veto.ground:
No veto. I recomputed every date in the orders, the other moves and the public statement, and none fails either of my two binding grounds.

(1) No order's value rests on a ready year before launch plus development years, or on an Open Fan ready before 2045. All five orders are hold. The Ducted is ready in 2041 (2035 + 6). Partner Embraer counts from 2042 (2035 + 7). The GEnx has been ready since 2033 (2030 + 3) and counts on the widebody from 2042. No Open Fan is ordered; launched now it would be ready in 2060.

(2) No statement or move gives a date that no test backs. The only engine year is 'ready since 2041', which is on the public record. RISE gets no date of any kind. No year is given by which the Ducted's durability will be 'proven'. Last round's line 'durability proven before entry into service, hot and harsh conditions included' is gone, replaced by a forward standard and a plain 'We claim no result here.' That meets my recorded wording veto. The Board report 'at its next regular meeting' promises a report, not a result, so it passes.

Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My own words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results. Under the team rule a failed test binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

board_review.note: No Board items: every order is the default.

other_moves.move: Fleet first: the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and the GTF fleet; Hot Section kit sold at value; fleet spares ahead of new hardware where they compete for the same parts
other_moves.detail:
The fleet comes before any new hardware [PX-0080][PX-0084].
- The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign or capacity answer [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100].
- Fleet spares and MRO material are allocated ahead of NGSA OE, ahead of any new Airbus capacity step and ahead of any Joint Venture block hardware where they compete for the same parts.
- We fix forward through shop-visit upgrades. Any durability fix for the NGSA engine enters as a shop-visit kit under configuration control, after its own test.
- Pacing parts and spares for the gear and the core are being sized to every Joint Venture engine that carries them, not only to our counted share, and to the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits.
- OE allocation is agreed jointly with Airbus, and we tell Airbus early where we fall short [PX-0099][PX-0066].
No date is given for any ramp or recovery. The move has no effect on the game board.

other_moves.move: Answer to Airbus's next capacity step: P&W commits capacity, in steps, sized to Airbus's own firm volumes, standard terms, no exclusivity, fleet spares protected
Standing answer to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus: the in-service Joint Venture engine as one engine source, on standard terms, no launch-style discounts
other_moves.detail:
This answers Boeing's standing invitation, which now names the Joint Venture as one of two engine sources in its plan at launch. It is Boeing's plan, not a selection, and nothing is booked on it.
- We offer the Joint Venture engine, ready since 2036, in the standard now in service on NGSA, with each partner standing behind its own modules.
- Standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The same terms apply on NGSA.
- On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven, the contract condition Boeing has set.
- A newer block would be a new development with its own durability proof. None is promised.
- A rival's price, including CFM's new engine and its Embraer partnership, does not move the offer [P-0768].
- Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and nothing is aimed at Boeing's timing, either way.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture governed to its published terms; 'never' restated as the public floor
other_moves.detail:
The formed Joint Venture runs to the terms published in 2035 and restated in 2045:
(1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces.
(2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233]. Gear and core modules are repaired in P&W's network under P&W data.
(3) A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share. It is never credited with P&W technology, and never with cash beyond equal shares.
(4) The engine in service is GTF2's tested configuration. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions. No date is given for any block.

other_moves.move: Closing whole-programme NPV review to the Finance Committee
other_moves.detail:
Final decision year. Mitchill presents; all derived figures labelled derived, Finance only, never booked, never public.
(a) Booked: -0.14 = engine value +1.86 less R&D 2.00 charged undiscounted, unchanged since 2045 (rounded table re-discounted gives +1.85, a rounding difference). 'Capitalise on the GTF' is reported as NOT MET, exactly as the GM reports it, with no re-measurement and no substitute figure.
(b) Run rate: +0.6 a year nominal over 2046-55 (8.8 against 8.2 in 2050), +0.7 in 2056. Nominal cumulative above the status quo +12.0 by 2056, crossing $2.0B nominal in 2041 (derived, not a payback claim). On the board's convention, cumulative PV reaches only +1.85 by 2056: no PV payback inside the count.
(c) S2 at -0.75, -0.61 below S1 (against -0.59 in 2045). The code-7 slot books nothing (EIS 2060, after the count ends in 2056); removing the last two slot-years moved the gap by only -0.02. Mitchill's arithmetic (inference): placed in 2051-56 it needs 134 engines a year lost while NGSA is above its ceiling; placed in 2038-49, when Boeing had 160-275 free slots, it needs about 28 a year. Read as a re-score of delivered years through the two-airframe preference rule, not cash at risk in 2051-56. Booked as neither. It becomes cash at risk only if NGSA's backlog drains below Airbus's ceiling: a watch item.
(d) Against a buyback (PV 0): -0.14, not met. Against Do Nothing: no grid row; direction only. Without a new P&W engine ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS, our NB OE flow would have run toward zero as the A320neo wound down; the 876 a year now carry about $8.8B a year of lifecycle value at 2050 prices. The 2030 grid priced 'NGSA without us' at -16.25: order of magnitude only, not rolled forward or booked. The programme sits far above Do Nothing and just below a status quo that assumes the A320neo flies our GTF forever.
(e) Derived, R&D discounted at 10%: +0.77 (spent evenly 2030-35), +1.01 (2035 lump), +0.49 (2030 lump).
(f) The lesson on the record: our 2030 and 2035 grids had no CFM column. In 2035 we put the low end on Airbus moving NGSA to code 5; the loss came from CFM's ducted engine (2041) and Embraer partnership (2042), about 3.9 pp of NGSA, half from us, which took the 2035 +0.48 to -0.14. The 2035 'Rolls-Royce commits' upside (+2.63) never showed. A grid shows one round of rivals' moves; we put the low end in the wrong place, and I own that.

other_moves.move: In-service durability report and Rolls-Royce block gate to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
other_moves.detail:
Bad news first: after thirteen years in service, the time-on-wing record we would need to say the NGSA engine is where it needs to be is not in front of us. No time on wing by environment, removal intervals, severe-environment or fleet-leader findings, life-limited-part lives against full life, AOG count, shop-visit rate or turn times appear on the record we hold. What the record shows is narrower: no P&W fleet, AOG or quality event in any public bulletin 2037-2050, and our 876 counted engines delivered each year at Airbus's rate. That is OE supply at rate, not durability, and we claim nothing more [PX-0022].
The Committee gets the data as they exist: time on wing cooler against hot-and-sandy; removal intervals against Block D and the Advantage; life-limited-part lives against full life; configuration percentages, AOG, shop-visit rate, turn times and pacing parts, run daily and reported weekly. If the data show a shortfall, the disclosure says so and fleet lift goes ahead of the Airbus step.
Rolls-Royce block gate, unchanged: joint configuration board with P&W sign-off on every interface to the gear and core; no intermix until the block is certified and its own spares stocked; at least 3x base-programme testing at severe-environment conditions; time on wing no worse than the fitted standard, with gear-and-core interface load tests; full-life parts at EIS; Rolls-Royce parts capacity qualified before rate; support in place before EIS; data to the Committee; no date. If the data are late, the block waits [PX-0035][PX-0073].
For Finance and the Committee: the Joint Venture's MRO split. Under term 4 the engine in service is GTF2's configuration, so shop load on the half counted to Rolls-Royce may fall on our network today. Shown, priced at value, and our fleet first.

other_moves.move: Airbus capacity capex and shortfall pricing to the Finance Committee
other_moves.detail:
Capex for the Airbus step comes to Finance as a capital item, released in tranches only against Airbus's firm extra volumes, inside the roughly $6B self-funded envelope with the dividend covered; the one-time stretch is not used [PX-0081][P-0686].
Internal illustrative unit, never public: each 10 NGSA a month is about 240 engines a year, about 88 counted to P&W and about 175 gear-and-core sets (+10% on about 1,752), plus later spares for that fleet; about $0.88B a year nominal of lifecycle value at 2050 prices, off the board and not booked.
Pacing parts (Eddy, inference from the company record): turbine airfoil castings (shared with the Hot Section kit and GTF heavy visits; CFM competes for castings), powder-metal disks (life-limited, full life at ship), forgings, and the gear, where we hold no capacity data. Lead time to add forging and casting capacity: 2 to 2.5 years in the company record, read as a floor.
Shortfall pricing, part by part when it bites: a lost install costs about $10.05M of lifecycle value and does not come back; a fleet shortfall costs AOG compensation plus about $3.8M of aftermarket at risk per flying engine, plus the credibility the in-service engine now carries. We cannot net the two without AOG data. The tie-break stays fleet first where parts compete [PX-0080]; the way to avoid the trade is to size the spares for the larger fleet before each OE step.

other_moves.move: Closing update of the enterprise risk register
other_moves.detail:
(1) Rolls-Royce alignment: its public answer to Boeing, 'Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine', and 'The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service' are recorded as alignment on one engine on the public record. The Boeing half of our private written-confirmation request is closed by that record. The block-route half (through the joint configuration board and our gate) stays open as a Joint Venture configuration-control document. The watch is kept, not retired. Tells: a block bringing its own gear or core [P-1875]; any request for gear or core data, repair data included; an offer to Boeing by product name; pressure to put Rolls-Royce content in service before its proof.
(2) In-service durability of the NGSA engine: data gap after thirteen years; owner Eddy.
(3) CFM share pressure on NGSA (ducted engine and Embraer partnership).
(4) Airbus capacity commitment against fleet spares, airfoils and disks first.
(5) S2 preference shift: cash at risk only if NGSA's backlog drains below Airbus's ceiling.
(6) Heavy-visit wave: about 12,100 GTF engines delivered since 2026 (derived; excludes the pre-2026 fleet, spares and retirements) and about 16,250 Joint Venture engines carrying our gear and core by end-2050.

other_moves.move: Counsel review of the GTF paragraph and the full disclosure
other_moves.detail: Given the derivative claims over GTF oversight and the compliance monitor, counsel reviews the GTF paragraph before release. The 2045 draft sentence 'We make no claim that the GTF investment has paid back' is taken out on Mitchill's advice: it characterises a private result and could read as an admission. We make no payback claim by making none.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Bad news first. The new single-aisle market is more contested than when we committed. CFM's new engine has been ready since 2041, and CFM has a partnership with Embraer. We have no birthright on any aircraft, and we earn our place every day. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new hardware where they compete for the same parts.

We control what we can control. The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, built on GTF2's tested configuration, has been ready since 2036. It is fitted on Airbus's new single-aisle, which has been in service since 2037. Time on wing is the name of the game. We report that engine's durability as the in-service data show it, and not ahead of them. We are sizing parts, spares and shop capacity to the fleet we support: the GTF fleet coming into heavy shop visits, and the gear and core we build for every Joint Venture engine.

Airbus has asked both its engine sources to commit capacity for its next step. Our answer is yes, on conditions. We will commit capacity, in steps, sized to Airbus's own firm volumes, with no exclusivity, on standard terms, with the allocation agreed jointly with Airbus and our fleet's spares protected. Where we fall short, we will tell Airbus early. Airbus speaks for its own rates and dates.

The Joint Venture shares risk and investment equally. It never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, under its own type data. A partner's technology is credited through its own modules and an equal share, never through ours. Under the Joint Venture's terms, any Rolls-Royce content would come only on a later block, and it would not enter service until its own durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decisions.

Our answer to Boeing's invitation stands. The Joint Venture engine is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, as one engine source, in the standard now in service, with each partner standing behind its own modules. It is offered on standard terms, with no launch discounts. On a new airframe it will not enter service until its durability is proven. The airframers speak for their own programmes and dates.

The dividend comes first. This year's plan needs no new engine development spending and no change to the dividend or to our path on debt.

DECISION, 2050 (last decision year): gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr hold. These are the only legal values in the brief (round4.md section 3), so no Board item arises. premium_b 0, overrides empty.

1. TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
- Start from Eddy's proposal: hold, hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
- Binding vetoes on the orders: none. Mitchill finds ground 1 not engaged ($0 new R&D), ground 2 not engaged (no live unselected GTF2; it folded in 2035), and grounds 3 and 4 not engaged by the package as drafted. Eddy passes both grounds: readiness 2036 against NGSA's 2037 and S2's 2060; no live fleet, quality or supply problem on the record.
- Conditional vetoes, honoured in the package so that none is engaged:
  - Mitchill ground 3 (any Joint Venture discount to Boeing; Airbus exclusivity, concession or penalties beyond standard; any credit to Rolls-Royce beyond equal shares).
  - Mitchill ground 4 (any payback claim, any durability claim beyond the data, a Boeing selection or Rolls-Royce block stated as fact, any derived figure made public).
  - Eddy's binding ground-2 veto on Airbus option (c), committing capacity without protecting fleet spares. I had already struck it, and it stays struck.
  - Eddy's ground-2 watch on the Airbus step. His conditions are written into the move: steps, commitment below qualified capacity, spares for the larger fleet sized before each OE step, no new source at rate before qualification, and each partner committing its own modules. So the watch is not invoked.
- Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. The engine in service is ready. No Rolls-Royce block and no new-airframe entry goes ahead of its proof. Then optimise: one row, so it is the best grid plan in both columns.

2. MY TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036; NGSA's EIS was 2037 and S2's is 2060.
- Visible demand: no capital order on the board. Off the board, the Airbus capacity answer is sized only to Airbus's firm volumes [PX-0109].
- Miss a cycle: not engaged. We are on NGSA, and code 7 already includes the Joint Venture.
- Responsible bet: no doctrine-favoured order differs from the only order. Premium $0.
- Dividend: $0 of new R&D, 0% of the roughly $6B envelope, stretch unused. Mitchill confirms the dividend is whole and debt stays on its pre-ASR path [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669].
- Value, not share: standard terms to Boeing and Airbus, no exclusivity, the Hot Section kit sold at value [PX-0055][PX-0100].
- Objectives: credibility MET; capitalise NOT MET at -0.14. PV given up for either: $0.

3. GRID AND WEIGHTS
The single row is -0.14 (S1) / -0.75 (S2). I keep S1 0.55 / S2 0.45, so the expected PV is -0.4145, about -0.41. The expected column is S1.
- Mitchill's 0.50/0.50 gives -0.445, the Board's 0.60/0.40 gives -0.384. Each 0.10 moved to S2 costs $0.061B, and the row is negative at any weights.
- Boeing's own words pull S2 up: technology and Boeing are 'ready', the 737 is at its ceiling, and Airbus's backlog is growing.
- But Boeing's last word on the record is 'not launching one this year' and 'no fps date and no launch commitment'. I don't get out ahead of an airframer's guidance [PX-0062].
- The $0.03B between Neil and me moves nothing.

4. CLOSING ACCOUNT (my scratch check reproduces Neil's)
- Booked: -0.14 = +1.86 less 2.00, unchanged since 2045.
- Nominal cumulative above the status quo: +12.0 by 2056, crossing $2.0B in 2041. Cumulative PV is only +1.85, so there is no PV payback inside the count.
- The S2 gap: I take Mitchill's reading as inference, not a booking. It is a re-score of delivered years through the two-airframe preference rule (about 28 engines a year in 2038-49), not cash at risk in 2051-56, while NGSA stays above its ceiling. It becomes cash at risk only if NGSA's backlog drains below that ceiling.
- Against Do Nothing: direction only. Far above it.
- Against a buyback: below, at -0.14.
- The lesson: no grid of ours had a CFM column. I own that.

5. BAD NEWS, PLAINLY
After thirteen years in service, Eddy has no time-on-wing, life-limit or AOG data to show me. I cannot say the fleet is where it needs to be, so the disclosure claims nothing beyond the data. The Governance and Public Policy Committee gets what exists, and a shortfall would put fleet lift ahead of the Airbus step.

6. DISCLOSURE EDITS TAKEN
- 'Where they compete for the same parts', added (Mitchill).
- The payback sentence taken out (Mitchill; counsel).
- 'In steps' added to the capacity line; 'sizing' kept; no 'proven', 'dependable' or 'mature' (Eddy).
- 'Each partner standing behind its own modules' added (Eddy).
- The Boeing line is framed as an answer to its invitation, not a selection.

7. BIASES I WATCHED
- Date optimism: no date for any block, step or recovery.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2's configuration stays the standard only until Rolls-Royce's proof is in.
- Supply-first caution [PX-0085]: I commit to Airbus rather than stall its gate.
- Incrementalism on Boeing's timing.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: my record is Low on the Joint Venture and silent on Rolls-Royce. Joint Venture governance follows company doctrine [P-1233][P-1240][P-1875], Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test. On readiness, parts and capacity I defer to Eddy. 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] and demand visibility [PX-0109] are RTX-wide sayings applied here by inference.

NGSA (Airbus) has been in service since 2037 on code 7, with CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce fitted.
- Its ramp is 'now reaching its planned rate'. Airbus says its own factory ceiling now limits deliveries and its waiting backlog is growing.
- It is preparing a next capacity step with no rate and no date, taken only once three gates are met: NGSA holds its rate with no open quality finding; both engine sources commit capacity; no supply crunch is reported.
- Its engine supply agreements cover its own volumes only, with no exclusivity. The A320neo transition is completing on the Alt plan.

The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine has been ready since 2036. GTF2 and UltraFan NB solo both folded into it in 2035.

CFM:
- Its ducted engine has been ready since 2041, and its Embraer partnership has counted since 2042.
- RISE stays technology, with no date.
- It has answered Boeing's invitation 'on product'.

Boeing:
- No fps. 'The market case is better than it was. It isn't there yet... Technology is ready, and Boeing is ready.'
- It has updated its engine requirement to 'a choice of two engine sources at launch, CFM and the Joint Venture' (code 7), with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition.
- The 737 is back at its 57-a-month ceiling, KPI-gated. Its NB delivery share has recovered from 26.6% (2044) to 36.3% (684 a year, 2047-49).

Rolls-Royce:
- 'The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service.' Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, with no date.
- Its answer to Boeing is now 'Rolls-Royce's part of the Joint Venture engine' on standard terms.
- Its own partner-shop support plan is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service and is sized for a second airframe.

Observed NB engine shares, 2047-49: CFM 53.5%, P&W 23.3%, Rolls-Royce 23.3%.

OUR POSITION (private brief):
- ΔPV -0.14 $B: engine value +1.86, less R&D 2.00 charged undiscounted. Yield 99.87%, unchanged since 2045.
- New R&D in 2050: $0. GTF2's $2.0B was booked in 2035 and counts toward our Joint Venture share, with no write-off.
- NB engines: 892 (2045), then 876 a year from 2046 (23.3%). The board counts NB engines to 2056.
- Run rate above the status quo: +0.6 a year nominal over 2046-55 (8.8 against 8.2 in 2050), +0.7 in 2056.
- My scratch arithmetic, derived and for Finance only, not a payback claim: the nominal cumulative above the status quo is about +12.0 by 2056 against $2.0B nominal, crossing it in 2041.

OBJECTIVE STATUS:
- Restore credibility (a new P&W engine in service on a new airframe by 2050): MET. The Joint Venture engine is on NGSA, in service since 2037, and its in-service durability now carries this objective.
- Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV ≥ 0): NOT MET, at -0.14 (S1) and -0.75 (S2). It is reported exactly as the GM reports it. No order can change it, so the PV given up for either objective this round is $0.
