decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on Airbus's new single-aisle. Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our support through partner shops is ours, and it is in place before any Rolls-Royce content enters service. Our answer to Boeing stands: Rolls-Royce's part of the engine, on standard terms, with durability proven and support in place before entry into service. On Airbus's next capacity step, we commit Rolls-Royce's own part, for Airbus's own volumes, with no exclusivity and no concession: our support capacity, and our share of the Joint Venture's investment and risk. Only what we are sure to deliver. We speak for Rolls-Royce, not for our partner. On the widebody, we look after the Trent fleet through time on wing. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. There's no change of strategy. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields. Orders: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This is my proposal unchanged. Both colleagues recommend the same orders. None of the orders is a Board item, so none can be vetoed.

1. THE GRID (item = row minus 'UltraFan NB: hold', column by column; the grid already includes the formed Joint Venture)
- 'UltraFan NB: hold': +9.61 / +9.61 / +9.61 / +9.96. Worst column +9.61. Best in every column.
- Trent 1000 upgrade: row +2.88 / +2.88 / +2.88 / +3.33.
  - Item -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.73 / -6.63.
  - Before the $5B strain: -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.73 / -1.63, worse than 2045's -1.48 because the counting window is shorter. It counts only from 2053.
- UltraFan WB: row +0.61 / +0.61 / +0.93 / +1.64.
  - Item -9.00 / -9.00 / -8.68 / -8.32.
  - Before the strain: -4.00 / -4.00 / -3.68 / -3.32. Ready 2056, a year after a 2050 Re-engine's entry into service.

2. WEIGHTS (no selection to weigh; the columns are rivals' moves; P = 0.1 for 'nothing on the record', inference)
- C, mine and McCabe's: S1 0.80, S2 0.05, S3 0.10, S4 0.05.
  - Hold +9.6275. Upgrade -6.725 (-1.725 before the strain). UltraFan WB -8.934 (-3.934 before the strain).
- B, the Board's S1-heavy set (0.75 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05): identical, since S1 = S2 in every row.
- U, uniform, and R, Re-engine-heavy (0.40 / 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.25):
  - Hold +9.6975. Upgrade -6.705 (-1.705). UltraFan WB -8.750 (-3.750).
- No vote changes on any set. Calculation: /tmp/wargame-rolls_royce/dash-2050-sd/work/r4_decide_calc.py.

3. WORST COLUMN AGAINST OWN BILL (final round, so every worst column is final)
- Upgrade: -6.73 against a $2B bill, 3.4 times the bill.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 against a $4B bill, 2.25 times the bill.
- Both fail in every column. Both fail even before the strain, which in the final round could never be lifted.

4. VETO CHECKS
- McCabe withholds her co-signature on both `launch` orders, and that binds. Neither is ordered, so no revision is needed.
- Her balance-sheet vetoes are not triggered: Do Nothing commits no new programme money. No equity, no borrowing, no change in leverage. Narrowbody spend ended at $5.71B, all booked in 2035.
- Watson finds no Civil ground on the orders, the draft statement or the draft other moves. His veto on the final text is conditional, so I wrote the final text to his three grounds:
  - (a) no date, year, rate or 'no earlier than' for the Rolls-Royce block, for Rolls-Royce content on any airframe, or in the Boeing or Airbus answers;
  - (b) nothing counts on our modules entering service by a year, on a Rolls-Royce block supplying Airbus's extra volumes, or on Rolls-Royce content being on the fps at its entry into service. The capacity answer commits support capacity, our share of the Joint Venture's investment and risk, and castings and forgings for what we make. It says plainly that we do not speak for the engine's output;
  - (c) the capacity answer never draws on block test hardware, the spare-engine pool or the intervention team. P&W's shops and allocation never stand in for our plan. The Boeing answer keeps support in place before entry into service.
- `overrides` is empty.

5. RED-LINE FLAGS
- McCabe flagged that `ultrafan_wb: launch` with no Re-engine on the record would break 'no UltraFan launch without a programme that can fly it'. Confirmed and struck: the order is hold.
- The overlap red line does not bite (no UltraFan in development). The money grounds alone reject the upgrade.
- No other flag was raised. I find no breach in the final orders, statement or moves:
  - no early date;
  - no concession;
  - nothing spoken for P&W or any airframer;
  - no orphan programme: the Joint Venture flies on NGSA.

6. WHY, IN MY TERMS
- Cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054].
- Both widebody items lose more than their own bill in every column, under any weights. The end of the game is no reason to buy share past the counting window.
- My pull to the 787 is real ('Why not?' [RX-0117]), and the grid answers it. The lever is time on wing, inside the envelope.
- If S3 or S4 arrives at this round's adjudication, there is no round left to answer it. I accept that knowingly: even in S4, UltraFan WB loses $3.32B before the strain.
- Actually, I've seen this movie before [RX-0087].

7. WHAT CAN BE COMMITTED AT NO NEW PROGRAMME SPEND (unpriced; no payoff effect)
- Boeing: the answer is renewed on standard terms. S2 adds 0.00, because any fps launched in 2050 enters service after the 2056 narrowbody window. Nothing is worth conceding.
- Airbus's capacity step, Rolls-Royce's part only, sized to Watson's read:
  - he can confirm partner-shop support, our share of investment and risk, and our castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers;
  - he cannot confirm Joint Venture engine output, which P&W's gear and core pace, with fleet spares first;
  - so we commit our part, never P&W's. Internal headroom stays internal.
- McCabe's conditions are written in: capacity not stock, inventory against firm volumes, no prepayment, rate guarantee or exclusivity discount.

8. S4 +0.35
McCabe's read: about +0.23 of it is roughly 9 more Trent engines a year (58.0% against 55.2%), and the rest she cannot place from the brief. No order of ours moves it, and we book none of it.

9. DOCTRINE, NOT RECORD
- My record has no launch decision in the final cycle and no Joint Venture terms. The bars used are team and company doctrine (inference): item against hold, a $3B premium cap with a $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB, and worst column against own bill.
- The capital frame, price over share and 'commit only when sure' are my record [RX-0242, RX-0081, RX-0124].

10. OBJECTIVES
- Narrowbody entry: met (25.1% in 2045, 23.3% in 2050).
- Widebody dominance: met (55.2% at the low point, 58.0% in 2050 in S4).
- Bounded narrowbody risk: not met, locked at $5.71B. That is the Solo's 2030-2035 spend, folded into the Joint Venture, and no order moves it.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0 strain, kept by holding both widebody items.
- We do not trade the strain objective in the final round for a widebody programme that pays in no column.

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed in full, and decisive on readiness, support and capacity. He concurs on Do Nothing and finds no Civil ground on the orders or the draft.

His conditional veto on the final text was treated as binding guidance. The statement and every public move were checked against his grounds (a), (b) and (c): no date or rate, nothing counting on Rolls-Royce modules or a block supplying Airbus's volumes, and nothing drawing on block test hardware, the spare pool or the intervention team.

His capacity read sized the Airbus answer. We commit only what he can confirm: support capacity, our share of the Joint Venture's investment and risk, and castings and forgings for what we make. We do not commit Joint Venture engine output, which P&W paces. The 84% load figure and the headroom stay internal.

His read on P&W's spares-first rule is taken up: it slows the block and cannot compress the proof, and it does not reach our pool or team. His internal ask (our spare-pool modules counted as fleet spares) becomes an internal move, framed as an ask and not a concession.

He credits the 23.3% to the Joint Venture engine under the equal-share rule, not to Rolls-Royce modules in service, and I report it the same way. His widebody read (55.2% at the low point, no durability reason for a programme) holds the core inside the envelope.

Readiness against each live airframe's EIS (brief §1, bulletin):
- Joint Venture engine: formed 2035, ready 2036. It took the folded GTF2's full six years (2030 + 6). NGSA EIS was 2037, so it had 1 year of margin. In service since 2037. Pass.
- Any fps launched in 2050: EIS 2057 (launch_7yr) or 2060 (launch_10yr, via Embraer). The engine has been ready since 2036. Pass, and both dates stay internal.
- UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade: not launched. Nothing to test.

(a) Maturity: not compressed. Pass. Nothing in the orders shortens a test programme. The Rolls-Royce-module block keeps its own gates through to EIS, with no date: module rig, full-engine endurance including hot and harsh conditions, life-limited parts at full life, certification, then support live. The CEO reports them to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee as a private move. P&W's spares-first rule can slow our block hardware. It cannot compress the proof.

(b) Early date: none. Pass. I checked every date in the final text:
- Statement: no date for the Rolls-Royce block, NGSA, the fps, any Re-engine, any rate or the capacity step. 'Rolls-Royce content enters service when its own durability is proven, and not before. We give no date for it.'
- Public other moves (Trent time on wing, the partner-shop plan, the Boeing answer, the Airbus capacity answer, standard terms, the capital frame): no dates and no rates.

(c) Support before EIS: in place. Pass. The partner-shop plan (Singapore model, qualified repairs, spare-engine pool, intervention team) has been live since before the 2037 NGSA EIS. It is Rolls-Royce's own and sized for a second airframe before that airframe's EIS. The Boeing answer keeps support before EIS as a condition. P&W's shops add capacity only after that, never in its place.
Reading for the record: the Airbus answer lists the spare-engine pool as support capacity sized ahead of the volume and also says it 'never draws on' the pool. I read that as follows: the pool grows as fleet support and is never raided for OE or block hardware. That is my memo's own reading, and it is not a ground.
